━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
𝟯. 𝗪𝗛𝗔𝗧 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗖𝗢𝗠𝗣𝗔𝗡𝗬 𝗔𝗖𝗧𝗨𝗔𝗟𝗟𝗬 𝗗𝗢𝗘𝗦
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Two real cash businesses today, plus a cluster of newer bets.

𝗔. 𝗛𝗲𝗮𝗹𝘁𝗵𝗰𝗮𝗿𝗲 / 𝗗𝗶𝗮𝗴𝗻𝗼𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗰𝘀 / 𝗠𝗲𝗱𝗧𝗲𝗰𝗵 ("𝗟𝗼𝗿𝗱𝘀𝗠𝗲𝗱")
Now the story the market is sold.

𝗜𝗻-𝘃𝗶𝘁𝗿𝗼 𝗱𝗶𝗮𝗴𝗻𝗼𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗰𝘀 (𝗜𝗩𝗗)
Rapid kits, serology, biochemistry reagents, ELISA kits, instruments. A new 14,000 sq ft IVD plant at Vasai (East) was commissioned in June 2026 (said to be two months early), on top of an existing 20,000 sq ft unit — 34,000 sq ft combined. The new unit is described as making 56 ELISA kits plus rapid tests, with an R&D wing dedicated to molecular/genetic work.

Company claims include:
• Large number of CDSCO / CE / related IVD approvals (investor deck language: "200+ approvals").
• India's first supply mandate for an AI-based sickle-cell rapid test into primary health centres — a government volume story, not yet a proven annuity in the reported P&L.
• Platforms named Onco Spectra and TB Truth — commercialisation talked about from FY28, not FY27.

𝗦𝘂𝗿𝗴𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘀𝘂𝗺𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲𝘀, 𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗵𝗼𝗽𝗮𝗲𝗱𝗶𝗰𝘀, 𝗵𝘆𝗴𝗶𝗲𝗻𝗲
Plant in Dadra & Nagar Haveli / Silvassa: looms, dyeing, 38 stitching machines, elastic-adhesive coater. Portfolio includes crepe and elastic adhesive bandages, cannula fixators, wipes, lumbar belts, cervical collars, braces, slings, immobilisers. Brand Lord's Joy for wipes.

US FDA registration (Oct 2025) is for this surgical / ortho / hygiene range — not for the AI dialysis machine or IVD kits. That is a real export door, but it is establishment/product registration, not an FDA approval of a novel device. The company has a US vehicle, Lords Mark Global LLC (Texas).

𝗥𝗲𝗻𝗮𝗹𝘆𝘅 — 𝗱𝗶𝗮𝗹𝘆𝘀𝗶𝘀
Acquired 85% of Renalyx Health Systems Pvt. Ltd. (Bengaluru) in Nov 2025. Product: an indigenous AI-labelled haemodialysis machine plus RenalOS software. Claims: "world's first AI-powered smart haemodialysis / renal-care ecosystem." Treat that as company positioning. Independent validation, installed base, and service economics are still being built.

Recent regulatory step (28 Sep 2026): UK MHRA registration of the haemodialysis system (GMDN 58131), with export talk from January 2027. Also CE language in older interviews. An ecosystem was launched at Shakti Super Speciality Hospital, Ahmedabad (May 2026). Plan: 50 company-run dialysis centres by March 2027. Dialysis order-book commentary has cited 500+ machines.

𝗢𝗻𝗰𝗼𝗹𝗼𝗴𝘆 / 𝗵𝗼𝘀𝗽𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗹𝘀 (𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗹𝘆 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲)
New subsidiary Lords Mark Medicure Ltd: two pilot 70-bed oncology hospitals in Vapi and Solapur, funded by a planned ₹200 crore debt raise in December 2026. Collaboration with C-MET on an AI breast-screening device; BARC technology-transfer language for oral-cancer testing without biopsy. These are pipeline, not current revenue engines.

Q1 FY27 mix (company commentary): healthcare ~55% of revenue, ~20% EBITDA; energy ~45%, ~11% EBITDA. That mix is why management wants a demerger — so the market can put a healthcare multiple on the healthcare piece.

𝗕. 𝗥𝗲𝗻𝗲𝘄𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗴𝘆, 𝘀𝗼𝗹𝗮𝗿, 𝘀𝗺𝗮𝗿𝘁 𝗟𝗘𝗗
B2G contractor / supplier: solar rooftop, solar street lighting, smart LED for Smart City-type work, solar pumps, "solar tree" lights. Clients cited: UPNEDA, APDCL, and more recently L1 / letter-of-offer language with CREDA (Chhattisgarh). Investor materials talk of a ₹3,000+ crore renewable order pipeline. That is a pipeline, not booked recognised revenue.

text:
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗔𝗜 𝗗𝗲𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗼𝗿 𝗔𝗻𝘀𝘄𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗪𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗴 𝗤𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

Machines have been writing text for more than seventy years. In 1952, Christopher Strachey programmed the Manchester Mark 1 to write love letters. In the mid-1960s, Joseph Weizenbaum at MIT built ELIZA, a program that played a therapist by turning patients' words back into questions. His own secretary asked him to leave the room so she could talk to it in private. Story generators followed in the 1970s. From 1990 until 2019, the Loebner Prize held a yearly contest for the chatbot judges found most human-like. The prize for a program judges couldn't tell from a person was never won. Now it's a business to catch them.

With chatbots like ChatGPT, the question of who wrote this has moved to the forefront.

Enter the AI detector.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗮𝗻 𝗔𝗜 𝗗𝗲𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗼𝗿 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗗𝗼𝗲𝘀

An AI detector looks for patterns in the prose that suggest a computer generated it. Pangram, a leading detector, was trained on millions of examples of human and AI writing until it learned to tell them apart. "We're reverse-engineering their stylistic fingerprint," its CEO, Max Spero, told The New York Times. It doesn't read for meaning. It doesn't check facts, judge arguments or ask whether anything in the piece is new.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺 𝗔𝗿𝗲 𝗪𝗲 𝗧𝗿𝘆𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗼 𝗦𝗼𝗹𝘃𝗲 𝗛𝗲𝗿𝗲?

One of my bosses always asked, whenever someone suggested some new software to write: What problem are we trying to solve here? Quite often the room got very quiet. Nobody had really thought about that.

In trying to detect what role AI had in a piece of writing, we should ask the same question.

𝗥𝗲𝗴𝗮𝗿𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗣𝘂𝗿𝗽𝗼𝘀𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝗪𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴, 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺𝘀 𝗗𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗮𝗻 𝗔𝗜 𝗗𝗲𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗼𝗿 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗦𝗼𝗹𝘃𝗲?

Basically nothing.

You want the best possible writing, original ideas, things worth reading. You can ask a chatbot those questions without a special tool. I do this with all my own writing. I ask: "What is original about this piece?" or "Read, Analyze, Critique" or "Thoughts?" (works great).

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗔𝗿𝗺𝘀 𝗥𝗮𝗰𝗲

Now there is an arms race between AI detectors and AI humanizers. An AI humanizer is designed to make an AI-assisted piece undetectable.

The humanizers are doing well. In a University of Notre Dame study, not yet peer reviewed, once AI-written text went through a humanizer called Undetectable AI, more than 96% of it passed as human. Undetectable AI offers a money-back guarantee if its output gets flagged, and it claims more than 22 million users.

The same study found the opposite problem for honest writers. Research abstracts that had only been lightly edited with AI were flagged 64 to 80% of the time. Pangram says its newest version fixed that; nobody outside the company has checked.

Honest AI editing carries more risk than paid evasion.

𝗦𝘂𝗺𝗺𝗮𝗿𝘆

At best, a detector score tells you one thing: AI touched the prose. It can't tell you whose ideas they are, whether the facts are right, or whether the piece is worth reading. Honest writers get flagged, anyone who pays for a humanizer walks through, and a ghostwritten book passes.

My old boss would ask: what problem are we trying to solve? For a reader, the only problem is whether a piece is worth their time. A chatbot can help answer that. A detector is not designed to.

Pangram will probably score this piece near 100% AI-written.

It can't tell you whether it is worth reading.

Read the full article, including the history of machine writing, the problems detectors claim to solve, and the ghostwriting and slide rule comparisons: https://t.co/brzaK25hmz

Happy Wednesday all!

If you missed the past 24 hours in crypto and stocks, here's your full recap:

🚨 Major Headlines & Market Moves 🚨

Bitcoin held near $83,000 as higher U.S. yields and oil prices kept pressure on risk assets. 

The 30-year Treasury yield rose to its highest level since 2002, while the 10-year sat near 5.25%.

U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs posted 8 consecutive days of inflows. BlackRock ETF clients bought another $51.09 million of $BTC.

Bitcoin is on pace for its second-strongest September on record. 

About 82% of Bitcoin addresses are now in profit, and the Bitcoin RSI bounced off its bottom, a setup that has often marked the start of a stronger move.

Bitwise said pensions, endowments, foundations, and sovereign wealth funds bought Bitcoin during the last bear market, and that none of the institutions interviewed were selling. One sovereign wealth fund was selling gold reserves to fund Bitcoin purchases.

$9.2 billion ETF provider HANetf launched the first euro-hedged Bitcoin exchange-traded commodity.

Tom Lee said crypto has entered a bull market.

Coinbase received CFTC approval to launch its own U.S. crypto derivatives clearinghouse.

Robinhood launched crypto and stock perpetual futures trading for U.S. traders.

Illinois released draft rules to tax crypto transactions regardless of profit or loss, starting in 2027.

The White House blamed Democrats for failing to pass the Crypto Clarity Act.

Cboe and S&P Dow Jones Indices are exploring tokenized options contracts.

The People’s Bank of China injected 833.5 billion yuan ($131.79 billion) through overnight reverse repo operations.

Australia hiked rates 25 bps to 4.60%, its fourth increase this year.

The U.S. offered up to 40 million barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. President Trump said oil prices will tumble.

Iran said it will discuss the nuclear issue only after the Strait of Hormuz issue is resolved and Washington lifts the blockade. Iran’s rial collapsed to a new all-time low.

Only 40.8% of S&P 500 stocks are above their 200-day moving average, the lowest since May 2025. Market breadth is getting thin.

$AMD agreed to acquire World Labs, founded by Fei-Fei Li, in an $8.2 billion all-stock deal focused on robotics and physical AI.

$FICO had its worst day since 1989, falling about 27% after FHFA moved to put VantageScore on more equal footing in mortgage pricing.

$MDB fell 18.5% after CEO CJ Desai resigned immediately to take a senior role at $META.

OpenAI is targeting a $30 billion funding round at a $1.4 trillion valuation. It also canceled the planned GPT-6.1 Astra release after the model failed internal safety and alignment checks.

Carnival posted record results, with revenue of $8.44 billion and 2027 occupancy and pricing already at record levels.

CarMax beat estimates with revenue of $7.88 billion and adjusted EPS of $1.16.

Summit Therapeutics surged after AstraZeneca agreed to invest $2 billion and take roughly a 12% stake.

Jim Cramer said a bond short squeeze could occur.

President Trump said a new Super Intelligence Czar will be named soon.

About $193 million in long positions were liquidated across crypto in 24 hours.

📊 Altcoin Market Updates 📊

Avalanche led all chains in 30-day RWA market-cap growth with +$266 million, more than the next two chains combined. It also saw $131.2 million in tokenized stock inflows over seven days, more than all other chains combined, led by Securitize.

Brazil’s CSD BR partnered with Ripple to mirror securities ownership records on the $XRP Ledger, starting with BTG Pactual fund shares.

Binance Pay launched $USDT payments at millions of PayPay-supported locations across Japan.

Bitwise’s spot $NEAR ETF went live on the NYSE.

$ETH flipped $BTC for the highest open interest on Hyperliquid.

If you enjoyed this daily roundup, make sure to follow me, I'll see you tomorrow!

Trump rejected it.

“Most of the ships that go through do go with Iranian consent.”

That gives Iran something more useful than simply closing Hormuz: a pressure valve it can tighten gradually.

The negotiations serve another purpose.

Marandi says demonstrating that Iran remains willing to return to the MoU strengthens Beijing’s hand as China deals with Washington. Tehran can tell its partners it offered a settlement and Washington refused it.

None of that makes him optimistic.

The probability of renewed U.S.-Iran military conflict is now “substantial,” potentially before or after the midterms.

So Tehran’s strategy appears to be running on two tracks:

Keep offering Washington an exit.

text:
🇯🇵 August's industrial output and retail data suggest Japan's economy is cooling while the Bank of Japan (BOJ) is raising rates. That makes an October hike less certain, and it means intervention, US yields and politics now matter more for the yen than the data does.

Industrial output fell 1.7% from July, against expectations of a 1.3% gain. Yearly growth was 3.4%, well below the 6.8% consensus. This is the second straight monthly decline, caused by an earthquake that disrupted factories in Kyushu and by higher costs from the Middle East conflict. Cars, machinery and petroleum saw the biggest drops.

Manufacturers now expect output to rise 3.2% in September and 3.1% in October. Treat these projections with caution. In July, the same survey projected a 6.4% gain for August, and output actually fell 1.7%. The earthquake effect is temporary, so some rebound is likely, but these surveys tend to be overly optimistic.

Consumers are also slowing. Retail sales grew 2.7%, below the roughly 3.2–3.3% forecast and down from 4.0% the month before. Large-scale retail grew just 1%, down from 2%. Headline inflation was 1.9% in August, so after adjusting for inflation, real spending is barely growing.

Impact on the BOJ

The BOJ raised its rate to 1.25% on September 18, the highest level since 1995. The decision was split 7–2, with board members Asada and Sato voting against. A former BOJ official had recently suggested another hike in October was possible because of inflation risks. Today's data strengthens the dissenters' case: growth is weakening and core inflation is still below 2%.

History offers a warning. In August 2000, the BOJ ended zero rates despite a weak economy and had to reverse course within months, a move still regarded as a policy mistake. In August 2024, a BOJ hike combined with weak US data triggered a carry trade unwind. The carry trade is when investors borrow cheap yen to buy higher-yielding assets abroad. During that unwind, the Nikkei fell 12% in a single day.

The difference today is that inflation is also coming from oil and a weak yen, not just domestic demand. That gives the BOJ less room to pause.

The yen puzzle

Weak data normally weakens the yen, but political pressure is supporting it. Tokyo and Washington have already intervened together to support the currency. The yen also rose 1% after Japan's finance minister said Trump raised concerns about its weakness in a meeting with Prime Minister Takaichi. USD/JPY fell from about 158.9 to around 156.5 this week.

My view is that the fear of intervention above and the US–Japan interest-rate gap below could keep USD/JPY range-bound. Today's data is negative for the yen, but probably not strong enough to break that intervention-driven ceiling.

The effect on the Nikkei is mixed. Weak output hurts autos and machinery. A lower chance of a BOJ hike would weigh on banks but help exporters.

Scenarios (my estimates, not guarantees)

Base case (~50%): The BOJ holds in October and looks to December or January. USD/JPY stays in a 155–159 range.
Hawkish (~30%): A strong Tankan (the BOJ's quarterly business survey) and firm Tokyo CPI, plus worries about yen weakness, lead to an October hike. USD/JPY falls below 155, and the risk of a carry unwind rises.
Dovish slide (~20%): September output also disappoints and US yields keep climbing. The yen weakens toward 159–160, where intervention risk is highest.

What to watch

Catalysts: The Tankan survey in early October is the most important. Also watch US PCE today, US jobs data on Friday, Tokyo CPI, revised industrial output and the late-October BOJ meeting.
Levels: USD/JPY support at 156.5 and an intervention zone at 158.9–160; the 10-year JGB yield around 2.95%.
Main risks: The BOJ hiking into a weakening economy and repeating the 2000 mistake, or a sudden carry-unwind rally in the yen.
Possible surprise: If September output rebounds more than 3% as manufacturers expect, August's weakness will look like a one-off earthquake effect, and October hike odds will rise again.
Would confirm this view: A weak Tankan, soft Tokyo CPI and a softer tone from BOJ officials.
Would invalidate it: A strong Tankan, rising services inflation, or the yen sliding toward 160 and forcing an early hike.

text:
Why Defense Data Breaches Aren't Just About Identity Theft 🧵👇

Pentagon Breach Exposes Data On 3 Million+ Military Personnel—the biggest threat isn't just someone opening a fraudulent credit card in your name.

It’s counterintelligence.

Here is why exposed PII and job metadata in defense databases like the Defense Manpower Data Center (DMDC) pose a massive national security risk:

1. Organizational Mapping
By linking Social Security numbers to specific Military Occupational Specialties (MOS), pay grades, and unit assignments, hostile actors can map out entire command structures, identify active/former special operators, and trace involvement in sensitive programs.
2. Hyper-Targeted Social Engineering 
Standard phishing is spray-and-pray. Intelligence-driven phishing is surgical. Detailed job history lets foreign intelligence craft hyper-believable spear-phishing campaigns, fake job offers on LinkedIn, or tailored social media contact.

3. Exploitation of Deceased Personnel 
Records of deceased service members are a goldmine for espionage. Hostile services use them to create synthetic identities, generate "ghost" credentials, or attempt impersonation across administrative systems.
4. Coercion & Leverage
When adversaries combine stolen government HR data with commercially bought data broker profiles, they can spot financial strain, family connections, or vulnerabilities—building precise leverage points for intelligence recruitment or blackmail.

The Operational Bottom Line: 
Security isn't just about firewalls; it's about personnel security. Credit freezes, strict OPSEC on public profiles, and zero-trust authentication are no longer optional—they are frontline defenses.

text:
NVIDIA Pushes for Faster Progress on Glass Substrates as AUO, Innolux and Other Taiwanese Suppliers Gear Up

NVIDIA is evaluating glass substrates for next-generation AI chip packaging, prompting Taiwan’s supply chain to accelerate technology development and position itself for major orders

September 30, 2026

Reports that NVIDIA is evaluating the use of glass substrates in its next-generation AI chip packaging have drawn renewed attention to the efforts of Taiwanese display-panel makers and glass-processing companies to enter the emerging market.

AUO has teamed up with Corning to showcase glass core substrate (GCS) technology, while Innolux continues to work with customers on the development and validation of through-glass via (TGV) technology. G-Tech Optoelectronics and TPK Holding are also investing in related processing technologies and pilot production.

Industry players caution, however, that the technology still faces major hurdles before it can reach large-scale commercialization, particularly in process yield and customer qualification.

According to South Korean media reports, NVIDIA is evaluating glass-substrate solutions and is working with supply-chain partners including German equipment maker SCHMID. NVIDIA is also reportedly pushing substrate suppliers in Taiwan, South Korea and Japan to complete technology development within two years, with adoption potentially beginning as early as 2028.

The reports also said NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang had discussed next-generation semiconductor cooperation with SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won, while NVIDIA has also encouraged TSMC to develop glass-substrate technology. Details of the partnerships and any potential adoption timeline have yet to be confirmed by the companies involved.

Glass substrates offer high flatness and strong dimensional stability, making them well suited to increasingly large semiconductor packages while also helping reduce the risk of substrate warpage.

AUO said this year that it intends to deepen its presence in advanced semiconductor packaging by combining its capabilities in large-format glass processing, precision metallization and redistribution layers (RDL).

The company is advancing the technology in stages, including TGV formation, via metallization and reliability validation, while working with key partners to optimize materials and manufacturing processes.

During SEMICON Taiwan this year, AUO and Corning jointly showcased their glass core substrate technology, combining Corning’s semiconductor-grade glass materials with AUO’s RDL process capabilities.

The technology is designed to address rising demand for high-density interconnects and low-loss signal transmission as core chips used in AI servers continue to grow larger.

At Innolux, its chip-first packaging business has already entered mass production. The company is continuing to explore materials and large-panel designs for TGV technology while working with customers on product development and validation in preparation for future demand for larger chip packages.

Innolux said the technology and its end-market applications are still at a stage where process capabilities and customer requirements are being aligned.

Glass-processing specialist G-Tech Optoelectronics is also developing thermal-forming technologies for TGV and package-substrate applications and has filed related patents.

The company aims to work with major glass-material suppliers and provide outsourced processing services. The technology, however, remains in the development stage and is currently making only a limited contribution to its business.

TPK Holding began researching TGV technology about two years ago, seeking to leverage its accumulated expertise and talent in glass processing to develop a new business.

The company has been adding equipment throughout this year, and its pilot production line in Zhongli began operations in early September. TPK has also started cooperating with semiconductor packaging and testing companies.

TPK acknowledged that while it has achieved some initial progress, commercialization and mass production are still some distance away. The company expects its development efforts to begin producing more tangible results over the next two years.

text:
My take: SEIU, SF Labor Council, Bay Resistance, Tech Workers Coalition — more than a dozen orgs outside OpenAI's DevDay with one demand: drop the ICE contract. Political framing noted. The substantive accusation underneath it is the part worth watching.

Organized Labor Plants a Picket Line Outside OpenAI's DevDay

OpenAI's annual DevDay opened on September 29, 2026, not with demos but with a protest rally outside Fort Mason in San Francisco. More than a dozen organizations — including the Service Employees International Union, the San Francisco Labor Council, Bay Resistance, Tech Workers Coalition, and San Francisco Rising — assembled at the venue entrance. Protesters marched in front of signs spelling out "PEOPLE OVER PROFIT" and chanted "Sam Altman, get off it, put people over profit." A large orange sign carried a single specific demand: "Drop the ICE contract."

The coalition composition is worth reading carefully. This is not ambient tech-skepticism or a loose gathering of generically concerned citizens. SEIU and the San Francisco Labor Council represent organized labor with institutional infrastructure; Bay Resistance and SF Rising are community coalition groups; the Tech Workers Coalition operates inside the industry itself. That mix — labor, community, and tech-adjacent — assembling around one named contract is a sharper action than general protest noise.

The ICE contract is the substantive accusation underneath the political framing. "People over profit" is political-claim register — the speakers are labor and immigration coalitions whose incentives are transparent and worth noting. That transparency doesn't make the demand wrong; it means the political packaging and the substantive charge need to be separated. The charge itself — that OpenAI has contracted with ICE in a way that harms people — is the thread worth tracking. The chants are how that charge travels, not the charge itself.

OpenAI chose to sign whatever this contract is. The protest is a downstream consequence of that decision, not of positioning or mission language. The article supplies no technical detail about what the contract delivers or prevents, which means no verdict on its actual effects is possible yet. What the article does supply: the government-partnership question, previously visible as background context around equity offers and political deal-making, now has a picket line attached to it — in OpenAI's own city.

Sam Altman is named on the sign and in the chant, which tells you who the coalition holds accountable. His production record is unchanged; ChatGPT ships, the lab operates. But the ICE contract accusation is the most concrete government-entanglement signal yet on his ledger. Whether the contract exists as described, and what it actually does, is the fact layer that would move the needle. Until that information surfaces, the pattern is noted and the verdict on the contract itself is suspended.

text:
The opposition’s job is not to applaud a working government. It is to test whether the body that elects that government still works. Two of three Election Commissioners putting objections on record is not “engagement.” It is the institution flagging itself.
BRICS is not an answer. Hosting Putin and Xi, or offering help on Ukraine, does not close questions about voter rolls. Diplomacy abroad does not immunise the Election Commission at home. And the claim is inflated: Modi did not “mediate between Russia and China.” They already sit together in BRICS. What was offered was good offices on Ukraine.
“Regard the decision as unanimous” is a slogan, not proof. The EC says SIR decisions were unanimous. Reports say Sandhu and Joshi objected, repeatedly, to orders issued without their knowledge. Those two lines cannot both stand unexamined. Lawfulness is shown by the paper trail—who signed, who was copied, what the notes said—not by a minister declaring it.
Calling public discussion of that dissent “unconstitutional” inverts the Constitution. Article 324 exists so the country can trust elections, not so internal disagreement becomes a state secret. After a 2023 law that already lets the government pick the referees and shield them, telling the public not to talk about a split inside the Commission is not constitutionalism. It is opacity.
If the process was clean, publish the objections and the signed orders. Until then, “it was unanimous and talking about it is unconstitutional” is not a defence.

text:
Proposal

Dear Alexander Shenderyuk-Zhidkov

I would have liked to have had a brief chat with you in Istanbul, but unfortunately we missed each other. You were, however, kind enough to allow my wife to take a photograph with you.

I would like to put forward an idea to you below; it may be a little naïve, but given the current, appalling situation between our countries, I simply feel I must do something, that I must make a stand: Not all Germans are as Germany currently appears to be.

My mother came from Silesia and was driven out of her home out of her beloved Silesia by the Red Army. And yet she brought me up in the spirit of love for the ‘Russian soul’, as she always put it. I grew up with music that has accompanied me throughout my life like a fundamental tone: Tchaikovsky, Rimsky-Korsakov, Swiridow, Rachmaninoff.

For me, the end of the Cold War was linked to the hope of a united Europe… from Lisbon to Vladivostok… that may not be entirely accurate geographically, but it is fitting in the spirit of peace and understanding amongst nations.

But the pieces on the Eurasian chessboard were moved differently.

As your President once said – I believe it was during an interview with Tucker Carlson – “when it comes to soft power, you (Americans) are unbeatable”. In Iran, they have found a very successful opponent in the form of the Lego videos. Such things have significance, make an impact and generate sympathy.

Unfortunately, I cannot suggest any measure quite as effective as this that might finally cast Russia’s image, even amongst my more narrative believing fellow citizens, in the light where it truly belongs; but I would like to put forward an idea to you which could at least reach the more educated, curious and book-loving among them, and which might also leave its mark on Western historical scholarship.

My suggestion is inspired by a post by @rinalu_ .  She is active on X and regularly shares posts about Russia, Russian and European history, which reveal a very different view of history from the one I, having been born in the Rhineland a long time ago, grew up with. When asked where one might read and verify her claims, she wrote:

“Sorry… either you can read Russian or you’re out of luck… not because I’m mean, but because the vast majority of Russian historical literature simply hasn’t been – and isn’t being – translated.”

This statement shocked me somewhat and raised the question: what if we could walk into a bookshop from Moscow via Berlin, New York and Beijing and find, in the books, at least the same facts, even if the interpretations differed? It seems we are a long way from that state of affairs. If I am interpreting Rina Lu correctly, and if what she writes is true, it seems that the Iron Curtain has never ceased to exist, at least in that respect.

To put it another way: we in the West, my fellow citizens – even those who are open to Russia – are blind in one eye… and what is presented to the other eye does not always, and under all circumstances, correspond to the historical events that actually took place… to put it very, very diplomatically.

Here, then, is my suggestion:

Many years ago, the “Project Gutenberg” (https://t.co/9eh5dHIWKG) was launched. Works in the public domain are made freely available to everyone there. For anyone who wishes to do so, a large part of our cultural world is open to them… free of charge.

How about launching a “Nestor” project to publish translations of Russian historical works (please include German translations too; we Germans are in desperate need of a refresher course). Even if such a project were limited to public domain books, it would at least offer those of good will – those willing to be open to different arguments – a new perspective on the world in which we live today… and how we came to be here.

In the past, this would have been a colossal and expensive undertaking; today, in the age of AI and translation programmes, it should be a straightforward and financially viable endeavour.

The fate of RT deeply moved and affected me at the time, both because the channel on my satellite receiver remains off the air to this day and because it shows the depths to which we – the free, open and democratic West – have already sunk. In this respect, such a project will certainly face opposition, but as it lies in a grey area between academia and popular science, there are surely ways to bridge that gap.

First and foremost, however, this would of course be a decision on the part of your country to be open to such an idea.

I would like to conclude with the heartfelt hope that we, the citizens of Germany, will wake up, remember our shared history, our responsibility and draw the urgent conclusions that must be drawn from it.

I do not know whether I will live to see it, but I do not wish to give up on it: the dream of your presidents, also shared by our presidents and chancellors, Chirac, Kohl and Schröder – the dream of a united Europe living in peace and prosperity from Lisbon to Vladivostok

With warm regards from the Rhineland to Kaliningrad

text:
𝗧𝗶𝗺𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗠𝗮𝗿𝗸 𝗖𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗲𝘆 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗖𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗱𝗮 𝘁𝗼 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗙𝗿𝗲𝗲 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝗹𝗱 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗗𝗲𝗳𝗲𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗛𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀

I read every day that Mark Carney is the grown-up in the room. The steady hand. The adult the free world has been waiting for while the Americans throw tantrums. Fine. I'm convinced. The job is open, and there's a live test case at the mouth of the Red Sea.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗛𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗱

In the past few weeks the Houthis took the port of Mocha, then Perim Island, the rock that splits Bab el-Mandeb into two shipping lanes. They announced a blockade of Saudi oil headed to Asia. Saudi Arabia shut its East-West pipeline after drone strikes, and this week Houthi missiles were fired at Yanbu, the Red Sea port where that pipeline's oil gets loaded.

The President of the United States, standing in Dublin, said the Houthis had called him, didn't want to fight America, were letting most ships through, and had a problem with only "one country." His Vice President said the administration was monitoring the situation. Translation: not our strait, not our oil, not our war.

𝗪𝗵𝗼𝘀𝗲 𝗢𝗶𝗹 𝗜𝘀 𝗜𝘁?

This is the serious part, and it's simple. They need the oil. We don't.

For seventy years, the U.S. Navy guaranteed that oil reached Tokyo, Seoul, Rotterdam and Marseille, and the countries receiving it never bore the real cost. They hosted some bases and paid some bills, but the warships, the risk and the casualties were American. Their most reliable contribution was the occasional lecture about American arrogance. That arrangement just paused. The people who need the oil are now the people who have to protect it.

𝗘𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗱𝗲𝗿 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗙𝗿𝗲𝗲 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝗹𝗱

Canada's navy has twelve Halifax-class frigates, commissioned in the 1990s. It has no destroyers; the last one was retired in 2017. The replacements are due in the 2030s. Its four submarines spend most of their lives in refit. When the U.S. assembled Operation Prosperity Guardian against the Houthis in 2023, Canada contributed a handful of staff officers. Not ships. Officers.

I propose the following campaign plan. Phase one: a strongly worded communiqué. Phase two: a coalition summit in Ottawa. Phase three: a second communiqué, more strongly worded. Phase four: the frigates arrive, sometime after the new destroyers enter service.

And Carney has had plenty to say. In March 2025 he declared the United States "no longer a reliable partner" and said the old relationship of tight security and military cooperation was over. This spring he told Canadians that "hope isn't a plan." Last month, after trade talks collapsed, he said America's signature is sometimes "written in pencil." Fine. Take him at his word. If America is unreliable, this is the moment for the reliable partners to show up. Hope isn't a plan in the Red Sea either.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗖𝗼𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗔𝘀𝘀𝗲𝗺𝗯𝗹𝗲𝘀

Canada's new friend is nearby too. Having concluded that America is no longer a reliable partner, Ottawa cut a deal with a more dependable one: Beijing. Chinese electric cars in, Canadian canola back to China. Surely a reliable partner will help out. Conveniently, China's only overseas military base is also in Djibouti, right at the mouth of the strait. The People's Liberation Army Navy has been sitting there since 2017, watching the world's shipping go by.

So picture it: a Canadian frigate, a Legion detachment and a Chinese naval base, all within sight of Bab el-Mandeb, united in defense of the rules-based order.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗙𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁 𝗩𝗼𝗹𝘂𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗲𝗿

As I was writing this, one stepped forward, and it wasn't Canada. France announced it will send soldiers, radars and air defenses to protect Yanbu, hours after Houthi missiles were fired at it. Credit where due. But Macron was explicit: this is to protect a site, not to engage in the conflict. Britain has offered the Saudis aerial refueling. France will guard the pump. The strait stays in Houthi hands.

What to Watch

But strip away the satire and this is Trump's point, and it's a fair one: help out. It's your oil, your trade, your sea lane. Europe has time for standing ovations and new membership categories. Canada has time to lecture Washington and cut deals with Beijing. Nobody has time to send a warship to the one strait that feeds them. The only way the free world grows up is if its designated adult stops doing its homework for it.

Prime Minister, the Houthis are on line one.

text:
🧠 You've been hearing about tokenization for months, things heating up, big numbers like trillion and quadrillion being thrown around.

Read this article to get a very concise, simple to understand explanation of tokenization.

We live in an age where an email takes milliseconds to reach the other side of the planet, yet transferring ownership of a stock, a piece of commercial real estate, or a trade credit bond still takes days or weeks. 

Why? Because global finance runs on a patchwork of disconnected, proprietary databases. 

Every bank, broker, and registry maintains its own ledger, requiring an army of middlemen, custodians, and clearinghouses to manually cross-check who owns what. 

This friction locks up trillions of dollars in idle capital just waiting for trades to settle, leaves high-value assets completely illiquid, and forces heavy compliance costs through manual checks. 

Furthermore, governments and institutions cannot simply adopt open digital networks without guarantees around sovereign control, strict tax oversight, and automated AML/KYC enforcement.

Tokenization solves this foundational infrastructure problem once and for all.

At its core, tokenization on Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT) transforms static, real-world assets into programmable digital deeds. 

Think of DLT as a shared, tamper-proof global ledger. When an asset is tokenized, an issuer locks the physical or traditional asset in a secure, audited vault, and mints digital tokens on the ledger that represent direct, verifiable ownership. 

Because these tokens are programmable, rules regarding compliance, dividend distributions, and transfers are baked directly into the digital code itself. 

An asset can now only move if regulatory conditions are met automatically. This unlocks instant atomic settlement—swapping the asset and the money at the exact same second—eliminating settlement risk, enabling fractional ownership of previously inaccessible asset classes, and opening up 24/7 global liquidity.

This is precisely where enterprise pioneers like Ripple have strategically positioned themselves to lead the transition. 

While much of the crypto industry chased consumer speculation, Ripple built a end-to-end, bank-grade tokenization stack tailored specifically for conservative financial institutions and sovereign regulators. 

Through its institutional custody solutions (via Metaco and Palisade acquisitions), Ripple allows institutions to safely hold the underlying physical assets and manage keys with custom compliance rules. 

On the ledger layer, the XRP Ledger offers native, protocol-level tokenization features, avoiding the security vulnerabilities of third-party smart contracts. 

To handle the cash side of the trade, Ripple introduced RLUSD, a fully backed, regulated stablecoin that enables instant, two-sided settlement—asset on one side, digital dollar on the other. 

By integrating custody, compliant asset issuance, and instant liquidity into a single turnkey platform, Ripple has engineered the exact gateway traditional finance needs to migrate trillions of dollars in real-world assets onto modern digital rails.

text:
here is Grok's response:

Charging more than a posted shelf price violates weights/measures accuracy rules (NIST Handbook 130, ~98% standard) in nearly every state and can count as false advertising under state consumer laws. California (BPC 12024.2) and Michigan require the lowest posted price (or bounties). Basic contract law treats tags as invitations to offer, so isolated errors often need not be honored for the sale itself.  Yes, bait-and-switch is illegal under federal FTC Act §5 and the Guides Against Bait Advertising (16 CFR 238).

The funny thing about laws .. there is never "just one" that covers something.  It's generally a patch work of stuff.

text:
The Unsweet Spike: 6 Everyday Vegetables That Quiet Blood Sugar Without Tasting Like Salad Punishment
—————————————————
A meal does not need to taste sweet to send blood glucose soaring. Large servings of rice, bread or potatoes deliver a hefty starch load that the body rapidly converts to sugar. @DocPriyamMD , highlights six cheap, familiar vegetables that help when they replace part of that starch rather than sit on top of a full plate of it.
1. Spinach adds fibre and folate with almost no digestible carbohydrate; slip a generous handful into soups, omelettes or stir-fries so the rice portion can shrink. 
2. Okra is similarly low-carb and high-fibre; roast or sauté it and pair it with protein plus a modest starch serving
.3. Cauliflower is the most versatile swap: rice it, mash it with potatoes, or use it as a base so the total carbohydrate count of the meal falls. 4.Cabbage supplies inexpensive bulk and fibre in salads, soups or stir-fries, making a smaller pasta or rice serving feel complete. 
5. Green beans offer fibre with far less starch than potatoes; load roasted trays with more beans and fewer potatoes
6. Cucumber is mostly water; a cucumber-tomato salad adds volume and almost no calories.
The physiology is simple. These vegetables contribute fibre, water and physical bulk while contributing very little rapidly digestible carbohydrate. Fibre slows gastric emptying and intestinal glucose absorption, flattening the post-meal rise. The critical detail is replacement, not addition: piling vegetables onto an unchanged mountain of rice changes little.
As a clinician -  I consider this advice practical and evidence-aligned. Non-starchy vegetables remain a first-line dietary tool for glycaemic control in diabetes, prediabetes and insulin resistance. The emphasis on swapping rather than stacking is what most patients miss and what actually moves the needle. The suggestions are culturally adaptable, inexpensive and easy to implement at home. They are not a cure or a licence to ignore overall calorie balance, protein, activity or prescribed medication. Individual glucose responses differ; people who use insulin or oral agents should still monitor their own readings and adjust with their own doctor. Used consistently as part of a larger pattern, however, these six ordinary vegetables reliably reduce the starch burden of everyday meals and make steadier blood sugar more achievable.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​ #MedTwitter #MedEd #MedX @IhabFathiSulima @ajaykraina @mekarora @sowmiyasid @ravikarkara

RINO Republican Shows His True Colors

Washington state lawmaker to resign 3 days before the election

Sept. 29, 2026

In a surprise announcement, Republican state Rep. Skyler Rude of Walla Walla, LD-16, said Tuesday that he will resign from office days before the election to start a NEW job with Democrat Secretary of State Steve Hobbs.

Rude, a moderate (mainstream) Republican, said he will step down Oct. 31, 2026 and begin work the next day as Hobbs’ legislative director.

The timing means Rude’s name will be on the ballot for the Nov. 3 election. Until Tuesday, he had been expected to win a fifth term against a Democrat challenger, Derek Sarley.

Rude said in an interview that the job opportunity arose after ballots arrived for the August primary and the offer became final a few days ago. He said he considered and decided against waiting until after the election to tell constituents in the 16th Legislative District which encompasses parts of four counties, Walla Walla, Franklin, Benton and Grant.

“The timing is difficult given the proximity to the general election. The politically safer decision would be to announce after the election,” he said in a statement. “I entered office committed to acting honestly and transparently, and I’m not going to change that commitment now as I complete my elected service.”

If Rude wins, Republicans will have essentially two vacancies to fill — one to complete the lawmaker’s current term and one that would begin in January when the new two-year legislative term starts.

If Sarley wins, the GOP could appoint someone to serve the final weeks of Rude’s term until the Democrat is sworn in.

Sarley said late Tuesday that even though it had seemed like the incumbent had not been actively campaigning he was “quite surprised” by the news.

Sarley now hopes voters understand that if Rude wins, they will have no say in who is appointed to the job. That’s up to Republican precinct officers and elected officials in four counties.

“I don’t think this is the kind of decision that should be made by county commissioners,” he said.

Rude wants his party to retain control of the seat.

“Voters who want a Republican appointed to replace me should vote for me,” he said. House Republicans, he continued, are “fighting hard to make Washington a more affordable, safer place to live” even as Democrats outnumber them 59-39 in the chamber.

“An imbalance that large diminishes the voices of moderate Democrats and Republicans alike,” he said. “It gives the most extreme voices outsized influence and reduces the need to build consensus on public policy.”

Rude won his House seat in 2018. He is the assistant floor leader for his caucus and the ranking Republican on the House Education Committee. He also serves on the Appropriations and the Postsecondary Education and Workforce committees.

In addition to leaving office, he will be shutting down a stagecoach tour business he ran in the Walla Walla Valley.

“Serving our district for eight years has been the honor of my life,” he said. “Leaving is bittersweet, but I’m grateful that my next role brings together two things I care deeply about: Washington’s history and the integrity of our elections. The Secretary of State’s office safeguards our state’s historical records and helps administer the elections on which our democracy depends.”

text:
Clipping. Not even close.

I run clipping campaigns for a living so I'm biased, but I'll show you how I'd run one for a business nobody in this space would ever touch

There's a veneer clinic in Miami I've seen go viral a few times. $20k a set. Full smile makeovers. They do at least one of these a day. Maybe more.

I'd bet my house they're spending 5 figs/mo on Google at $60+ CPC and posting their before & afters to 8k followers on IG, then calling it in. 

The "Turkey teeth" meme boosted the entire country's tourism industry with zero paid ads.

Before & after is the most viral format that exists. This clinic makes a fresh one every single day and only posts it to their IG feed. 

If they hired me tomorrow this is what happens:

Consent form at check-in. (They probably already have this) Film short clips of every patient, the reveal and the reaction. 30 days later we have tons of raw footage

You could start with 50 clippers. $1 per 1k views. $1k max payout. They get the footage, a brief, and go to war cutting infinite before & afters with a hundred different hooks across 250 different pages. 

If their clips flop I pay nothing. When a format hits and does 4m views overnight, I pay $1k for 4M eyeballs on a $20k offer. 

Here’s the thing marketers get wrong when they try this and then tell everyone clipping "doesn't work"

Nobody is buying $20k of teeth off a random clipper's page. Clipping isn't there to sell

It's there to make people search you

Every clip tags the clinic in description, the text  on screen says DM @ clinic  "SMILE" for a free smile design. Clinic runs a DM automation, viewer sends 3 photos of their teeth, gets a mockup of how hot they can look in 24 hours. Now it's personal, a deep emotional need for this product. Of course we offer financing, $400/mo. Painless. 

Deposit paid. Customer books the flight

You’re just farming follower count and inbound DMs 

After 2 weeks I know exactly which 5 clips hit. The algorithm told me for free

Those 5 go straight into Meta as ads with an actual button, targeted to the metros people fly from, retargeting everyone who touched the page. This is the part where the money gets disgusting

$10k gets you 10M views. One sale pays for the whole campaign twice. And I haven't even opened Meta ads manger yet 

I've never seen a single clinic do this. Not one. Everyone still thinks clipping is for streamers and casinos

Which is exactly why the first guy who does this will eat 

Same play works for other niches. Anything expensive with boring marketing

Now that I’ve posted this some agency kid is going to run it and print. You’re welcome.

text:
VENICE AND GENOA COMBINE
For Venice, so far so good: Florence, Naples, and Milan had been ruined. But ironically, the same dumb Valois and Hapsburg giants which had taken out three dangerous rivals were now to turn like Frankenstein’s monsters on the wily new Romans. Venetian manipulations were about to boomerang in the form of an alliance of all of Europe against Venice. This was the famous crisis of the War of the League of Cambrai, which was assembled in 1508-1509. The opposing coalition was made up of the pope (by then the Genoese Giuliano della Rovere, as Julius II), the Holy Roman Emperor Maximilian I, France, Spain, Savoy, Mantua, and Ferrara. The announced purpose of this alliance was to expunge Venice from the face of the earth. It nearly worked. At Agnadello, near the Adda River, the Venetian mercenary army was crushed by an army composed predominantly of Frenchmen. The Venetians were driven all the way down the Po Valley to Padua, and they soon lost that as well. Machiavelli exulted that on the day of Agnadello, the Venetians lost everything that they had conquered in more than 800 years. Machiavelli was himself engaged in operations against Venice, bringing a grant of Florentine cash to the aid of the Franco- Imperial forces holding Verona. With nothing left but the lagoons, the Venetian position was desperate. The doge sent a message to the pope asking for mercy, and announcing that Venice would vacate territory taken in the past from the Papal States. Inside Venice, Agnadello brought on an orgy of hysterical self-flagellation among the terrified patricians. The banker Girolamo Priuli wrote in his diary that Agnadello had been a punishment for the sins of the Venetian nobility, among which he numbered arrogance, violation of promises, lechery in nunneries, sodomy, effeminate dress, and luxurious and lascivious entertainments. Antonio Contarini, newly appointed patriarch of Venice, gave a speech to the Senate in which he characterized the Serenissima as a thoroughly amoral city. The defeat was a punishment for the city’s sins, he said. Nunneries were catering to the sexual needs of the rich and powerful. Homosexuality was so widespread that female prostitutes had complained to him that they had earned so little during their youth that they had to keep working far into their old age. But more significantly, the shock of Agnadello set into motion a strategic review in the Venetian intelligence community which led to very far-reaching conclusions, some of which were not obvious before several decades had gone by. The first Venetian ploy was to attempt to dismember the Cambrai coalition. They started with Pope Julius II. This pontiff was, as already noted, Genoese. Genoa and Venice had engaged in a series of highly destructive wars up till about the end of the fourteenth century, but after that, Genoa gravitated toward the status of junior partner and close associate of the Venetians. The Venetians had bested the Genoese by virtue of superior connections in the East, but otherwise their was a broad area of agreement. The symbol of Genoa was St. George the dragon-slayer, in reality no saint at all but a thinly disguised version of Perseus saving Andromeda by slaying the sea monster, a legend that is centered on the coast of Lebanon. The “George” is said to come from the Gorgon Medusa, whose head Perseus was carrying. Perseus is in turn nothing but a westernized variant of Marduk, the Syrian Apollo, a deity associated with the most evil forces of ancient Assyria and Babylon. The Venetians had their own Marduk cult, although subordinated to St. Mark, on the island of San Giorgio Maggiore, home of a Dominican monastery and today of the Cini Foundation, one of the highest level think tanks in the world. The modern British preference of Gorgons is too well known to need comment. What probably accounted more directly for Julius II’s decision to reverse his alliances was a deal mediated with the Venetians by Agostino Chigi, the Siena Black Guelph banker from whose financial empire the infamous Siena Group of today derives. He proposed that the Venetians stop buying alum, needed in textile and glass manufacture, from the Turks, but contract for a large shipment at higher prices from the alum mines at Tolfa in the Papal States – mines for which he, Chigi, was acting as agent. To sweeten the pot, Chigi offered the Venetians tens of thousands of ducats in much-needed loans.
The Venetians, fearing a rapid French offensive, accepted. Their own state finances were in total shambles. Only the Chigi loan allowed them to hire enough Swiss mercenaries to hold out against the French and the Imperial Landsknechte. To provide a plausible cover for his move, Julius II suddenly discovered that the real issue was not Venice after all, but the need to expel the barbarians (primarily the French) from Italy. Julius stipulated an alliance with Venice. He then set up the slogan of Fuori Barbari! (Kick the Barbarians out!) which is still recorded by credulous writers of Italian school books as the beginning of the struggle to unify Italy. Even the Venetian mercenaries, mostly Swiss, began using the battle cry of “Italy and Freedom!” Thus the post-Agnadello crisis was overcome. Some years later the Venetians tried the same tactic in reverse, this time with more lasting success. By 1525 the prevalent barbarians in Italy were the forces of Emperor Charles V, who had defeated the French at Pavia, capturing King Francis I. The French lost their hold on Naples and Milan. At this point Doge Andrea Gritti, whose portrait by Tiziano speaks volumes about his personality, decided to agitate once again the banner of Italian freedom. This took the form of the Holy League of Cognac “for the restoration of Italian liberty,” uniting France, Venice, Milan, Florence, and the Papal States under Pope Clement VIII Medici. After having set up this alliance, designed to play the French against Charles V once again to destroy Medici-controlled Rome, the last intact Renaissance center, the Venetians retired into defensive positions to await the outcome. Venetian capacities to manipulate Charles V were formidable indeed. The emperor’s bankers and intelligencers were the Fuggers of Augsburg, a banking house and a city that must be regarded as Venetian satellites, within a context of very heavy Venetian control of the cities of the Danube valley. Virtually every young male member of the Fugger family, and of their colleagues the Welsers as well, was sent to Venice for a period of apprenticeship at the Fondaco dei Tedeschi. This was the case with Jacob Fugger the Rich. Venice was the pivot for Fugger metals trading, especially toward the East. Thus, the Venetians stayed in their phony war posture against Charles V, while the imperial army of Lutheran Lanzi under Georg Frundsberg devastated Italy. The sack of Rome in 1527 was the direct outcome of this combined Venetian diplomacy and manipulation. To make Charles V’s triumph complete, the Genoese Admiral Andrea Doria, commanding the French fleet, defected to the imperial side. A Doria coup in Genoa then established a permanent de facto alliance with Venice. In 1530, Charles V was crowned as Holy Roman Emperor and King of Italy in a ceremony at Bologna. Garrisons of imperial troops were shortly stationed in every major city. Thanks to the tenacious policy of the Venetians, the main centers of the Renaissance had been subverted or destroyed. Venice was the only major Italian state which had retained real sovereignty. With the end of the Renaissance, Venice could feel free to start a delphic Renaissance among the throngs of intellectuals seeking asylum in the lagoons.

THE CREATION OF THE JESUITS
The “long autumn of the Italian Renaissance in Venice” during the rest of the sixteenth century was only one deployment among several. Another was the promotion of the Protestant Reformation. The more immediate controllers of Martin Luther have yet to be identified, but this is something of a secondary matter. Luther’s agitation in Wittenberg was merely one more example of protests against the papacy and the Curia that had been chronic and endemic for decades. What gave Luther and the rest of the Protestant reformers real clout was a publicity and diffusion of their ideas that owed much to the Venetian publishing establishment. The Venetian presses quickly turned out 40,000 copies of the writings of Luther, Calvin, Melancthon, and the heresiarch Juan Valdes, especially popular in Italy. Pope Leo X publicly denounced the University of Padua as the hotbed of inspiration of the German disease of Lutheranism. Clearly, Venetian interest was well-served by a schismatic movement that would embroil Germany, France, and the rest of Europe in a series of easily profiled conflicts. In addition, a conflict between reformers and counter- reformers, all owing allegiance to Aristotle, would severely undercut the influence of Erasmus and others like him. Venetian influence on both Reformation and Counter- Reformation can be seen most clearly in the remarkable career of Gasparo Contarini, who did not let the fact that he was a Protestant in theology, well before Luther, prevent him from founding the Society of Jesus. Contarini was the scion of one of Venice’s most prestigious Longhi families. The Contarinis had produced seven doges, and Gasparo had his sights set on being the eighth, before he was tapped to serve Venice as a member of the College of Cardinals. He served the Serene Republic as ambassador to the court of Charles V, and as ambassador to the Vatican, where he took a role in setting up the Medici Pope Clement VII for the 1527 sack of Rome. Toward the end of his life, Contarini was sent as papal legate to the Imperial Diet at Regenburg, where he represented the Roman point of view in debates with schismatics like Melancthon. There, he had a hand in destroying any compromise between the Lutherans and the Emperor Charles, which would have helped to end the bloodshed and dissension of the Reformation years. What does this sublime Venetian patrician have to do with the founding of the Jesuit order by that itinerant and deranged mystic, Ignatius of Loyola? Ignatius was the creature of Venice, and of Contarini in particular. In 1521, Ignatius was wounded while fighting the French in one of the wars of Charles V. During his convalescence, he underwent his much-touted mystical crisis, after which he took up the life of a hobo. Making his way around Europe seeking funding for a pilgrimage to the holy land, Ignatius found his way to Venice, where he camped out in St. Mark’s Square and lived by begging. One evening the Venetian oligarch Marcantonio Trevisan was sleeping in his golden palace, and had a vision. An angel came to him asking, “Why are you sleeping so soundly in your warm bed, while in the square there is a holy man, a poor pilgrim who needs your help?” Trevisan rushed downstairs to find Ignatius, who became his house guest, fleas and all. One of the requirements of the Beast empire is that it be a democratic nation born of Templar French Freemasonry, the father of modern democracy.
Michael Baigent, co-author of The Temple and The Lodge, has traced the movement of the Templars to America. He discovered that Sionist English Freemasonry reigned supreme in Boston until a higher degree Templar lodge was warranted in 1756 by Grand Lodge Scotland. "There were thus two rival Provincial Grand Lodges in Boston," says Baigent, "St. John's, under the aegis of the Grand Lodge of England, and St. Andrew's, under the aegis of Grand Lodge of Scotland.... And on 28 August 1769, St. Andrew's conferred, for the first time anywhere in the world, a new Freemasonic degree - specifically called the Knights Templar Degree."23
Shortly thereafter another form of Templar Freemasonry came to America. The quasi-Jacobite Grand Lodge of York warranted lodges in Virginia.24 York Rite Freemasonry created additional degrees in the New World until it reached the 13th and final degree, known as the Knights Templar degree.
Thirteen-degree Templar York Rite Masonry, having ceased operation in England after establishing its base in the New World, exists today only in North America. Michael Baigent was able to trace the westward migration of the Templars by following their esoteric number "13." As you recall, the original Templar order consisted of thirteen degrees. The number "13" also commemorates Friday the 13th, 1307, the day persecution of the Templars began. In 1314, Jacques de Molay, the Grand Master of the Knights Templar, was burned at the stake. Only in America, says Baigent, has the Templar Grand Master received his most flattering and lavish public homage, in the form of a youth organization sponsored by Freemasonry, the Order of DeMolay.

Templar Military Lodges
The Templars also stealthily entered America through military lodges. Of particular significance are those chartered by the Irish Grand Lodge, which offered the higher degrees of Jacobite Masonry. Later these lodges incorporated the French Templar Scottish Rite degrees, further dividing colonial America between two rival forms of Freemasonry. While British politics in the colonies was dominated by English Masons in the Northeast, her military was under the influence of French Templar Field Lodges throughout the colonies - not a stable union for governing "13" rebellious colonies.2

European Templars Settle America
Another identifying characteristic of the Beast's revived Roman empire, according to our analysis of Daniel 7:7-8 in chapter 26, is that it must be populated by immigrants from the territory governed by the old Roman empire. Of course colonial America was populated by peoples from a Europe shaped by ancient Rome and later by the Holy Roman Empire. Templar influence in America began after Prince Charles Edward, the Young Stuart Pretender, failed to regain his British throne. As you recall, in 1746 he was soundly defeated, forever dashing the hopes of Scottish Templars recapturing England. As a result, many Irish and Scottish Templar Jacobites who had fought with Charles Stuart fled to America. Those who returned to France with the Prince founded the Scottish Rite of Freemasonry.
Between 1745 and 1753, the British and European Templar population in the New World had increased dramatically. In 1754 Benjamin Franklin attempted to relieve population pressure by proposing a plan for the union of all 13 colonies. The British government rejected Franklin's proposal, fearing a united America would be difficult to control. Subsequently, the exploding population was forced to move west into French territory, which precipitated the French and Indian War in America, a phase of the Seven Years War on the continent of Europe. During this war the French military brought to the New World the Templar Scottish Rite, first setting up base at Boston, then Charleston, S.C.26 Michael Baigent, in The Temple and The Lodge, explains:
Prior to the Seven Years War, most of the Freemasonry in North America was orthodox pro- Hanoverian, warranted by Grand Lodge [London]. During the Seven Years War, however, "higher degree" [Templar] Freemasonry, by means of regimental field lodges, was transplanted on a large scale to the American colonies and quickly took root. Boston - the soil from which the American Revolution was to spring - exemplifies the process of transplantation and the friction that sometimes arose from it.27

Benjamin Franklin: Templar Spy Master
Benjamin Franklin became a Mason in February 1731 and Provincial Grand Master of Pennsylvania in 1734, and again in 1749. In 1756 he was inducted into the Royal Society in absensia. (The Royal Society, you may recall, was an English Masonic front organization for the Rosicrucian Priory of Sion.)
Between 1757 and 1762, and again between 1764 and 1775, Franklin spent considerable time in England and France. While in England, he discovered English Freemasonry's "Secret Doctrine" for America. Franklin was in London in 1775 when he was made aware that war between the colonies and Great Britain might break out at any moment, so in March he returned to Philadelphia. Later that year he attended the Second Continental Congress, through which he helped draft the Declaration of Independence. In 1776 he was sent to Paris where he came in contact with the Illuminati. Franklin learned of the esoteric significance of the number "13" and the Illuminati plan for the "13" American colonies. He stayed in Paris only a short while, returning to America with this important information. On the afternoon of July 4, 1776, he, with two other Masons, were appointed by the Continental Congress to design the Great Seal of the United States of America, which would include the Seal of the Illuminati.
Baigent suggests that Franklin favored the Illuminati plan to create a New World democracy, a "Philosophical Atlantis," over the British plan for an oligarchic expansion of empire. When Franklin was in France, he began to build a spy network in preparation for America's independence from England. Baigent gives us the details:
On 9 November [1777], a special committee - the "Committee of Congress for Secret Correspondence" - was appointed to establish a network of contacts among "our friends abroad." This committee consisted of Robert Morris, John Jay, Benjamin Harrison, John Dickinson and Benjamin Franklin. It was to operate extensively through Freemasonic channels and to lead to the creation of an elaborate spy network. At the same time, and quite coincidentally, it was to overlap a British spy network which ran parallel to it and also operated through Freemasonic channels. Because it afforded access to virtually all letters, all communications, the position of Postmaster-General was also traditionally that of spymaster. And during the American War for Independence, their experience as Postmasters-General was to stand both Dashwood and Franklin in good stead.
In his dual role of spymaster and colonial ambassador to France, Franklin established his centre of operations in Paris. Franklin's Templar Masonic friends in the postal service and in the military also had Templar sympathizers in the British Parliament. Temple of Olympian Zeus, Athens

Just a short walk from the Acropolis stands one of the largest temples ever built in the ancient Greek world. The Temple of Olympian Zeus may now survive only in ruins, but the remaining columns still give a remarkable impression of its original scale.

The temple was dedicated to Zeus and took centuries to complete, finally being finished during the Roman period under Emperor Hadrian.

The site offers plenty to appreciate:
•The enormous surviving columns
•Views towards the Acropolis
•Hadrian's Arch nearby
•The surrounding archaeological landscape
•A glimpse into Roman Athens

Standing beside the columns makes their size much easier to appreciate than photographs ever can.

The temple's history is equally fascinating. Construction began in the 6th century BC but was repeatedly interrupted before finally being completed many centuries later.

Hadrian played an important role in its completion and inaugurated the finished temple in AD 132.

Today, the site provides an interesting contrast to the Acropolis. Rather than the relatively intact silhouette of the Parthenon, here you see fragments of something that was once enormous.

Walk around the site slowly and look towards the Acropolis. The two monuments create an extraordinary visual connection between different periods of Athens' history.

It is another reminder that in Athens, history isn't confined to a museum. It is woven directly into the modern city.

Did you stop here during your visit to Athens?

text:
In 1998, Warren Buffett gave a 1-hour masterclass on how to never lose money investing.

Here are the 22 most valuable lessons from his lecture:

1. You only have to get rich once. If you have $100 million and can make 10% unleveraged or 20% leveraged, the difference between $110 million and $120 million at year-end means nothing to your life, your family, or anything. But the downside, especially with other people's money, is disgrace, humiliation, and facing the friends whose money you lost. The equation never makes sense.

2. To make money they did not need, they risked money they did have and needed. That is just plain foolish, Buffett says, regardless of your IQ. If you hand him a gun with a million chambers and one bullet and offer him any sum to put it to his temple and pull once, he will not do it. There is nothing on the upside that justifies the downside. People do this financially all the time without thinking.

3. The smartest people in finance went broke, and that is the most fascinating story Buffett knows. Long-term Capital Management had 16 people with possibly the highest average IQ of any business in the country, 350 to 400 combined years of experience, and most of their own net worth in the firm. They still went bankrupt. Buffett says if he ever wrote a book, it would be called why smart people do dumb things.

4. Beta and sigmas tell you nothing about the real risk of going broke. The LTCM team relied heavily on mathematics and believed a six- or seven-sigma event could not touch them. They were wrong. History does not tell you the probabilities of future financial events. The real risk is not volatility. It is a permanent, irreversible blind spot in something crucial, often caused by knowing a great deal about something else.

5. Invest only in businesses you can understand. That one rule narrows the field by about 90%, and that is fine. Buffett can understand Coca-Cola. he cannot value an internet company, and he says if a student handed him a valuation of one on a final exam, he would flunk them. People thought Enron was incredible because it had a good track record, but almost nobody understood how it made money. That was the signal to avoid it.

6. You want a business that is a castle with a wide moat around it. Inside the castle, you want an honest, able, hard-working duke. The moat can be low cost, like Geico in auto insurance, or brand, or patents, or location. But a wonderful castle will always be attacked, so the job of every manager Buffett owns is one thing: widen the moat. Throw crocodiles and sharks into it to keep competitors out.

7. Moats change slowly and invisibly, but they change. Thirty years ago, Kodak's moat was as wide as Coca-Cola's. They had share of mind; the little yellow box meant best in everyone's head. Then they let Fuji into the Olympics and narrowed their own moat. Coca-Cola's moat, by contrast, is wider now than 30 years ago. Every time infrastructure gets built in a country that is not yet profitable, the moat widens a little. You cannot see it day by day, but in 10 years, the difference is enormous.

8. Share of mind beats share of market. When you say Disney, every person in the room has something in their head. Say Universal Pictures or 20th Century Fox, and you have nothing. A mother with two kids will pick the $17.95 Disney video over the $16.95 alternative because she knows it will be fine and does not want to preview ten videos to decide. That little bit of certainty in the customer's mind is worth a fortune.

9. The best businesses have pricing power and require little capital. see's candy sold 16 million pounds at $1.95 when Buffett bought it for $25 million. The entire thesis was whether the price could go to $2.25 without hurting sales. It could, because nobody wants to hand their valentine a box of candy and say, "This year I took the low bid." Today, See's makes $60 million on the same formulas and still takes almost no capital. Compare that to GM, which had to reinvest every dollar into better factories and whose stock barely moved over 50 years.

10. The best businesses earn a royalty on other people's capital. Coca-Cola sells a formula and collects a royalty on every drink. American Express takes a few percent of every dollar you spend. You put up the capital, they take a cut. Low capital intensity is one of the most underrated qualities in a business and one of the surest paths to durable wealth.

11. Define your circle of competence and stay inside it. The size of the circle does not matter. Staying inside, it does. If you know which 30 companies out of thousands you actually understand, you are fine. Buffett understood H.H. brown shoes and Frank Rooney, so he closed that deal in five minutes. If you do not know enough to understand a business instantly, you will not understand it in a month either.

12. Ignore the macro entirely. Buffett has never bought or skipped a business because of a feeling about interest rates, the economy, or any macro forecast. If Alan Greenspan and Bob Rubin both whispered exactly what they would do for the next 12 months, it would not change what he pays for anything. You want to focus on what is important and knowable. The macro is important but not knowable, so you ignore it.

13. Inactivity is the strategy, not a flaw. Wall Street makes money on activity. You make money on inactivity. A broker is like a doctor paid by how often he changes your pills. If everyone in a room trades their portfolio with everyone else every day, they all end up broke, and the intermediary keeps the money. Buffett looks for one good idea a year and rides it to its full potential. He measures Berkshire by how little turnover there is, like a church where the same people fill the seats every Sunday.

14. If you understand businesses, diversification is a mistake. For the 99% who will not evaluate businesses, Buffett recommends a low-cost index fund and extreme diversification. But if you bring real intensity to evaluating companies, owning more than six is a terrible idea. Very few people got rich on their seventh best idea. A lot of people got rich on their best one. Buffett keeps about half his money in what he likes best.

15. Buffett's biggest mistakes are mistakes of omission, not commission. The times he understood a business well enough to act and instead sat there sucking his thumb. He passed on healthcare stocks during the Clinton plan and on Fannie Mae in the mid-eighties, each a multi-billion-dollar miss. Accounting never captures these. The $2,000 he put into a Sinclair service station as a young man, money he lost, has an opportunity cost of about $6 billion today.

16. Focus on what will happen, not when. Coca-Cola went public in 1919 at $40 a share and dropped to $19 within a year. There was always a reason not to buy: the great depression, world war, sugar rationing, thermonuclear weapons. But one share bought then and reinvested would be worth about $5 million. If you are right about the business, you will make a lot of money. The timing is the tricky part, so do not focus on it.

17. When hiring, look for integrity, intelligence, and energy. But if the person lacks the first one, you actually want them dumb and lazy. Because a person with intelligence and energy but no integrity will destroy you. Buffett borrowed this from Pete Kiewit. The trait everyone screens for last is the one that matters most.

18. Here is a thought experiment Buffett gives students. Imagine you could own 10% of one classmate for the rest of their life. You would not pick the highest IQ or the best grades. You would pick the person you respond to best, the one who is generous, honest, gives credit to others, and has leadership qualities. Now imagine you also had to short one classmate. You would pick the egotistical, greedy, slightly dishonest one. The qualities that decide both are not talent. They are character.

19. Every quality on the admirable side is achievable, and every quality on the repellent side is removable. The things that make you want to own 10% of someone are not the ability to throw a football or run fast; they are behavior, temperament, and character, all of which anyone can choose. Buffett's point: you already own 100% of yourself, so you might as well become the person worth betting on.

20. The chains of habit are too light to be felt until they are too heavy to be broken. Buffett sees people in their forties and fifties trapped by self-destructive patterns they can no longer change. At a young age, you can choose any habits you want. Ben Franklin and Ben Graham both did exactly this, looking at people they admired and simply deciding to behave like them. There was nothing impossible about it.

21. Take a job you would take if you were already independently wealthy. Buffett told a 28-year-old at Harvard who wanted a consulting job "to look good on his resume" that it was like saving up sex for your old age. There comes a time to just start doing what you love. Buffett offered to work for Ben Graham for free, was told he was overpriced, and kept pestering him for years. Take the job you would jump out of bed for. You cannot miss.

22. You won the ovarian lottery, and that should shape how you think. Buffett imagines a genie 24 hours before your birth letting you design the world's rules, with one catch: you do not know which of 5.8 billion balls you will draw. Born here or in Afghanistan, with an IQ of 130 or 70, male or female, able-bodied or not. If you could put your ball back and draw one of 100 random others, most people would not, because they are already in the luckiest 1%. Buffett knows he is perfectly wired for a market economy that pays him like crazy, while an equally good citizen leading scout troops and teaching Sunday school is not, purely by luck.
