text:
Seedance 2.5 Prompt
Create a 30-second Japanese sword-action comedy: reference-style 2D anime characters composited into photorealistic Shibuya. Synchronized dialogue, music and effects. Use the selected aspect ratio.

REFERENCES
A = black-haired heroine from @Image 1; her voice uses @Audio 1.
B = white-haired heroine from @Image 2; her voice uses @Audio 2.
All enemies use the design from @Image 3.
Preserve exact faces, hair, costumes, accessories, proportions and reference art styles. Images define identity, not poses or sheet layouts. Equal heroine heights, excluding ornaments. A and B are allies; ONE of each. Replicate only enemies.
Audio references define timbre and natural pitch, not scripts. Never replay recorded words or swap voices. Enemies are silent.
STYLE AND LOCATION
A, B and enemies retain their reference illustrated styles, clean lines and cel shading. Never turn them into live-action people or 3D figurines.

Photorealistic Shibuya Scramble Crossing at night after rain: diagonal zebra stripes, station frontage, curved commercial buildings, LED screens, wet asphalt and realistic glass, concrete and steel. Screens show abstract colors, no readable brands.

Integrate the illustrated characters through matching light direction, soft contact shadows, wet-road reflections and colored light on their cel shading. Keep their faces and linework sharp. Buildings, airborne debris, dust and destruction have realistic materials, weight and lighting. Sword energy remains vivid anime-style light.

Only heroes and enemies occupy the streets; no civilians or moving traffic. Establish Shibuya in the first frame before the destruction.
OPENING SPECTACLE AND CONTINUITY
Begin directly with a combined ultimate attack; no title or long setup. Both swords are already charged in the first frame.

TEN THOUSAND enemies fill the crossing and roads in deep layered ranks. A's teal slash and B's violet slash visibly merge into ONE gigantic crescent, expanding into a pressure wave that blasts enemies AND buildings outward.

Each heroine has one right-hand silver katana and a waist scabbard. Left hands may support the grip. Keep blades rigid and clear of each other.

Show contact before displacement. Enemies stay down. Close combat uses three to six attackers, preserving @Image 3. Sparks and knockdowns; no blood or exposed wounds.

SHOT 1 — COMBINED ULTIMATE ATTACK, 0–3 seconds
Low wide view across the crossing: A left, B right, side by side, facing a vast enemy formation. Their charged blades and wet road reflections glow teal and violet.
A slashes diagonally upward, B downward, in separate spaces. Energy trails cross ahead and fuse into one white-gold crescent. Bodies and blades never collide.

Around 0.1–0.8 seconds, A uses @Audio 1 and says:
「いくよ！」

Around 0.9–1.6 seconds, B uses @Audio 2 and replies:
「あわせる！」

These are the only lines; accurate lip sync. At 1.6 seconds the crescent launches the front ranks. Show merger and impact clearly.

SHOT 2 — TEN THOUSAND BLOWN AWAY, 3–8 seconds
High oblique view over the crossing and roads. Both heroines stay grounded at the origin; debris flies away from them.
The pressure front lifts successive enemy ranks and drives thousands of silhouettes backward with spinning weapons. It also strikes buildings along both roadsides, blasting them away from the heroes.

Show a traveling chain reaction, not an instant disappearance. At wave contact, windows shatter, signs tear away, and buildings rip from their foundations and fragment. Huge concrete sections and steel frames fly OUTWARD with the army. Show collapse spreading building by building, never an unrelated explosion.

Briefly slow the airborne peak, then resume speed. Illustrated enemies and photorealistic building fragments fill the sky. Keep silhouettes readable through dust.
SHOT 3 — BACK-TO-BACK GUARD, 8–11 seconds
Low medium-wide: the heroines slide back-to-back, feet grounded. The army stays down. Keep buildings ruined throughout.

A fresh @Image 3 squad enters over distant rubble; show their arrival, no respawning. The heroines exchange a glance and face them.
SHOT 4 — LOW/HIGH TEAMWORK, 11–16 seconds
Full-body lateral tracking. A advances into three attackers, ducks an incoming sword and sweeps low. Show blade contact, sparks and the attackers losing balance.

B leaps above A's crouched shoulder, clearly separated, and strikes another attacker. Show contact and its backward fall. B lands ahead as A rises.

Hold leap and landing continuously, keeping blade paths distinct.
SHOT 5 — MUTUAL PROTECTION, 16–22 seconds
Wider three-quarter view. An enemy attacks A's rear. B steps in and visibly parries above A's shoulder. A pivots beneath the clash and strikes the attacker approaching B's side.

They turn back-to-back and simultaneously slash outward into opposite sectors. A short teal-and-violet shockwave knocks down the remaining close attackers. This follow-up is smaller than the opening ultimate attack.

Dust clears. The main army remains down, the reinforcements are defeated, and ONE last enemy is standing several meters ahead. Both heroines lower their blades.

SHOT 6 — TOO POLITE TO FINISH, 22–27 seconds
Stable wide three-shot on the crossing: A left, B right, last enemy ahead. Stop the action music.

A offers the last enemy with her empty left palm, right-hand katana lowered. B returns the gesture. Both stay serious, looking at each other.
The enemy quietly lays its sword on a zebra stripe, backs away and runs out of frame. Show this continuously.

A and B turn back together and discover only the abandoned sword. Hold an awkward pause. No dialogue explains the joke.

SHOT 7 — THE FAMILIAR FACE, 27–30 seconds
Frontal close-up of anime A against a blurred photorealistic ruined Shibuya skyline. Preserve her exact face and hair. Wide eyes, small pupils, raised brows and lips slightly parted once, then held still: her familiar stunned, uncomprehending expression.
A looks toward camera. Push in; hold the final full second, sword out of crop. No blush, crying or speech. End on A.

SOUND AND MUSIC
After the two opening lines, no dialogue, narration, grunts, gasps, screams, laughter or vocal breaths from anyone.

Instrumental drums, strings and brass drive combat. Synchronize swords, impacts, collapses and landings. Opening: huge bass impact and cascading crashes.

Cut music at Shot 6. Hear the sword, retreating steps, settling debris and wind. No choir, vocals, comedy sting or canned laughter.
No text, subtitles, logos, watermarks, HUD, hero clones, mixed identities, extra limbs, fused bodies, morphing swords, costume changes, persistent afterimages, uncontrolled camera spins, realistic human faces, 3D character redesign or chibi.

text:
Prologue: Professor B.S.
Professor B.S. suffered from eternal insomnia. He sat before his television screen, far too alert.
3:21.
An interesting hour. Even more so when read in reverse. A basketball game murmured in the background, entirely irrelevant.
B.S. was contemplating the critical ethics of eating during a lecture. Not the students eating; that was perfectly legitimate in his eyes. He was thinking about the lecturer eating, mid-presentation. Nothing heavy, like beef and potatoes. Something light. A pleasant little salad. Perhaps a can of something carbonated on the side. But the students might take offense. The pretentious ones would likely file a complaint with the faculty.
Ridiculous. It’s for their own benefit, B.S. mused.
It would allow him to survive the mid-lecture hypoglycemia and bring the entire performance to a crescendo.
Perhaps he could bring in a patient while he was at it. Well, at least an actor. He could demonstrate meningeal signs on them - bend the neck until they screamed their soul out in pain.
Unpleasant.
Meningitis is undeniably unpleasant. Fortunately, only the actor must suffer.
Professor B.S. considered breaking his routine tomorrow to perform a ward round. A 'Peacock Walk,' just to remind everyone he was still among the living. Perhaps he would bark at someone regarding a botched chest X-ray interpretation, or, more amusingly, offer a rare word of praise to the department’s most incompetent resident. It was always good for a laugh.
The mere thought caused a twitch in his left flank. Or his right. Or both. Dealing with the actual practice of medicine was a dangerous business. Too demanding. Better to stick to lectures and remain entombed in his office. The air conditioning was sublime this time of year. Airy weather.
It was already four in the morning. Not good; sleep was no longer an option. Better to get dressed and brew some coffee. The morning would arrive soon enough.
***
Chapter 1 – Beep. Beep. Beep.
Beep. Beep. Beep.
White noise.
Beep. Beep. Beep.
White noise.
Dr. Eran Datner, the miserable resident on duty in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) at 'Sharona' Hospital, glanced at his watch. 3:23. A digital watch. A toy for the new generation. He disliked the time staring back at him, something too symmetrical about it. Either too early to get up or far too late.
In any case, he wondered why he had woken up. The background drone of the monitors was a poor excuse. It was barely audible from behind the on-call room door in the NICU. It must be something else.
Ring. Ring. Ring.
The phone. The nurse Susan. Susan Schell.
That never meant anything good.
That American only spoke up to rant about vaccines or bark about resuscitation.
Resuscitation.
He leapt out of bed, nearly forgetting to put on his shoes, and bolted from the room. His thinning hair was disheveled, and he was wholly dazed and bewildered. He did not know what awaited him.
***
Datner nearly stumbled over the nurses' desk before truly opening his eyes. He felt sour. Like a lemon squeezed into a margarita that had sat in the sun for far too long.
He knew what he had to do.
Too late.
Washing his face now would make the nurses look at him strangely. Combing his hair was out of the question; he had never owned a comb (he knew he did not have much to comb anyway). It was time for action.
Room 11.
The resuscitation in Room 11.
Susan had said it explicitly, that unhinged American from hell.
Too harsh. Just an unhinged American, then. Still tough, though. American, the harshest curse of all.
Resuscitation.
He pulled back the curtain of Room 11.
***
A large incubator. Transparent. Horribly generic.
The baby was unmistakably blue.
It had a name, but no one cared about that at this stage. At this stage, it wasn't even clear what the baby’s sex was. A few things were clear to Datner now. The monitor above the incubator showed a low oxygen saturation of 76%, and the baby looked distinctly blue.
The pulse and blood pressure were not being read by the monitor, and there were too many nurses around the small incubator. At least three nurses. At least one of them was Susan Schell. That couldn't be good.
Worst of all, the incubator had not yet been opened. That really annoyed him.
He pushed his way past the flustered nurses, opened the incubator, and shouted at Susan - "The Ambu, now." He began ventilating. 'Not too hard,' he recalled the advice of his old mentor, Prof. B.S., 'Gently, so you don’t burst the baby’s lungs.'
The lungs, surprisingly, did not resist at all. The air pushed by the Ambu flowed easily into the small body, which gradually turned pinker and pinker.
"What are the blood pressure and pulse?" Datner called out into the air, stifling a small smile at the saturation rising to 99%. Even better than 100, better symmetry. The sound the monitor emitted became much more tolerable. Almost melodic. Harmonic. The Beach Boys at their peak. God Only Knows.
"Still not reading," a voice from outer space replied.
That alien irritated Datner.
"Bring me a tube, size 2.5. And a laryngoscope with a small blade," he practically grumbled, disappointed by the slow flow of the event.
He did not fail to notice that Susan was working flawlessly. With all her faults, she was still quite experienced. She handed him the laryngoscope and the tube.
He put down the Ambu and inserted the laryngoscope.
'Straight up at a right angle. With the patient’s eyes facing the ceiling,' he recalled another piece of advice from Prof. B.S. Advice for all time. A Man for all seasons.
He wondered where B.S. was now.
Probably sitting at home watching TV and getting annoyed about his low salary. Who watches TV at this hour? Is the man a psychopath?!
Never mind. Moving on.
The vocal cords were clearly visible. A piece of cake. He inserted the tube quickly. Now, fixation.
This was the part he hated. He always felt the nurses would cause him to pull out the tube at that moment. Susan, however, didn't panic. "At 9.5 centimeters, Doctor?" she asked, almost affectionately.
"Yes," he mumbled, slightly surprised by her positive approach. He connected the Ambu to the tube and squeezed gently, compressing the small bellows only slightly, so as not to burst the lungs.
Meanwhile, the pulse returned. Approximately.
The monitor showed something that looked approximately like an ECG tracing in Lead 2. Not quite.
The stickers! They had fallen off the baby’s chest. Nurse Miri was attaching them now. Other than that, she was useless. She should learn from Susan.
Pulse 150. A small smile.
"And blood pressure?" Datner almost whispered.
"Wait, I'm changing the cuff, the previous one is too big," Susan answered. He almost began to like her. Not really, but still, a little, given the situation and the alternatives. Better unhinged and efficient than sane and harmful.
Another half a minute passed. Thirty seconds is a long time when you are waiting. He began to remember how tired he was. A big yawn. Overt. For everyone to see. The questionable scent of his breath forced him to stop the show. If you eat something after midnight, it’s best not to have it spicy or with a lot of garlic. Crucially, it's best not to have both ingredients, Datner noted. Failed note.
Meanwhile, the tube fixation was finished, and he turned to adjust the parameters on the ventilator. He never quite understood how to choose the numbers, the ventilation metrics. Strange names for pressures – ‘PIP’, ‘PEEP’, and all sorts of other 'peeps' ran through his head. He also had pressure in his bladder. A sudden need to urinate. Fortunately, he sorted that out relatively easily here. Almost a coincidence. Dumb luck.
"Blood pressure 60/30," Susan cried, almost shouted, in a tone of joy, into the space.
It won't get better than that, Datner decided.
He barely knew what to do with himself now that he was no longer holding the tube or calibrating the ventilator. Nurse Miri smiled. Like a calf that had been given excellent straw.
Nurse Susan was frowning. Despite her advanced age, something of the Southern American beauty in which she had once excelled remained. The Texas beauty queen forty years ago, no doubt. He didn't recall her being originally from New York.
"What about Dextro?" Datner barked.
"Immediately, Doctor," Susan replied submissively. She clearly had excellent training and manners that were out of this world. Foreign to the place.
He almost decided to go out to the stairwell and steal a few puffs of a cigarette.
Maybe it is better to update the on-call physician first.
But first, read the chart, he concluded.
He knew nothing about the infant who had just returned to life and certainly didn't know why this delicate creature had nearly collapsed completely. The on-call physician would not like a call about resuscitation without concrete information about the patient. He wasn't even sure if it was a male. He thought he saw testes during the ventilation, but he wasn't prepared to swear to it.
Still, a cigarette first. The on-call physician was certainly asleep now, and there was no reason to rush and call her before everything was known.
The watch showed 3:53. Still too symmetrical.
***
"What do you mean, the baby in Room 11 almost died?" the voice on the other end gasped. Datner wasn't sure if Dr. Katya Pavlichuk, the on-call neonatologist, was shouting or talking in her sleep. Maybe it was a combination of both? And what difference did it make anyway?
"He was perfectly fine this morning when I left him," the on-call physician continued, starting to wake up, grumbling about the uninvited wake-up call and the news it brought.
Datner glanced at his watch, 5:15, still symmetrical.
He thought that if he waited long enough, the on-call physician would appreciate the extra sleep time he had allowed her, and it would slightly dull the criticism of his ignorance regarding the chart.
He had tried earlier to read a little in the record, but everything was written in a particularly sloppy handwriting, worse even than his own, and most days there wasn't even a visit note. Only nurses’ comments alongside growth metrics and medication logs.
He gathered it was an infant (it was, after all, a male, those indeed were testes), a 29-week preemie who had been in the NICU for two weeks, receiving some TPN (total parenteral nutrition; nutrition through the vein. The 'T' standing for Total - meaning exclusive IV nutrition, although the baby had already started receiving some formula).
And that was it.
Most of the time, the baby had been idling and lying in the incubator between visits, however many of those were conducted.
This was exactly what the on-call physician, Dr. Katya Pavlichuk, was lecturing him about now.
Datner wasn't really listening. He knew the ways of senior neonatologists. She would dump everything at him, regardless. Better to keep quiet and scowl. Healthier for his coronaries.
After a few more seconds (about two hundred, in Datner's estimation, who had begun to develop a slight, involuntary twitch) of a lecture on the essence of life and the fact that the baby had been perfect that morning when she left, Dr. Katya finally got around to asking something. It sounded like a question. Datner wasn't really listening.
Hello, hello, Datner, are you there?!" Katya shrieked.
"Yes, certainly," Datner replied.
He was entertaining thoughts of early retirement. Considering his age (33, well-balanced), his professional status (a pediatric resident in his third out of four years), and his family status (unhappily married with two daughters who were probably very nice, he didn't really know them), these were premature, idle thoughts.
"How is the baby now? Is he ventilated? Does he need inotropes? Did you take cultures? Did you replace the central line? Did you start antibiotics?"
This was roughly what Dr. Katya rattled off. Datner wasn't really sure he cared.
"The baby is fine, easily ventilated, no inotropes, and no antibiotics," he replied, trying to avoid revealing the fact that he had failed to insert a central line and hadn't managed to take more than one blood culture. As for urine and cerebrospinal fluid cultures, forget about it. Let the morning shift do that. They rested all night.
He didn't tell Dr. Katya all of that, of course. She hadn't asked specifically. A small, harmless white lie, in Datner's opinion. She said she would arrive in about two hours (funny, that was the usual time for the morning meeting anyway) and that until then, he should update her if there was anything new. Anything at all.
"Yes, of course," Datner answered in an authoritative tone, his thoughts were far less polite.
***
Dr. Katya Pavlichuk thought life was once more beautiful. When she was a child, still in Moscow, she dreamed of becoming a doctor. A pediatrician. She had always been the best student in school, the best student in medical school. Until she arrived in Israel. Straight to 'Sharona'.
When she arrived in the country, they told her 'Sharona' Hospital was in the Sharon region, as the name suggests. 'Two minutes from Tel Aviv,' they said. That was a crude lie; the drive was at least thirty minutes from Tel Aviv, and that was only if you drove at night, with zero traffic. No less. It wasn't really in the Sharon either; it was more in the Coastal Plain. She wasn't sure, and anyway, there was no one to complain to. But that’s where they assigned her, and she, being the good girl she was, did as she was instructed.
That was over twenty years ago already. Like another lifetime.
She tried to feel like she belonged from the start, but they didn't exactly make it easy.
For the first time in her life, she wasn't the popular success. She would hear them mocking her strange accent behind her back. Funny, in her eyes, the Israelis at 'Sharona' had the diction of Orientals. Mongolians. Descendants of Genghis Khan. Almost Mongoloid, she thought, a word she knew she shouldn’t be using. She remembered someone once told her that Dr. Down was a vicious, consummate racist. He was the one who gave the name 'Mongoloid' to babies with three sets of chromosomes 21 and slanted eyes. A smart fellow. A great racist, like all puffed-up Brits, but smart. He probably had crooked teeth. All smart Brits had crooked teeth. Even the not-so-smart ones. And they were all racists.
Only Dr. Renana treated her nicely, back then, when she first arrived at 'Sharona'. They became better friends. Renana was still sometimes happy then. Until that incident.
Now, as a veteran, Katya had learned to live in 'Sharona'. She no longer tried to excel. Excellence at 'Sharona' meant a death blow. A sign on your back. A mark of Cain.
She got out of bed and walked toward the bathroom. That Datner, she thought to herself. Couldn't he have waited another hour before telling her about a deteriorating baby?!
And why was the baby deteriorating anyway? He was perfectly fine this morning.
She would blame Datner for everything at the morning meeting. That was good for his character development.
The urine flowed relatively easily. In all cases. For Katya, Datner, and the temporarily stabilized preemie.
Relief.
Dr. Katya did not remember to check why the deteriorating baby was not given antibiotic treatment without reason, or what work-up was done to identify the possible infection. It was as if, in the heat of the events, she missed Datner's answer. Too bad; distraction was uncharacteristic of her.
***
Chapter 2  -  A Collection of Amateurs
"A collection of amateurs," I snapped. "Just a bunch of amateurs. Not a single one of them belongs in a professional organization."
The phone rang. It always rings in the bathroom, and always while I’m reading an article about the only soccer team I care about, FC ‘Sharona Sharks.’ A team with no luck; a fan with no luck.
I didn't know who was on the line. I’d replaced too many phones in recent years, and when one of the backups crashed, I just stopped trying to sync contacts. My call log was a graveyard of digits. Most names no longer appeared identified, just numbers, like Holocaust survivors. Those who merited a name, everyone deserves one, after all, were usually labeled as "Blocked," "Do Not Answer," "Do Not Answer 3," or the more recent "Blocked, Do Not Answer Forever. New."
It was Datner. A pleasant enough fellow. I'd known him since he was a young, enthusiastic student. He was a good man, back during his internship. Pediatric residency hadn't done him any favors. His fair hair had receded and turned a premature gray, and his zest for life had almost completely evaporated. He was no longer light-hearted. I’d even known him while he was mourning his mother, and even then, he was more optimistic than he was now.
"Datner, I'm not a consultant for the NICU. Take your madness elsewhere. I had intended to spend the day in glorious, uninterrupted indolence," I shot back before he could even draw breath. Better to set the record straight before the request to claim my soul arrived.
He didn't stop. He was always stubborn. He apologized at length, babbling something incoherent about having been on duty in the NICU three days ago. Now, there were two isolates in a baby’s blood culture. The infectious disease specialist had dismissed it as contamination, but Datner feared it was real. He was truly sorry, he said, but maybe I could take a look?
It sounded like typical nonsense. I told him so. He insisted I come. Even just for five minutes.
I insisted I felt like hell. That was true; I hadn't felt well since the late 1980s. It didn't help. He insisted. The boy was relentless. I told him to shut up and let me drink my coffee, and that I’d be there in fifteen minutes.
"Promise?" he asked. "A sailor's promise, diseased with syphilis," I replied.
He hung up. Slow to take a hint, that one. But a good guy.
***
A few minutes later, I was already nodding my head towards several familiar faces from the past. A gaggle of nurses who I had no idea were still alive. I didn't know any of their names, of course. Except for one, Susan Schell, who stood at the edge of the ward, near the kitchenette. "Is she still alive?" I wondered internally (or perhaps I shouted it, I'm not sure). She hadn't changed much at all. Maybe a wrinkle here, a white hair there, but still the beautiful Susan. An American from hell.
I adopted what I call my 'Dreamy Genius' expression, the one that says 'don't interrupt my profound thoughts' and strode briskly toward the place of the incubator in question, ignoring the astonished gazes of all the occupants. Datner was already standing there, beside the incubator containing a small body and many tubes.
"The little guy doesn't look good, friend," I opened with an immediate taunt.
"Aging fast," the impertinent student replied.
"You were somewhat economical with the truth regarding the patient’s status," I bristled.
"It happened recently, just this morning," Datner tried to defend himself.
A weak, apologetic response. Total surrender.
At this point, I grew tired of the intellectual chess game. More accurately, the easy victory prevented me from feeling any sense of satisfaction, so I decided to get to the point. This way, I would at least significantly cut down on my stay in the NICU, a unit I hadn't tolerated, along with its people, for over sixteen years. I glanced at the patient's chart and even managed to read a few lines before returning to torment Datner. It’s important to arrive prepared for battle; otherwise, there is a danger that the opponent might have a fair chance of success, heaven forbid.
I remember being a young student, not even a resident, when I heard people speaking respectfully about me behind my back. Rumors were circulated about the new genius on the ward, who knew everything during rounds, even before the attending physician. I will reveal the secret of the aforementioned magic to you, even though a proper magician never reveals his secrets. The whole secret lies in arriving half an hour before everyone else, opening all the charts of the new admissions from the night, and memorizing the admission details. Especially numbers of vital signs and selected lab indices. That's it. That’s the whole secret. A little memorization and spurting out the numbers before everyone finishes their coffee, and the title 'genius' is thrown your way without a problem. The art of illusion. The art of the lie.
"So, I see we have a small preemie, ventilated on inotropes, with a borderline pulse and unstable blood pressure, oxygenating with difficulty, and prone to ending his visit on planet Earth. And you say the little prince wasn't like this until your shift?" I fired quickly. That's always my method. Stun them before they regain their composure.
If the fight is fair, there's a good chance you'll lose. After all, I was in enemy territory.
Datner was about to open his mouth when Dr. Katya appeared behind him.
***
"Exactly, Prof. B.S., exactly. Simply appalling. Seventy-two hours ago, this was a completely healthy baby. And now? What a disaster," she almost sobbed. Since when did she get so worked up? I remembered her as a cold fish, not spicy fish stew.
"How are you, dear Dr. Katya?" I mustered my most empathetic tone. I remember not tolerating her 20 years ago, when she first arrived at 'Sharona'. She was already a senior, and I was just a young, clueless resident. This whole meeting felt strange and unwelcome to me.
She didn't answer. She considered making a stinging comment but knew I'd fire back immediately. She gave up. Instead, Datner launched into a speech about cultures. I wasn't listening. There was a medical chart next to the incubator, and I picked it up and saw the problem immediately. I silenced Datner with a finger, and immediately burst forth with the following sentence:
"Gram-positive cocci in chains and Gram-positive bacilli. In the same culture. From the same time. Strange. Definitely strange."
***
"What do you say, Datner? Can you explain to Dr. Pavlichuk and me the possibilities in the differential diagnosis?"
Datner puffed out his chest. It was clear he had prepared for this. He launched into a monologue so long it felt like movie exposition.
"Three big possibilities. All of them are quite strange. First, contamination. The two growths are meaningless. This doesn't explain the child's condition, but it eliminates the need to understand the strange culture result." I smiled; there was an echo of my own words from the past in his reply, it was clear the youth enjoyed quoting me. He continued:
"The second possibility is that only one bacterium is real, and the other is a contaminant. In that case, we need to analyze each possibility regarding each bacterium."
"And the third possibility?" I decided to intervene, even though it was completely unnecessary.
"Both bacteria represent real infections, which are not necessarily related, and may not even have been acquired in the same way, but both led to the child's deterioration." The defense rested.
"I feel almost superfluous here, Datner and Katya. It's clear you've considered all the options. I'm sure you've already discussed the possible identity of the bacteria," I said, injecting a hint of mild insult into my words.
"Of course," Katya shrieked.
That woman needs sedatives; I decreed to myself. I nearly had a heart attack because of her sudden franticness.
"And?" I pressed.
"Datner, tell him," Katya said, with a semblance of quasi-authoritativeness.
It was clear to me that she was afraid of making a mistake, and even more than that, trembling with fear at the possibility that I would correct her.
"The Streptococci are probably GBS," Datner began lecturing, "That's the most common cause of neonatal sepsis, even this late."
"And...?" I continued to press.
"It could also be Enterococcus, though you taught me that without risk factors, it almost never does anything," chirped the visibly unshaven student. This didn't bother me; I had made a point of not arriving clean-shaven at work for over twenty years. I always replied to supervisors' questions about my poor shaving capabilities with the same answer: "When I have time to sleep, I'll shave and maybe even shower." I liked Datner's answer, even though he didn't list every possibility in the world. I decided to let it go and not press the point right now. This was uncharacteristic of me.
"And the second bacterium, Datner?" I continued...

Illinois has released draft rules explaining how a proposed 0.2% tax on digital-asset transactions could apply across several areas of the cryptocurrency market. The guidance addresses stablecoins, decentralized finance platforms, blockchain bridges and transfers made through self-custody wallets. The treatment of DeFi and cross-chain transactions may be particularly important for users and businesses whose activities do not fit traditional exchange-based models. Stablecoin transactions and wallet-to-wallet transfers could also face questions about when a taxable event occurs and which party would bear reporting or payment responsibilities. Because the measure is state-level, its direct effects would be limited to activity subject to Illinois jurisdiction, but the proposal could contribute to broader debate over how governments tax crypto transactions that occur across decentralized networks. Market participants will likely monitor the final language, implementation timetable and any exemptions or compliance obligations introduced during the rulemaking process.

text:
The Guardian drops a bombshell: one of the Fairford suspects called police and led them to the group

The Guardian today published details that recast the security incident around RAF Fairford in western England in the early hours of Sunday. The base, used by the United States as a launch pad for bombers in operations against Iran, became within hours the scene of a major security operation — then a political and security riddle after the five men were released on strict bail.

A call from inside the group

The paper reported that one of the five detained men — a Briton in his twenties living in London — dialled 999 before officers reached the scene. His call was among the information that triggered the armed response, alongside a later alert from a local farmer returning from a night out who saw three vans and masked men near the village.

The first narrative, which framed the episode as a chance discovery after a British farmer spotted the vans and hooded men and called police, now collapses. The new account says one of the suspects himself called emergency services first. The question is no longer only who saw them first. Investigators must now weigh the caller’s intent: to control the scene before patrols arrived, to send a signal inside an unfinished operation, or to confuse the picture after sensing the group had been exposed. Those three possibilities sit at the centre of the inquiry, not at its edge.

Petrol barrels and empty drums

The Guardian said the first officers found several barrels in the three vans. One contained petrol; the others were empty. After extensive examination with military specialists and forensic teams, counter-terrorism police said no improvised explosive devices were found. That finding shifted the case from a suspected imminent bombing to a wider inquiry into intent, context and a possible foreign link.

The vans carried the logo of a fuel-haulage firm that later denied any connection to the vehicles or the men. The suspects are British nationals aged 23 to 25; four live in Westminster and one in Camden.

Washington accuses, Tehran denies, London holds back

President Donald Trump criticised the bail decision, saying he “wouldn’t have done that,” and hinted at an Iran link without detail. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called it “a very serious threat” and said the case “clearly involves the hand of a foreign actor,” tying it to Iranian threats against US interests. Washington offered no public evidence.

Iran’s embassy in London rejected “unfounded and malicious speculation.” British authorities have not officially confirmed a foreign link. Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said the response followed “a range of information”

text:
Talks between the U.S. and Iran have hit a dead end, pushing both sides right back to the brink of direct military conflict. A push by Qatari mediators to hammer out a compromise between Washington and Tehran went nowhere, with neither side willing to give an inch.

The real show was playing out behind the scenes at the White House. On Monday morning, U.S. officials were cheerfully leaking to reporters that the talks were constructive, hinting that Iran was ready to budge on its nuclear program and that Trump was open to easing sanctions and unfreezing assets. Just hours later, while the Qatari delegation was still in Washington meeting with Jared Kushner and Vice President JD Vance, Trump hopped on Truth Social and blew it all up, posting that he hadn’t offered Tehran a thing.

The core sticking points haven't moved. The Iranians flat-out refuse to scale back their nuclear program until the U.S. lifts its naval blockade and honors the June memorandum of understanding. Meanwhile, Washington thinks the pressure campaign is working and Tehran will fold on its own, so they see zero reason to compromise. In response, Mohsen Rezaei, the head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, called Trump out, saying he’s trapped in a quagmire where he can neither negotiate nor fight.

The diplomatic window is slamming shut fast, and regional mediators are getting visibly fed up with both sides digging in. If nothing gives, signs point to the White House potentially pulling the trigger on a major military operation right after the midterms.

text:
IRGC’S OPEN LETTER TO AMERICANS: CUT ISRAEL LOOSE OR KEEP THE WAR  

On Tuesday, IRGC spokesman Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi did not address the White House. He addressed American scholars, students, journalists, and taxpayers. The letter’s offer is simple and brutal: Americans can live peacefully with Iran if they separate themselves from Israel. Everything else is an argument that Washington already lost the war it started.

WHO THE LETTER IS FOR  
➡️ Mohebbi salutes “the honorable people of the United States” and says the first casualty of America’s wars is always the truth.  
➡️ The Qur’an line he opens with is the whole pitch: God does not change a people’s condition until they change it themselves.  
➡️ The demand at the end is not a ceasefire memo. It is political: occupiers of Palestine leave, America distances itself from Israel, then coexistence becomes possible.

THE VICTORY CLAIM  
➡️ The letter dates the war to February 28, 2026 and calls it unprovoked.  
➡️ It accuses the United States of striking an elementary school in Minab and of killing Iran’s Supreme Leader plus members of his family, including a 14-month-old granddaughter.  
➡️ It puts Iranian dead at more than 3,600, “the vast majority” civilians, including 400 children, and lists eight universities, three hospitals, and eight schools as bombed.  

THIRTEEN AIMS, NO FINISH LINE  
➡️ Mohebbi’s test of victory is crude: who achieved their objectives?  
➡️ He says the first U.S.-Israeli aims were regime change and partition. After those failed, the list kept changing.  
➡️ The letter counts thirteen later targets: unconditional surrender, Kharg Island, occupation, Stone Age energy destruction, seizing Hormuz, a 20 percent toll, wiping missiles and drones, ending support for regional resistance.  
➡️ “Thousands of bombs,” it says, and still no declared objective secured. That is the humiliation thesis.

HORMUZ AND THE FLEET  
➡️ The strategic boast sits here: Iran claims it now holds operational control of the Strait of Hormuz.  
➡️ American warships, the letter says, were forced into the Indian Ocean. Not one U.S. vessel can dock at Fifth Fleet in Bahrain.  
➡️ It claims more than 200 strategic drones, 12 tanker and transport aircraft, 30 fighters, at least one AWACS, dozens of helicopters, and 18 bases reduced “to nearly zero.”  
➡️ Again: this is the Guards writing their own scoreboard. The point they want Americans to hear is reputational. The superpower look is gone.

WHAT “DEATH TO AMERICA” MEANS  
➡️ Mohebbi insists the chant is not hatred of the American people.  
➡️ He calls both nations victims of the same White House elite and “Zionist capitalists,” and says Iranians decided to fight that elite while Americans still finance it.  
➡️ Shared-pain list: 4% of world population and 20% of its prisoners; 1,300 Americans shot by police a year; billions in aid to Israel while poverty and a $40 trillion debt pile up at home.  
➡️ “Death to America,” in this telling, is a prayer against the ruling class, not against the taxpayer who pays for the missiles.

HOW THEY SAY THE WAR ENDS  
➡️ Force the government off Israel. Shut useless overseas bases. Stop the aid pipeline. Choose leaders who can pass a basic honesty test.  
➡️ If not, the letter warns of a regional fire and an economic earthquake that hits ordinary Americans first.  
➡️ The closer is religious and political at once: Palestine liberated, Mahdi and Christ with the oppressed — and a hope that Americans stand on that side.

text:
Privacy coins: OGs vs. Emerging tokens.

Things start with the new ATH of $ZEC, up roughly 2,496% over the past year. On Sep 22, ZEC crossed $1,600 for the first time. Driven factors are:

- Grayscale's spot Zcash ETF (ZCSH) launched Aug 25, 2026, and had pulled in over $463M by early Sep
- A long-pending SEC investigation into Zcash closed
- A Europe-listed spot ETP followed shortly after on Euronext Paris and Amsterdam

Over the time, the term privacy is now getting much clear - hiding the DeFi info including wallet address, token balance and transaction details.

In this post, let's compare the OG privacy coins like $ZEC and the new emerging privacy builds.

1. OG teams

- $XMR @monero: privacy is mandatory and default on every transaction; core tech include Ring signatures, stealth addresses, and RingCT

- $ZEC @Zcash: the only privacy coin with a US spot ETF, using zk-SNARKs with an "opt-in" model proving that selective disclosure was the right long-term bet

- $DASH @Dashpay: originally forked from Bitcoin, now more into payment than privacy which is a pratical usecase that most privacy protocols don't have

- $ZEN @horizenglobal: a zk-SNARK-based privacy chain that developed enterprise Web3 infrastructure and sidechains

2. Emerging teams

- $AZTEC @aztecnetwork: a privacy-focused zk-rollup built on Ethereum, privatizing arbitrary smart contract logic for deeper DeFi usecases like swap, lending and more

- $ALEO @AleoHQ: a Layer-1 built specifically for privacy-preserving general computation, using LEO language to let developers make inputs, computation, and outputs selectively private while still verifiable on-chain

- $ZAMA @zama: built on Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE), allowing computation to run directly on encrypted data; FHE theoretically offers stronger guarantees than zk-based

- $RAIL @RAILGUN_Project: a privacy middleware layered on top of Ethereum and other EVMs, using zk-SNARKs, built with compliance-adjacent design from the start

Which ones do I miss?

text:
The Plastic Chair 🪑

Let me tell you a story about a chair 🪑. It was a plastic one, in a circle of other plastic chairs, in a rehab clinic back home in England. A chair that saved my life... and this is how I got to it.

Some may find this self-indulgent. I get it... stop reading. But for me it is cathartic, so I don't care. All those times sitting in that plastic chair 🪑 taught me to talk about my story as much and as often as possible, because it is the talking that keeps me living.

Plenty of people have overcome far more than me. I fell into a deep hole through my choices and my decisions, and I own every one of them.

Today I'm a very different person than I was 20 odd years ago. I can confidently boast that I'm way nicer, more honest and caring now than I ever was then. Because, before 2005, which is the year my life started to improve, the year I first sat in that plastic chair 🪑... I was selfish, deceitful, and immoral.

As a kid I guess you would call me just "naughty" but by the time I was a teenager I was a total fucking nightmare. Smoking, drinking and taking drugs were my way of hiding the trauma I'd experienced (another story). I was forever getting into trouble and being punished: whether it was being kicked out of school, being flogged with canes and shoes by teachers (it was allowed in those days) or having the police come to my mum's house to pick me up.

When I was twenty, I found myself living in Bali making tie dye shorts and dresses for a friend's clothing company. Life started looking up. I remember, several weeks after arriving….on a cloudless June afternoon, standing knee deep in the sea with my hands outstretched like a preacher, looking out towards the bobbing boats on the horizon and shouting in utter joy: "Yes! This is the fucking life".

For the first few years I gorged on all Bali had to offer. I fell in love several times; and worked and partied with equal vigour. I had a lot to forget, and for a few years I actually believed that I had moved on and could live a rich and carefree life. For a while the partying was a lot of fun, it was innocent in a way but ultimately, it turned to misery. I was proof to the theory of how "one drug leads to another." Alcohol to ecstasy and LSD, to cocaine, crack, and finally my drug....my love: heroin.

I guess I was born without an "off switch" which if directed with care and forethought can be a positive attribute for some people. But for me it was a disaster. I hated it when the party was over or when the normal people went to bed. I would be depressed when the last line of coke was sniffed, or when there was no more ecstasy....it confused me and made me deeply sad. Heroin absolutely helped, it was like a friend that would comfort me.

Eventually my life in the paradise of Bali consisted of the pain, danger, and boredom of heroin addiction and the depressing monotony of endlessly trying to quit. A feeble attempt at suicide, friends dying, police drug raids and arrests and imminent jail all passed over me with little feeling and less worry. I would wake up in bed each morning with fear and anxiety as my two constant companions. I was a junky, the normal kind, the boring kind….penniless, lonely, and dull. Every day my first thoughts and energy were focused on one single-minded endeavour: finding money and buying some heroin so that I could function for the next few hours until the dreaded withdrawals started…then it was time to look for more. It was that simple and that depressing.

If I had no money I would sell my clothes, or I would beg, or cheat. I became an expert at deceit. I had no "life". I would find myself waking up on sidewalks outside bars at five in the morning, or on the floor of closed nightclubs with the cleaners sweeping around me. The white tiles around my toilet bowl were as much a place to sleep as my bed.

I thought perhaps that if I left Bali all would be fine – but then I found that it made no difference: I ran from police in Madrid, blacked out in Ecuador, got arrested in Paris and woke up stoned and drunk in a park in Singapore at dawn. It was not Bali that was the problem, it was me. I hated my life, I was dying. I desperately wanted to be clean. I wanted to be normal.

I went to rehabs but always only lasted a few weeks before running back to my dealers. I thought a girlfriend would help, after all love conquers all right? Wrong, when you are incapable of loving yourself then nobody can help you. I locked myself in rooms doing cold turkey, I tried meditation, methadone, everything….all potions, nothing worked. I felt I was irredeemable, a fucking mess forever, a desperate case.

But for some brief, rare moments I had an inkling that I could beat it. Hope was rare but I did glimpse it, fleetingly at times.

Finally, I entered what would be my final drug rehab with the belief that it was my last chance. I was extremely ill and after the compulsory medical at the clinic the doctor told me that I was dangerously malnourished. Some members of my family suggested that I should not bother going to rehab because I would be dead in a year anyway. Understandably they had given up on me and my few steadfast friends were wondering if I would ever sort myself out. This is when I first found that plastic chair 🪑, and weeks later, having endured endless group sessions, therapy and counselling, I left rehab clean and frightened with a commitment to finally do what was suggested, to finally listen to other people….They called it surrender; I called it the last of my nine lives.

I met my wife soon after leaving rehab and she was the rock I needed during those first couple of years back in the real world. A few years later we married and built a beautiful family.

Most of the friends and acquaintances I took heroin with in Bali back in the day did not make it; only a few of us have survived 😢. I was just so fortunate...so fucking lucky... They were put in jail and never came out. They were killed, committed suicide, overdosed or died of AIDS.

I'm not a religious man at all but the phrase: "There but for the grace of God go I" certainly helps to explain the humility I feel.

So that's my chair 🪑. A plastic one in a rehab clinic in England. I sat in it for weeks and it saved my life. My friends in Bali never got theirs. Their chairs are empty. I haven't had a drink or a drug since 2005.

text:
A NEAR-FUTURE AI-INDUCED UTOPIA?

by Bill Kochman   09-30-2026

Ha! These AI advocates claim that comfort,  material wealth and good health will soon be available for everyone, even for the working class, the poor and the downtrodden, without exception.

My friends, do any of you honestly believe that nonsense?

Promises, promises, promises! So many of these AI-promoting CEOs are pushing this very same line in the news, in online videos, in podcast interviews, on the social networks, etc.

But I guess Sam Altman of OpenAI is at least being a little bit honest by admitting that the near-future, AI-dominated world will be a global slave state with very little privacy. And, of course, there are other top-tier AI figures — such as Elon Musk and Dario Amodei — who are also warning that AI labs and engineers are ALREADY losing control of their creations. And yet they keep creating the stuff anyway!

But honestly speaking, my friends, isn’t the world already that way right now? In other words, divided between the haves and the have-nots where the have-nots serve the elite, and in many instances can barely survive on what they are paid?

These AI wishful thinkers sound like politicians who promise us the Moon in order to secure our vote, and then they backtrack on every single campaign promise they ever made.

The elite of this present world — including the very rich technocrats whose companies already earn billions of dollars — are motivated by money, profit, greed and an insatiable lust for more power. And yet they try to cloak it in altruism.

Anyone who believes these empty, pie-in-the-sky platitudes regarding a wonderful future world filled with comfort and ease for everyone where you no longer have to work anymore, is both naive and foolish. Please stop drinking the Kool-Aid!

Tell me something. Have the powerful and the elite ever shared their wealth with the poor? A few do, yes, but most of them don’t. They live their lives of luxury while we struggle.

And you think that they are going to suddenly start sharing their wealth now because of the advent of AI? Again, please wake up!

Sorry folks. Call me a pessimist if you like, but I will believe it when I see it, if I even live that long. I think I am just being a realist.

All of this current AI-related bogus altruism that is being put on display by the AI CEOs is a deception.

I honestly do not believe that we common people will ever be full recipients of the benefits which may possibly be derived from the advancements which are made due to AI. The elite will hoard such benefits to themselves, just as they do now.

BTW, there was a dude in Matthew chapter 4 who offered Jesus everything that the world had to offer, in exchange for total subservience to him. You know, “Just bow down and worship me. It is a small price to pay compared to everything I can give you.” Well, we know how that particular story went.

"And the devil, taking him up into an high mountain, shewed unto him all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time. And the devil said unto him, All this power will I give thee, and the glory of them: for that is delivered unto me; and to whomsoever I will I give it."
Luke 4:5-6, KJV

"Lest Satan should get an advantage of us: for we are not ignorant of his devices."
2 Corinthians 2:11, KJV

"For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? Or what shall a man give in exchange for his soul?"
Mark 8:36-37, KJV

BTW, to date, I have written 10 articles and series regarding Artificial Intelligence, AI-based chatbots, etc., both the good, the bad and the ugly.

If you don’t fully understand AI technology yet, and how it actually works under the hood, please visit the Bill’s Bible Basics website. Just google it. I explain all of it in easy-to-understand terms for the non-technical layman. Thanks!

🎥 | The #Manipur government on Wednesday paid tribute to Jana Neta Hijam Irabot on his 130th birth anniversary at a state function held at Irawat Square, Thangmeiband Lilashing Khongnangkhong in Imphal West.

Chief Minister Yumnam Khemchand led the commemorative ceremony and offered floral tributes to the revered leader.

The occasion recalled Irabot’s contributions to society and his enduring legacy of public service, social justice and commitment to the welfare of ordinary people.

His contributions to the cause of peasants and working people, social equality and communal harmony were also remembered.

In his message, Khemchand described Irabot as an enduring symbol of social justice and public service. He said the leader’s historic contributions and ideals continued to remain relevant for generations.

The Chief Minister called upon the people to reaffirm their collective resolve to uphold Irabot’s ideals and work towards building a peaceful, united and progressive Manipur.

He paid heartfelt tribute to Irabot, describing him as a great son of Manipur.

text:
No enemies but the Zeitgeist which has gone dark. 

 Mr Cogito’s Monster 

Zbigniew Herbert

1

The lucky Saint George
could judge the dragon’s
strength and movements
from his knightly saddle

strategy’s first principle
size up the enemy well

Mr Cogito’s position
is less advantageous

he’s seated in the low
saddle of the valley
wrapped in thick fog

in the fog you can’t make out
the burning eyes
the greedy claws
the maw

in the fog
you see only
the flickering of nothingness

Mr Cogito’s monster
lacks all dimensions

it’s hard to describe
it eludes definitions

it’s like a vast depression
hanging over the country

it can’t be pierced
by a pen
an argument
a spear

if not for its stifling weight
and the death it sends
you might conclude
that it was a phantom
a disease of the imagination

but it’s there
it’s there all right

it fills crannies of houses
temples bazaars like gas

it poisons the wells
destroys a mind’s constructs
covers the bread with mold

proof the monster exists
is offered by its victims

indirect proof
but sufficient

2

the sensible say
you can coexist
with the monster

just try to avoid
violent gestures
violent speech
when threatened
take on the form
of a stone or leaf

obey wise Nature
who urges mimicry

breathe shallowly
play we’re not here

Mr Cogito however
dislikes living as-if

he’d like to fight
the monster
on solid ground

so he goes out at dawn
to the sleeping suburbs
intrepidly fitted out
with a long sharp object

he calls to the monster
through empty streets

he insults the monster
provokes the monster

like the daredevil scout
of a non-existent army

he calls—come out you dirty coward
through the fog
you see only
the huge mug of nothingness

Mr Cogito wants to
join the unequal fray

this should happen
as soon as possible

before he is felled
by powerlessness
common death without glory
suffocation by shapelessness

text:
Cormorants: convenient scapegoats for Ireland’s salmon crisis

The Great Cormorant (Phalacrocorax carbo) is a much misunderstood bird which has been persecuted for centuries - just because it eats fish. These stunning and vulnerable birds are currently subject to hate campaigns by fishing groups calling for culls. However, there is no scientific evidence that culls would solve conflicts or replenish fish stocks. We need to stop blaming natural predators and address the real problems facing our aquatic ecosystems. 

Cormorants are native to Ireland, and their presence on rivers and lakes is entirely normal. It is a myth that they are a non-native invasive species that should not be here. The Irish names for cormorant are Broigheall or Cailleach dhubh. These birds have shared our rivers and lakes with salmon long before humans began managing them as fisheries. Both subspecies that occur in Ireland (P. c. carbo and P. c. sinensis) are native. 

These protected birds are part of our coastal and freshwater ecosystems, with as much right to inhabit a river as the salmon swimming beneath them.

The idea that cormorants are seabirds that have invaded freshwater because the sea has run out of fish is also a myth. They naturally use both environments and are more accurately described as waterbirds. Cormorants were intensively persecuted in the past, while pesticide pollution further damaged their populations. Legal protection and reduced pesticide contamination allowed depleted populations to recover from the 1970s onwards. Recovery is a conservation success, not evidence that a native species has become an invader. 

Cormorants do indeed eat fish, including young salmon. But seeing a bird swallow a fish does not establish that it is driving a population decline. Predation is a natural and ecologically important process alongside which salmon have evolved. 

Native predators like cormorants are not a key factor in the decline of salmon populations. The major pressures on salmon include deteriorating water quality, habitat loss and degradation, dams and other barriers, salmon farming, and changing conditions in the North Atlantic. Overfishing has also contributed historically, and salmon bycatch in other fisheries remains a problem. 

However, it is easier to blame cormorants than to address the real issues. They are conspicuous, their feeding is visible, and killing them offers a tangible action. Addressing sewage discharges, reducing agricultural runoff, removing dams, and confronting aquaculture interests are far more challenging. A dead bird can be presented as progress while the conditions responsible for declining fish populations remain unchanged.
 
Predation can matter locally, particularly where fish are concentrated, for example below a weir or dam. But this is a fish passage issue, and the solution should be restoring fish passage. When we channelise our rivers and remove all the riparian trees, then stock these rivers with hatchery-reared fish, we should expect problems from predators. The solution here is river restoration. 

The hostility and prejudice against cormorants have deep roots, and they have been unfairly hated for centuries. Milton used the cormorant to symbolise ultimate deception and malice when Satan disguises himself as a cormorant to sneak into the Garden of Eden. Even today, some anglers still refer to them as the “black death” and the “devil bird” and consider them to be key cause of the decline of fish like salmon in our rivers. But these claims are not supported by science, and cormorants can actually bring ecological benefits including controlling non-native invasive fish species. 

The fact that cormorants nearly went extinct in the mid-20th century should remind us how vulnerable they are. Their restricted breeding distribution makes them particularly vulnerable to persecution. Culling cormorants will not clean polluted water, restore damaged habitats, or remove the dams blocking salmon migration. Reducing cormorant numbers is not a practical or sustainable option, and it will not solve local conflicts or replenish fish stocks. 

A river is an ecosystem, not simply a supply of fish for people to catch. Native predators are part of its food web, and their right to exist should not depend on whether anglers welcome them.

Protecting salmon means restoring the conditions that allow wild populations to thrive alongside their natural predators. Every debate that ends with blaming cormorants, while leaving those conditions unaddressed, lets the real causes of decline off the hook.

On March 30, 1976, two young women, Sally Ivester and Barbara Savage, were with two men inside a motel room in North Miami Beach, Florida. The men, William Lee Thompson and Rocco James Surace, demanded the girls to call home and get some money to pay them. Although Savage got the amount of money she offered to pay to the men, Ivester only got $25, which fell short of the $200 to $300 she promised to pay. This incurred the anger of both men.[6][7]

In a fit of rage, Surace removed his chain belt and began beating Ivester. Thompson joined in the assault and used the belt to further beat and torture Ivester. Ivester was sexually assaulted by the pair, who used a chair leg to penetrate Ivester's vagina, which caused tearing to the inner vagina wall and internal bleeding. The men repeated the process of beating with other objects such as a night stick. The pair forced the victim to eat her sanitary napkin and lick spilled beer off the floor, and they burned her with lit cigarettes and lighters.[8][7]

Halfway through the brutal assault, Ivester was taken to a phone booth by Thompson, who instructed her to call her mother and ask for more money. During the phone call, Ivester's mother noticed that her daughter's voice sounded strange, as if it carried a "death rattle". Before ending her call, Ivester told her mother, "I'm all right. I'm all right. I'm going to be all right."[8][9] Afterwards, both Thompson and Surace continued beating and torturing Ivester, who died of multiple injuries and internal bleeding. Throughout the whole process, Savage witnessed her friend being beaten and killed by the two men, but she did not intervene due to her fear that the men would do the same to her if she tried to escape the motel room.[8][7]

Thomas Mapfumo, the legendary music "Lion of Zimbabwe", spent decades as the unyielding voice of the oppressed. 
His Chimurenga music was the soundtrack to a revolution, fiercely defying Ian Smith’s colonial government and later, after supporting Zanu PF before and after Independence, exposing the damaging effects of leadership failure and corruption of Robert Mugabe's regime. 
Mapfumo’s critical post-independence music targeted systemic corruption, economic mismanagement, and political repression under Zanu PF and Mugabe, and later President Emmerson Mnangagwa.
Mapfumo hit the Mugabe regime with many greats hits, including Corruption, Mamvemve (tatters), Disaster, Marimanzara (you have spawned hunger) and Varombo kuvarombo/Ndiani waparadza musha/Musatambe nenyika (poverty, you have ruined the nation).
Corruption, released in 1989, denounces greed, elite self-enrichment, and dishonest leaders.
Released in 1999/2000 on the album Chimurenga Explosion by Thomas Mapfumo and The Blacks Unlimited, Mamvemve is a sharp political and social critique of the Zanu PF government under Mugabe, bemoaning how the prosperous country people fought for during the liberation struggle has been reduced to a crumbling shell and ruins - a travesty.
Due to its harsh honesty regarding economic decline, corruption, and mismanagement, the song was banned on state-controlled national television and radio in Zimbabwe.
Disaster highlights the grim living conditions, suffering of the masses, and the erosion of the rule of law.
Serves as a direct call-out to the ruling elite to open their eyes to the plight and poverty of ordinary citizens.
Varombo kuvarombo/Ndiani waparadza musha/Musatambe nenyika critiques broken promises of post-independence socio-economic transformation and unequal resource distribution.
His later music underlined and criticised Zanu PF and Mugabe's unmitigated failures.
Mapfumo initially supported Zanu during the liberation struggle, but he grew disillusioned after independence as the party moved away from ota promises, ubuntu ethics and failed to uplift the working class.
His hard-hitting lyrics led to state radio bans, harassment, and property seizures, ultimately prompting him to relocate to the United States in 2000 when the economy collapsed after the chaotic and violent land reforms.
Even from exile and following subsequent leadership changes, Mapfumo has continued to speak out against ongoing repression, corruption, poor governance, and looting.
For years, Mapfumo chose exile, poverty, and artistic activism over silence, embodying the ultimate symbol of an unpurchasable artist. 
Yet, a controversial late-career return to Zimbabwe and sudden, uncharacteristic pivots towards the ruling establishment shocked his loyal fan base, serving as a sobering reminder that every man— no matter how revolutionary —has a price, whether paid in currency, comfort, or the desperate longing for home.
For more than two decades, Mapfumo lived in Oregon, United States, far from the collapse, chaos and electric energy of Harare. 
In exile, the financial realities of an aging independent artist hit hard. The massive stadium crowds of his youth were replaced by small diaspora venues. 
Back home, a new generation of musicians had taken over the airwaves.
Then came the twilight years. Aging, facing mounting financial pressures, and deeply homesick, the Lion grew tired of the cold Pacific Northwest. 
Behind closed doors, emissaries from the very ruling party he had vilified for 30 years made approaches. 
Initially, he refused.
But later they offered him what he could not resist: a triumphant return, cleared legal hurdles, state reception, and a massive financial payout - US$1 million - for some performances.
When Mapfumo stepped off a flight in Harare yesterday, he was not greeted by thousands of fans, but by state escorts, including ministers - clearly captured.
