text:
Podcast Summary | Armchair Expert with Dax Shepard: Jared Diamond Returns (on the science of leadership)

Overview
Jared Diamond returns with a framework for when individual leaders actually change history, and when broader forces swamp them. The core answer is conditional: it depends. Leaders matter most when they combine discretion, the formal power to decide, with timing, the moment when their actions can have outsized impact. Diamond applies this across politics, business, sports, and religion, using natural experiments and counterfactuals like the Hamlet test to separate genuine individual impact from luck, circumstance, and structural forces.

Key Themes
- History is not a contest between "great men" and impersonal forces; the real question is when and why individual leaders matter, and the answer is conditional.
- Discretion is formal decision power, and it varies enormously by role, from mayors and governors to presidents, dictators, and regulated utility CEOs.
- Timing is partly chosen, partly recognized, and partly accidental, which is why some leaders seize a moment and others simply happen to be standing in it.
- The Hamlet test asks whether anyone else could plausibly have produced the same outcome; it works in small, well-documented cases and breaks down in huge populations.
- Natural experiments, such as studying outcomes after leaders die, offer a way to estimate individual impact when controlled experiments are impossible.
- Great leaders often fail the Hamlet test while still putting a distinctive stamp on an industry or country, achieving what others could have achieved but in their own way.
- CEOs and coaches account for roughly one-third of outcomes, with the company, the industry, and the specific year accounting for the rest.
- Charisma is necessary but not sufficient to found a world religion; a movement also needs an organizer and sometimes a military figure.
- In democracies, voters routinely credit or blame presidents for economic conditions that presidents largely cannot control.

Detailed Summary
The book's premise is not to settle whether leaders or broader forces determine history. It is to ask when and why individual leaders matter at all. The answer is conditional. Leadership expresses itself through six factors, including timing and place, discretion, founder status, and whether a leader can persuade the public to do what it initially does not want to do. Guns, Germs, and Steel addressed why Europeans conquered much of the world, concluding that geography mattered more than great men. The new book turns to leaders across politics, history, sports, religion, and business to test where that conclusion holds and where it breaks.

Timing is partly chosen, partly recognized, and partly accidental. Bill Gates had said the time was not right for personal computing, then saw a January 1976 Popular Electronics cover and decided the moment had arrived with Paul Allen. Winston Churchill wrote in The Gathering Storm that becoming prime minister was the moment his life had been pointing toward. He did not cause Germany's invasion of France, but that invasion led to Chamberlain's resignation and Churchill's rise. Mark Zuckerberg, born in 1984 and a Harvard sophomore in 2004, was at the right time and place for founding a major social media company without necessarily knowing it.

Discretion is the formal power to make decisions, and it differs sharply by role. Mayors have less decision power than governors, governors less than presidents, and democratic presidents less than dictators. Democratic presidents have more power in wartime than peacetime. Public utility CEOs are tightly regulated and have little power, while CEOs of perfume companies and teenage T-shirt companies have greater freedom to respond to trends. College coaches generally have more discretion than professional coaches because pro players, owners, and general managers hold more power and continuity. Founders, whether of countries like George Washington and Lee Kuan Yew or of businesses, tend to have more discretion than successors.

The Hamlet test is a rare situation where one can plausibly identify whether anyone else could have done the same thing. Shakespeare had already written Romeo and Juliet and Julius Caesar and commanded the best London theater company and theater. Only about two dozen outstanding Elizabethan dramatists are known, and none wrote plays as good as Hamlet, so the comparison is tractable. With Jeff Bezos and Amazon, it is impossible to name all 340 million Americans who might have done what he did. The test is easier to apply in small, well-documented cases than in huge populations.

Hitler's chauffeur anecdote raises the role of contingency. In 1930, years before Hitler became chancellor, a speeding truck seemed about to hit his car; the chauffeur floored it and narrowly avoided what might have killed him. Biographers generally conclude Hitler made a difference because of his extreme anti-Semitism, his charisma, and his skill as a deceiver of Chamberlain, German industrialists, generals, and fellow Nazis. A.J.P. Taylor, perhaps the best-known British historian of the postwar period, concluded Hitler was a normal German politician who did what any German politician would have done.

Natural experiments offer a method for studying individual impact when controlled experiments are impossible or unethical. One compares outcomes after 47 prime ministers died natural deaths versus about 200 who did not. For CEOs, the death of a spouse or only child is linked to a large drop in earnings, sibling death also lowers earnings, and parent death lowers earnings less. Mother-in-law death is the only death associated with an earnings increase, but the sample is small, the effect is small, and it is not quite statistically significant. A Denmark dataset of 76,000 businesses showed earnings dropping roughly 13 percent within two years of a CEO's death. Across factors, the year accounts for only 1 to 6 percent of company earnings, while the company, the industry, and the CEO each account for roughly one-third.

FDR recognized the U.S. needed to prepare for war while the public did not want to, and gradually nudged the government in that direction. Charles de Gaulle got the French to leave Algeria in 1958 despite public reluctance, using shifting conditions around terrorist acts to move toward withdrawal. Clement Attlee produced the biggest change in British social policy in the 20th century but remained less famous than Churchill because he had about five skilled cabinet colleagues who shared the glory. Botswana began independence as a small colony of one million people with only 22 college graduates and seven miles of paved road. Seretse Khama, chief of the most powerful tribe, was the only chief who could abolish chiefly power, and diamonds were found on his tribe's land, allowing him to treat them as national treasures.

Kwame Nkrumah, first president of a new, poor nation, kept experienced British administrators, granted mineral rights to the people after diamonds were discovered, and had unusually high discretion. Rachel Carson wrote Silent Spring, described as one of the two science books in the last 170 years with the biggest impact on the world, alongside Darwin's Origin of Species. Carson was a scientist and a poet-like writer who read her prose aloud. Academics writing for the public faced the belief that they were washed up or prostituting themselves; the speaker says UCLA denied a promotion when he won the Pulitzer Prize.

Pomegranates were domesticated around 4,000 BC, but there was no U.S. pomegranate juice industry until 2002. The juice requires a three-story press to grind hard rind and fruit. Of 22 pomegranate farmers in California, 21 were ordinary poor farmers. Linda Resnick's husband bought central valley acreage and discovered 125 pomegranate trees. Linda Resnick invested 150 million dollars in researching medical value and launched the industry in 2002. Coca-Cola and Nestle then started producing what the notes call fake pomegranate juice, leading to another 120 million dollars in lawsuits up to the Supreme Court. The Resnicks passed the Hamlet test because they controlled half of U.S. pomegranate juice production, had their own money rather than a public stock company, and could lose money for 18 years before turning a profit.

Of 22 modern political leaders surveyed, only two retired voluntarily: Nelson Mandela and Lee Kuan Yew. The other 20 died, were assassinated, or were voted out. Business leaders Bezos, Zuckerberg, Gates, and Musk did not pass the Hamlet test. Yet they at minimum put their stamp on how their industries operated. Sears, Kmart, and Walmart operated differently from Amazon's online model. Great leaders often fail the Hamlet test while still achieving things others could have achieved, just in their own way. John Wooden, possibly the greatest coach in American sports history, won 10 national championships at UCLA and was credited with helping make basketball a major sport. His practices were intentionally faster than games, running two and a half to three hours with repeated instructions to run it again, faster. He taught players even how to roll up their socks. UCLA beat Duke despite averaging 6 feet 4 inches versus Duke's 6 feet 8 inches because UCLA players could jump higher. Wooden adapted to star players like Kareem Abdul-Jabbar rather than forcing his system on them, and after a losing season around his 14th year he re-examined what went wrong rather than blaming players.

Coaches and CEOs are estimated to make roughly a 30 percent difference to outcomes. Firing poorly performing coaches produces roughly the same improvement as retaining them, suggesting coach impact is closer to dice-throwing than skill. UCLA's athletic department is 155 million dollars in debt from repeatedly firing basketball coaches, and all UCLA basketball coaches since Wooden had winning records of about 65 to 70 percent. UCLA's football and basketball coaches were the highest or second-highest paid employees of the state of California, while the chancellor earns about one-tenth of their salaries. Alabama pays its coach three times what UCLA pays its coach and invests heavily in football, while UCLA has a better basketball arena and USC better football practice facilities, correlating with each school's strength. Four new religions in the last 200 years spread worldwide, all American: Mormonism, Seventh Day Adventists, Jehovah's Witnesses, and Christian Science, attributed to U.S. economic and military power. Every Mormon man is required to spend two years on a mission at age 18, aiding global spread.

Charisma is the only route to religious leadership, unlike politics where non-charismatic figures like Pinochet in Chile led through fear. Religions need charisma, or they go nowhere, plus a great organizer, and sometimes an army or general. St. Paul organized Christianity. Muhammad and the Mahdi of Sudan fulfilled all three roles. Brigham Young organized Mormonism after Joseph Smith's death, building infrastructure, mission, capital, and resources; without Young, Mormonism might not exist. Jim Jones illustrates the cult trajectory: a charismatic leader and outstanding organizer with a positive early side, including a large role in integrating Indianapolis and leading a movement to desegregate the city, but also negative sides including sexual predation, economic dishonesty, drug abuse, and ultimately driving his group to suicide at Jonestown, which was well protected militarily and well armed.

A natural-experiment database on leader deaths shows average economic effects roughly cancel out: about half of economies improve and half worsen after a leader dies. The database compares 83 heads of state assassinated since World War II with 140 who died of cancer and heart disease. When Mao and Mozambique's founding leader died, the economy got better. If a dictator dies during wartime, the war is more likely to end, because a wartime dictator faces likely death if he loses. Leaders matter through discretion plus timing, and good ideas can be ignored if the world is not ready.

Alfred Wegener, a German climatologist, postulated continental drift based on the fit of South America and Africa. He could not identify a working mechanism, suggested Earth's rotation, and died on a Greenland expedition in 1930. Continental drift was proven in the 1960s by seafloor spreading magnetic reversals and discovery of magma upwelling; a Harvard colleague in 1962 was first to see magma bubbling up along these lines with deep underwater vehicles. Mendel published his genetics paper in 1868, had it right, but was ignored until 1900, when three scientists independently rediscovered his work. The author declined to evaluate Trump or Angela Merkel because he only assesses leaders whose careers have ended. Merkel's decision to admit one or two million refugees into Germany was initially praised but is now viewed as pragmatically harmful for Germany, contributing to a rising far-right party.

Business schools justify 60,000 to 100,000 dollar tuition by claiming to teach CEO success through charisma, but there are many paths to success: mastering detail, terrifying people, being a good discussion leader, and picking good followers. Dictators' downfall is lack of feedback. The speaker ran a UCLA physiology lab for 40 years doing manipulative experiments on gallbladder and intestine with about five students, who corrected him when out of date. He was a Harvard postdoc from 1962 to 1966, during the time continental drift was proven. He turns 89 tomorrow and is a year and a day from 90. He won a MacArthur Foundation prize, and the foundation was reportedly disappointed he would continue studying gallbladder.

Diamond argues that in politics, especially in the U.S. and most democracies, people exaggerate how much a single leader, even a prime minister or president, can change the country. It is hard for a president to change the economy, harder for a governor, and hardest for a mayor. Voters credit or blame presidents for economic conditions even though presidents have limited control. External events, such as taking office on the day a global pandemic is announced, can sharply limit how effective one leader can be. The book is titled Prophets, Coaches, and Kings: When Do Leaders Matter. Diamond compliments the interviewers for doing their homework, expressing themselves vividly, understanding the matters, and asking good questions.

Look under the hood.
What the clip does not say is the size of the file Ottawa is playing with.
Bilateral goods trade with the United States is still in the $400-billion range. Energy trade alone was about $137 billion in 2025. The U.S. took 3.9 million barrels a day of Canadian crude. Canada supplied about 63 percent of U.S. crude imports and nearly all of the pipeline gas. Potash exports were $9 billion; about half of Canada’s potash still goes south. That is the commodity stack Jamieson Greer meant when he said there is no urgency in Washington: oil, gas, potash still move. The fight is not over those barrels. It is over the political layer Ottawa stacked on top.
August 21: Mark Carney pulled Janice Charette and Dominic LeBlanc out of the room. Greer said the U.S. had offered to cut steel and aluminum tariffs and kill the lumber tariff. Carney called it a bad deal and walked. Mexico stayed. Fifty-percent U.S. duties then hit about $20–28 billion of Canadian goods. Canada answered “dollar for dollar” on Sept. 8: 15/25/50 percent on more than 800 U.S. lines, Finance Canada’s own figure C$27.6 billion. Mélanie Joly said the quiet part: “We are picking products that will target states.” Ohio most exposed at about $3 billion. Michigan is Canada’s largest state customer, $43.5 billion in two-way goods, vehicles and Alberta oil. Maine seafood was on the first list, then partly pulled. Midterms are Nov. 3. Collins in Maine. Michigan Senate and governor. That is the map, not a metaphor.
Sept. 29: the next U.S. ban took effect. Not “about $1 billion” in the abstract. Jacob Jensen at AAF: $967 million on 2025 numbers. Eighty-seven percent of that is alcohol, because some provinces pulled American booze off the shelves first. Also whey, molasses, non-alcoholic beer, Can-Am three-wheelers from BRP. Capital Economics: 0.25 percent of Canada’s U.S. exports. Tiny in GDP. Loud in politics. That is the point of a ban instead of another tariff.
What is still not published: the annex Carney rejected. What is still flowing: crude, gas, potash. What Ottawa will not lock: Canadian steel in LNG Canada Phase 2. What CBC will not say when Frank McKenna blesses Mark Carney: McKenna has chaired Brookfield since 2010.
Lobbying K Street is not the file. The file is a mid-sized country using a $27.6-billion tariff list as a midterm instrument against the customer that takes most of its oil, then acting stunned when Washington answers with a ban and a closed door.
Mélanie Joly. Mark Carney. Janice Charette. Dominic LeBlanc. Jamieson Greer. Peter Navarro. The Liberals. Name them.
Kitchen table first.

You do not encounter this level of social rot in Russia because Russia is what functioning governance looks like: the state understands that order, social cohesion and the protection of young people are public responsibilities. This is why I always shed a few spontaneous tears before stepping back into the degradation that is South Africa after having travelled to people-centred Russia.

Meanwhile, here at home in South Africa, a drug culture is eating through the lives of the youth. Walk into clubs and bars in Braam and drug menus circulate with astonishing brazenness - cocaine, ecstasy, meth, ketamine and fentanyl are offered to th youth at competitive prices. Criminal economies flourish while the state looks elsewhere.

Then come the professional human-rights gatekeepers, many embedded in donor networks tied to Washington and the wider Western funding architecture, ready to police communities the moment ordinary citizens organise against the collapse around them. They have endless language for restraining popular anger, but remarkably little urgency about the forces destroying working-class neighbourhoods.

And why would they feel the same emergency? Many retreat each evening into secure homes sustained by two professional incomes, private healthcare, private schooling, alarms, walls and armed response while the wider society sinks deeper into the doldrums of unemployment, addiction, criminality and decay.

This is the obscenity of the neoliberal human-rights industrial complex: those most insulated from social collapse appoint themselves the moral supervisors of those forced to live inside it.

We are at the mercy of the United States a it is reflected in the cesspool below. Be afraid for your children. Be angry!

The stalemate bolsters the belief on both sides that a renewed military conflict is becoming more likely. U.S. officials think President Trump could order a return to major combat operations after the midterms.

Qatari officials will keep trying but are growing increasingly frustrated with both sides, two of the sources said.
Driving the news: Qatari mediator Ali al-Thawadi met Monday with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and his team in New York for several hours.

A source with knowledge said they discussed a two-page Qatari compromise proposal.
According to two other sources, the Qatari plan was aimed at addressing both Iran's demand for lifting the U.S. naval blockade and the U.S. demand for Iranian nuclear concessions.
On Monday evening, al-Thawadi held talks in Washington with Trump envoy Jared Kushner and other U.S. officials. Vice President Vance also attended a small part of the meeting.
The White House declined to comment.

On Monday morning, the White House was hopeful of progress.

U.S. officials briefed several media outlets, including Axios, that the talks were "positive and constructive" and that Iran "indicated they are flexible on the nuclear issues."
The officials even said Trump was willing to give Iran sanctions relief and release frozen funds in return for concrete steps to pare back its nuclear program.
But several hours later, while the Qatari officials were still at the White House, Trump posted on Truth Social that he offered nothing to Iran.

One of the sources said there was no significant movement in the talks on Monday.

"It is stuck. The Iranians are asking for things the U.S. can't accept and the U.S. thinks it is winning so there is no need for compromise," the source said.
Other regional mediators, including Pakistan and Egypt, urged Iran to agree to nuclear concessions. But the Iranians said they would only consider doing so after the U.S. agrees to return to the June memorandum of understanding, another source with knowledge said.

Iran's Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, said Tuesday that Iran has conveyed its terms to the U.S. but that "Trump is incapable of making a decision," per the Iranian press.

text:
Trump launches new AI-powered website to streamline access to the federal government | Carlos Garcia, Blaze Media

The effort was headed up by the co-founder of Airbnb, who quit his job to join the Trump administration.

The White House announced the launch of a new website powered by artificial intelligence that streamlines access to services offered by the federal government.

The "https://t.co/HRWsiPUUhi" website includes a chatbot of which users can ask questions and get directed to government resources from hundreds of agencies.

'We’re simplifying it. We’re glamorizing it. We’re making it what it should be.'

President Donald Trump signed an order directing government agencies to connect to the website on Friday.

"With https://t.co/HRWsiPUUhi, the federal government no longer stands in your way; it only stands at your service," the president said before meeting with tech executives.

"We’re simplifying it. We’re glamorizing it," he added. "We’re making it what it should be.”

Some of the examples included getting information about National Parks and changing one's official name, which previously would take far longer and be more complicated.

"For the first time, there's one place to get everything done across the entire government," said U.S. Chief Design Officer Joe Gebbia in a video post by the White House Rapid Response account.

"It's trained specifically on one official source of truth: the United States government," he added.

"So thank you to all the agencies government-wide, those 29,000 websites, 800 million pages, billions of pieces of information, that are now available in one easy-to-use website for every American."

The website is immediately available, but some agencies are still working to connect their databases for access.

A Blaze News test of the website found that it quickly and accurately provided answers to queries about submitting a Freedom of Information Act request and whether emails of government officials were available for media inquiries.

text:
A while back, I bought crap domains, pulled generic Apollo data, wrote bad copy, and somehow ended up booking a sales call with the founder of a $500,000,000 company.

For years, most of my business came inbound.

Then I got pimp slapped by algorithms.

Suddenly, the little client-acquisition machine I thought I owned turned out to be rented land.

But when I started writing copy for an advertising agency, something bizarre happened...

One day, they asked me:

“Do you know cold email lead gen?”

“Negative ghostrider” was my reply.

Anyway...

I bought .info domains, wrote poor copy, made weak offers, pulled generic Apollo data, and had basically none of the infrastructure, enrichment, or verification systems we use today.

By all reasonable logic, the campaign should’ve sucked.

Oddly enough, it didn’t.

One of those early campaigns booked us a call with the founder of a company doing roughly $500,000,000 a year.

Because if I could screw up that many parts of the process and still reach buyers at that level, what would happen if I learned how to do cold email lead gen the right way?

That question became an obsession.

ZZZZTTTTTTT…eureka!

A light bulb moment.

The biggest advantage in cold emailing isn’t the copy or tech.

Because the greatest cold email in the world is useless if it reaches the wrong company, the wrong person, at the wrong time, with an offer they don’t care about.

The reason most cold email campaigns fail starts before anyone writes a single word of copy?

They’re built on bad markets and bad data.

So I stopped thinking about cold email as a copywriting problem and started treating it as a market-message-fit problem.

Around the same time, I teamed up with my business partner Charlie, who is the technical prodigy behind a lot of what we now do.

Charlie knew how to turn those ideas into systems that could process thousands of prospects.

Like a late-night Taco Bell bender, things started to explode…

We started generating thousands of qualified leads for clients, booked 31 calls in two weeks for one campaign, helped another client generate 13 new deals in 45 days, and continued reaching buyers most businesses would assume are almost impossible to get in front of.

In fact, the client who booked those 31 calls had to pause the campaigns because they were struggling to handle the volume.

And the same basic question kept popping up:

“How are you doing this?”

Enter the Cold Gold webinar.

I wanted to pull apart the process Charlie and I use every day and show you what cold email looks like when you stop treating it like a clever writing trick and start treating it like a complete client-acquisition system.

If nothing else, remember this:

The goal isn’t to become good at sending cold emails.

The goal is to be able to look at a market, decide which companies you want as clients, and have a reliable way to start conversations with them.

text:
COFFEE WITH JESUS
September 30th, 2026

Do you remember what it felt like to be a child waiting on Christmas?

When I was little, we had a candy cane holder that hung on the door. Every day we got to take one down, one candy cane to suck on for that day, counting down to Christmas. So every day came with anticipation. Anticipation of the prize. Anticipation of the gift.

This week, we're in the middle of the feast, the in-between days. And if you think about it, we're always in the middle. Jesus came, and Jesus is coming again. We live every day in the in-between.

What if we learned to wake up every day in anticipation of the gift He offers us that day? It may not be a candy cane. It may be a conversation. It may be an answered prayer. It may be Him walking you through the storm you're in, or comforting you at the loss of a loved one while you grieve. It could be a new relationship.

We don't know the day, so we can't hang a marker on our door and count down. But we can wake up like we did as children, excited for life, because today we are one day closer.

Isn't that how we should be?

"In the morning, O LORD, You will hear my voice; in the morning I will order my prayer to You and eagerly watch."
— Psalm 5:3 (NASB 1995)

text:
The following Monday, Samuel received a phone call.

He answered.

“Hello?”

His expression changed.

He stood up.

“Yes, sir.”

Silence.

“Yes, I can do that.”

Another pause.

“Yes.”

He hung up.

I looked at him.

“What happened?”

He smiled.

“They want a meeting.”

“Who?”

He told me.

A company he had contacted eighteen months earlier.

They wanted him to manage their digital operations.

Not an internship.

Not temporary work.

A real contract.

But there was one problem.

They wanted him to start immediately.

Samuel sat down.

“I don't have the money to set everything up.”

“How much?”

He told me.

It was more than he had.

I expected him to panic.

Instead, he smiled.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You're smiling.”

“Because five years ago, I thought success would arrive looking like a job offer.”

He looked at me.

“I didn't realize it might arrive looking like a responsibility I wasn't financially ready for.”

He borrowed equipment.

Called people he'd helped over the years.

Asked friends for small loans.

His mother sold some jewelry.

His younger sister contributed her savings.

For the first time, his entire family wasn't asking when he would get a job.

They were helping him build one.

The night before his first major contract began, I found him outside.

“You scared?”

He nodded.

“Terrified.”

“Then why are you smiling?”

He looked at his house.

“Because tomorrow, my family won't wake up wondering whether I'm going anywhere.”

He paused.

“They'll wake up knowing I'm already on my way.”

CONFIRMED TONE: Risk is soft, and the weakness is broad across ES, NQ, and RTY. The important structural feature is location: all three equity-index futures are testing or sitting just above their overnight lows, not recovering from them. Meanwhile, WTI and gold are higher and trading in the upper portions of their overnight ranges.
DLMM READ: The market is approaching decision territory, not providing a completed directional trade yet. Look left: the overnight highs are clearly defined, but so are the lows. Sellers have control only while they can keep futures accepted beneath failed intraday bounces and press through the overnight floors. Buyers need more than a green candle; they need a reclaim of the failed auction and body acceptance back into the prior range. Until one side surrenders, treat early movement as an auction around major scheduled data.

WHY IT MATTERS

First: the 8:15 AM ET and 8:30 AM ET data cluster arrives with futures already leaning on overnight support.

ADP employment data is scheduled for 8:15 AM ET. At 8:30 AM ET, the market gets Personal Income and Outlays, including PCE inflation measures, along with the third GDP estimate. That is a concentrated event window before the cash open. With ES, NQ, and RTY all at or near their respective overnight lows, the reaction matters more than the headline. A weak initial move that immediately reclaims the pre-data range is a failed breakdown. A post-data bounce that cannot reclaim the pre-data decision candle is a lower-high setup, not strength.

Second: NQ is weaker than ES, and RTY is not providing confirmation from underneath.

NQ is down 0.33%, versus ES down 0.16%, while NQ is nearly exactly at its overnight low. That is relative weakness in the growth-heavy index. RTY is also down 0.31% and near its own overnight floor. The market does not have broad participation to the upside before the data. For bulls, NQ needs to stop being the weakest index and reclaim structure. For bears, NQ remaining offered while ES attempts to stabilize would preserve the pressure.

Third: commodity price strength is separating from equity-index price action.
WTI is up 1.51% and close to its overnight high. Gold is up 0.70% and remains elevated within its overnight range. Those are confirmed price facts, not a standalone equity-market explanation. The practical trading implication is that leadership is fragmented. Do not assume a broad index recovery will automatically lift every theme. The open may produce sharp pockets of relative strength and relative weakness rather than clean, broad index alignment.

Fourth: today’s calendar can turn overnight levels into intraday pivots.

TODAY’S EVENTS
8:15 AM ET: ADP National Employment Report
8:30 AM ET: Personal Income and Outlays, including PCE inflation data
8:30 AM ET: Gross Domestic Product, third estimate
9:45 AM ET: Chicago PMI

The 8:15 AM ET through 8:30 AM ET sequence is the first major test. The 9:45 AM ET Chicago PMI is the next potential expansion point. The 10:30 AM ET oil inventory report matters most for energy-linked names and for whether WTI can hold its early strength.

ROTATION MAP

PARTICIPATION: NARROW.

The rotation map is not showing broad leadership. It is showing a limited group of themes holding constructive range location while financials, small caps, defense, digital infrastructure, copper miners, and nuclear remain near the lower ends of their respective 20-day ranges.

Leadership is concentrated in semiconductor-adjacent areas.

Lithography and semiconductor equipment, represented by EUV, is the strongest rotation entry. It is up 1.98% over five sessions, up 7.85% over 21 sessions, and sits at 95.50% of its 20-day range. That is leadership by price location, though it is close to the 20-day high of $25.44 and requires clean continuation rather than late chasing.
Semiconductors, represented by SMH, sit at 91.60% of the 20-day range after a 9.73% 21-day advance. SMH is only down 0.09% over five sessions, which is materially more resilient than the broader benchmark over that period. The 20-day high is $613.27. Semis remain the best institutional-quality long-side group if they can regain intraday structure, but NQ’s premarket weakness means the group must prove it can separate rather than simply bounce with the tape.

Healthcare, represented by XLV, is the quiet stabilizer. It is up 0.49% over five sessions and holds at 60.00% of its 20-day range. It is not a momentum leader, but it is comparatively stable versus weaker cyclicals.

Quantum computing, QTUM, holds at 77.40% of its 20-day range but is down 1.66% over five sessions. The message is simple: semiconductors, equipment, cybersecurity, and selected defensiveness are the areas with room to lead. Financials, small caps, defense, data-center infrastructure, copper, and nuclear remain structurally damaged until they can build and hold higher lows.

LEADERS & LAGGARDS

There are no verified fresh individual premarket movers meeting the required freshness standard this morning.

That means there is no confirmed company-specific catalyst list to chase into the open. Treat stale quotes, isolated bid-ask changes, and yesterday’s closing prices as reference points only—not as fresh evidence of a tradable premarket move.

The actionable leadership and weakness today are group-based:

Leaders to monitor:
Semiconductors and semiconductor equipment remain the strongest rotation complex.
Cybersecurity remains a constructive secondary group.
Healthcare remains comparatively stable.
Laggards to monitor:
Small caps and financials remain near their 20-day floors.
Aerospace and defense, nuclear, copper miners, and digital infrastructure remain structurally weak.
Bitcoin miners remain fragile after pronounced five-day relative weakness.

DLMM TRADE MAP

BULLISH SCENARIO

The bullish case begins with rejection of the overnight lows, not merely a bounce from them.

ES must reject 7,719.50, reclaim 7,720.00, and then print candle-body acceptance back into the overnight range. The next meaningful proof is a reclaim of 7,756.50. A wick above that high is not enough. Buyers need bodies holding above it or a breakout, retest, and defended higher low.

NQ must first stop accepting below 30,512.25. A reclaim of 30,512.75 is only stabilization. The real bull case requires a sustained push away from the floor and eventual acceptance through 30,737.00. Without NQ participating, ES strength is vulnerable to failure.

RTY needs to reject 2,819.70 and reclaim 2,820.30. Acceptance above 2,842.20 would confirm that small caps are no longer merely following the downside auction.

Best long-side expression: semiconductor leaders only if they show relative strength against NQ and hold a higher low after the opening-range reaction. No pattern, no trade.

BEARISH SCENARIO

The bearish case is continued acceptance below the overnight floors after the scheduled data.

ES must break 7,719.50 with candle bodies holding below it, then fail on an attempted reclaim. A first break can be liquidity discovery. The short setup is the failed hold beneath the broken level, especially if a bounce stalls below 7,719.50 and rolls over.
NQ must accept below 30,512.25 and fail to reclaim that level. NQ is already at its floor, so it is the index to watch for momentum. If it breaks, reclaims immediately, and holds, the downside thesis is invalidated. If it breaks, retests from below, and sellers defend, that is surrender from buyers.

RTY accepting below 2,819.70 would confirm that weakness is broadening rather than contained in large-cap technology.

Best short-side expression: lagging groups that cannot reclaim their opening-range high while the futures remain below their overnight decision levels. Do not short into a flush without a failed bounce.

CHOP / NO-TRADE SCENARIO

Expect chop if ES remains inside 7,719.50–7,756.50, NQ remains inside 30,512.25–30,737.00, and RTY remains inside 2,819.70–2,842.20 after the data reactions.

If price repeatedly pierces a range extreme but closes back inside, that is rejection, not continuation. If the first 15- to 30-minute auction stays inside the overnight range with overlapping candles and no side can hold a breakout, stand aside. Momentum is born when one side surrenders. Overlapping candles are not surrender.

NAMES ON THE SCREEN

CONDITIONAL LONG BIAS

NVDA — Semiconductor leadership remains the cleanest broad theme. Long only if NVDA builds above its opening-range high while SMH holds a higher low and NQ stops accepting at its overnight floor.

AMD — Same semiconductor tailwind, but it must show clean price separation from NQ. Require a reclaim of the opening-range high, a higher low, and continued SMH strength.

MU — Memory has strong 21-day price performance but weak recent five-day performance. That makes MU a reaction trade, not a blind continuation trade. Long only after a failed breakdown or a clean reclaim-and-hold of the opening range.
INTC — Semiconductor equipment and chip leadership keep it on watch. Require a decision candle through the opening-range high and a retest that holds. If the breakout immediately falls back into the range, pass.

CONDITIONAL SHORT BIAS

PLTR — Software is not leading, and IGV remains below the stronger semiconductor complex on the rotation map. Short only if PLTR fails to reclaim an early bounce high while NQ remains below its overnight decision range.

TSLA — High-beta names are vulnerable when NQ is pinned at its overnight low. Require a lower high after the opening auction and a break of that reaction low. If NQ reclaims structure, do not force the short.

AMZN — Treat it as an index-sensitive short only if it cannot reclaim the opening range while NQ remains accepted below 30,512.25. A strong reclaim in AMZN while NQ stays weak is a reason to stand down, not argue with price.

TWO-WAY NAMES

AAPL — A liquid index-weight name for reading broad-market acceptance. Long only on an opening-range reclaim and hold with ES recovering from 7,719.50. Short only on a failed bounce while ES accepts below that low.

META — Use META as a two-way momentum name, not a directional prediction. A clean opening-range breakout with NQ stabilization favors the long. A failed breakout, lower high, and renewed NQ pressure favors the short.

SMCI — Semiconductor adjacency puts it on the long-side watchlist, but its individual structure must lead. Long on a higher low and opening-range reclaim with SMH firm. Short only if the semiconductor complex fails broadly and SMCI cannot reclaim its first meaningful bounce.

BOTTOM LINE

The premarket posture is cautious because every major equity-index future is near its overnight low ahead of a dense 8:15 AM ET and 8:30 AM ET economic-data window.
The market is not offering broad alignment. Semiconductor equipment, semiconductors, and cybersecurity remain the best areas of price leadership. Financials, small caps, defense, data centers, copper miners, and nuclear remain weak on the rotation map. That split favors selective trades over broad-market assumptions.

For bulls, the job is clear: reject the overnight lows, reclaim them with candle-body acceptance, and show NQ participation. For bears, the job is equally clear: break the overnight floors, fail the reclaim, and hold sellers in control.

Trade the reaction, not the level. If the data creates range expansion but price cannot hold outside the overnight structure, expect trap conditions. If one side holds acceptance beyond the range and the other side cannot reclaim, that is the move worth respecting.

text:
PLANETARY HYSTERESIS describes a state that, once established, keeps running under conditions that would never have started it from scratch.
A planet's interior is characterized by unbalanced fluxes of mass and energy, so its state is a matter of rates, of how fast heat leaves the core, how fast the lithosphere yields, how fast a magnetic field regenerates against diffusion, and a dynamical state is the standing pattern those rates settle into.
The ordinary picture of a threshold is symmetric, on above some critical value and off below it, but many driven systems instead have two branches, a weak or absent state and a strong self-sustaining one, and which branch a system occupies depends on its history rather than its present forcing alone.

A subcritical dynamical state is one sustained only because such a state existed previously. What sustains it is memory of one of two kinds: passive memory, a record that simply preserves what happened, and active memory, an imprint that feeds back on the process that made it. A stable isotope ratio is passive; a grain size is active, because it sets the viscosity that governs the next deformation. Only active memory makes a state subcritical; passive memory records one. The cases below are sorted accordingly, and two of them fit neither, one because it is a coupling between states and one because it is held by shape rather than by memory.

Several systems are subcritical in this sense, each held by an active memory. Hori and Wicht (2013) show the dynamo case in a modeled Martian core, where a strong dipolar field persists down to roughly a quarter of the Rayleigh number, the ratio of the buoyancy driving a hot fluid to rise against resisting thermodynamic factors, needed to grow the field from a weak seed, because the field reorganizes the flow into a pattern that sustains it, the field acting as a catalyst for its own induction, so that once the heat flux fell "it would have been very difficult to restart the dynamo after the heat flux recovered."

Weller and Lenardic (2012) show the tectonic case, where the lithospheric yield strength at which a stagnant lid breaks into plates is lower than the strength at which plates stop, leaving a window in which mobile and stagnant states coexist for identical parameters, so that a planet keeps its plates under stresses that could never have broken fresh lithosphere. Bercovici and Ricard (2014) supply the active memory that holds that window open: deformation reduces grain size, reduced grain size weakens rock, and the weakened zones persist as dormant faults that later subduction can reactivate, so plate boundaries are inherited rather than remade, and on a hot surface like Venus's, where grains heal faster than damage accumulates, the inheritance fails and plates never spread. 

Lenardic and Seales (2021) extend the logic to the whole planet, where the feedback is asserted rather than shown: if habitability is a process variable, like heat, rather than a state variable, like temperature, then planets should show bistable behavior with history playing a role, and their evidence is a pair of similar Jupiter-like exoplanets whose compositions differ because "their formation histories could be playing an important role."

These states do not run in isolation, and the link between them is not a subcritical state but the route by which a branch chosen in one system is inherited by another. Foley and Driscoll (2016) show that after an initial 1-2 Gyr window in which any young core cools fast enough to run a dynamo, a mobile lid keeps the core losing heat while a stagnant lid insulates it, so the tectonic branch a planet occupies decides whether its dynamo survives. The consequence for the divergence of similar planets is direct. Two planets alike in mass, radius, and insolation can sit on different branches of every one of these systems at once, and the branch each occupies was chosen when the first of them crossed its threshold.

Rotation offers a case of selection by history without memory. The coupling between core and mantle decides which state a slowing planet is caught in, and can be inferred from the states it escaped, but the state, once reached, is held by the planet's shape rather than by anything it made.
Peale and Boss (1977) showed that friction between a liquid core and the mantle can capture a spinning planet into a resonance, so strongly that for a wide range of core viscosities capture is certain, and since Mercury evidently slipped past the state where it would spin twice per orbit to reach its present 3/2 state, its core must lie outside that range.

The outcome hinges on whether the thin Ekman boundary layer where core meets mantle is laminar or turbulent, and the critical Reynolds number [ratio of a flow's inertial stress to its viscous stress] for that transition was unknown for a spinning core. They took it from Cham and Head's (1969) rotating-disk measurements, converting the disk values into 'momentum boundary layer' Reynolds numbers of 560 and 870, a measure built on the layer's own momentum deficit rather than any external length, and so the one quantity that can be carried from a laboratory disk to a planetary core; a second estimate from surface stress gave about 500, which they adopt.

The answer swings on it. Escape through a turbulent layer requires two things of the planet: that its equatorial asymmetry be small, with the difference between its two equatorial moments of inertia, B−A, no more than about a hundred-thousandth of its polar moment C, since that difference is what the Sun's gravity grips to hold a resonance; and that its tides dissipate energy fast, with a tidal Q [tidal dissipation factor; low values mean strong friction] below about 40, a value severe for a planet without shallow seas.

Every assumption behind the inference, an unstratified core, a smooth spherical boundary, weak magnetic coupling, near-zero obliquity, is a product of formation history, and "any additional core-mantle coupling would make it unlikely that Mercury could have passed through the 2n [2:1 spin-orbit resonance] with a liquid core of low viscosity." A planet's rotational history is a record of its coupling, and coupling in turn depends on what state the core and its boundary layer were left in.

The center of the planet holds both kinds of memory at once, a subcritical process and the passive record it leaves. Inner core crystallization is itself a subcritical process, since a liquid can hold below its freezing point until something starts it, after which growth proceeds on its own, and the solid it leaves cannot be undone by returning to the conditions that preceded it. What that growth leaves behind is a record. Deguen and Cardin (2009) find that "the secular chemical evolution of the outer core has been imprinted in the crystallizing inner core," an imprint they present as a record, with nothing in their result showing that it steers later growth. These authors consider deep inner core anisotropy as fossil anisotropy inherited from horizontal Maxwell stresses arising because of the magnetic field. That fossil anisotropy is passive memory, sensu stricto, a record of conditions rather than a feedback on them.

We are accustomed to think that the condition of a thing tells us how it came to be so. The planet teaches otherwise. Its magnetic field, its moving plates, and the solid growing at its center are not conditions that exist because present circumstances demand them. The genesis of a state belongs among the researcher's questions, not after them.
To understand the present, we must sometimes look for the moment the choice was made, and accept that the moment may have left no mark except the state itself.

text:
2/ "He was the first English speaking Jew who achieved a place in English letters… Next to Nordau no one was more prompt than he to proffer help to Herzl."

Zangwill Initially Opposed Palestine Location. With Herzl he was Palestine: the English voice at the Maccabean Club in 1895, the novelist who could sell Der Judenstaat in a London drawing room. After Kishinev, when Joseph Chamberlain offered a tract in British East Africa—the so-called Uganda scheme, actually highland Kenya—Zangwill took the emergency door. A mass of Russian Jews needed ground now. Herzl put the offer to the Sixth Congress in 1903 as a night shelter, not a replacement Temple. The Seventh Congress in 1905 killed it and bound the movement to Palestine only. Zangwill walked and built the Jewish Territorial Organization. ITO’s brief was blunt: a large territory, preferably under the Union Jack, wherever it could be had—Galveston as a funnel, Angola, Cyrenaica, Mexico later. Africa (and every other empty-looking imperial margin) versus Zion. He ran that opposition for a decade. Balfour in 1917 pulled him back toward Palestine, but only if the paper meant a state that governed, not a hostel that bought land by the yard under an Arab majority and a British High Commissioner.⁠

That is what he brought to Carnegie Hall on 14 October 1923. Stephen S. Wise’s American Jewish Congress invited him, promised he could speak unhampered after he refused to sail if they muzzled an article on Mexican land. He called the night the greatest labor of his life. The line that emptied the hall of goodwill: “Political Zionism is dead.” He reached for King David: when the child was sick the king fasted on the ground; when the child died he rose, washed, and anointed himself. Honorable defeat. Colonization without a territorial charter, buying square yards and bidding up the price against yourself, was “a monstrosity unknown to history.” National politics is might, and Jewish might did not exist. Palestine was the size of Wales; French imperialism had already lopped the north; at best it might hold a quarter of the sixteen million. The Arabs were not fools. They read their own papers. They knew the project meant swamping them and being masters in the house. He said a Jewish state had been possible in the hour when the Arab was a defeated enemy, glad to take a political impress—racial redistribution on the Lausanne model of Greeks and Turks, with pay for land. That hour, he said, had passed. Better to drop political hopes in Palestine “rather than kindle a conflagration which may ravage the whole world.” He even said the Ku Klux, absurd as it was, had more self-respect than a racial Jewry that had lost its soul. Weizmann, “as a chemist,” had delivered not Zionism but ersatz—cocktail-type, beer-type.⁠

Why the room turned. Wise, Straus, Untermyer, and the Palestine Foundation Fund were raising dollars and discipline for the mandate as it stood. They needed American Jews to believe Balfour plus Weizmann plus purchase-and-settle was the path. Zangwill told them it was a substitute, that the leadership would not say the word state, and that the only honest political program implied moving Arabs. Nathan Straus, who had put his life and money in the country, called it counterfeit Zionism and said he would denounce it if Zangwill were his son. Untermyer called him a destructive epigram factory. The Congress, next morning, disavowed the speech: Zangwill spoke for himself, not for them. Wise put “primarily for Palestine” into the resolutions so no one could miss the answer. Weizmann called the speech a betrayal. Zangwill’s reply at the Judeans: who betrayed whom—the man who took the whittled declaration or the man who said it was whittled? Coolidge had just wired sympathy for a “Jewish homeland.” That word was the fight. Homeland is a sentiment. Political authority is a government. Carnegie Hall was where the American movement chose the first and treated the second as an embarrassment.⁠NYTimes

What he had pushed for, and what happened. From 1905 to the war he pushed territory with title—Africa if Palestine was closed. After 1917 he pushed Palestine with sovereignty: state lands actually granted, immigration control, not “paying guests,” not a legislative council built to freeze a minority. He lost both fights in his lifetime. ITO dissolved in 1925. The mandate stayed Weizmann’s: cultural home, purchased dunams, British police, Arab majority on the ground. Zangwill died 1 August 1926 of pneumonia after a breakdown. Wise wrote the eulogy as if Carnegie Hall had been a family quarrel.

How much that stage still sits under Israel. The state that exists is the answer to Zangwill’s 1923 demand and the rejection of his 1923 despair. He said there is no Jewish state if Jews do not govern from above. 1948 made a government. He said the window was 1918–19, when the Ottoman order was broken and population transfer was thinkable in the same decade as Lausanne. That window closed; the state arrived after another war and another flight of Arabs—not the compensated Lausanne he sketched, but a war outcome. He said a national home without political authority was a monstrosity. The Zionist Organization after Carnegie Hall would not put state in the fundraising speech. The movement that built Israel after 1942–48 was the one that finally said what he said in 1923 and what Wise could not let him say in that hall without a disavowal the next morning. Carnegie Hall is the hinge in American Jewish politics: the night the official family chose the mandate’s language over the playwright’s, and then spent the next twenty-five years walking, by other means, toward the authority he had named.

Orthodox Scripture and Commemorations

Today’s commemorated feasts and saints
Hieromartyr Gregory, Bishop of Greater Armenia, Equal of the Apostles, Enlightener of Armenia (ca. 335). Ven. Gregory, Abbot of Pelshme, Wonderworker of Vologdá (1442). St. Michael, first Metropolitan of Kiev (992). Martyrs Rhipsime and Gaianḗ of Armenia and those with them (4th c.).
Hieromartyr Gregory, Bishop of Greater Armenia, Equal of the Apostles, Enlightener of Armenia
Commemorated on September 30
The Hieromartyr Gregory, Enlightener of Greater Armenia, was born in the year 257. He was descended from a line of Parthian Arsakid kings. Anak, the father of Saint Gregory, was a Parthian by birth. In his quest for the Armenian throne, Anak and his brother attacked their kinsman, King Kursar with their swords, leaving him mortally wounded. The King's servants found him still alive, and he was able to tell them what had happened. Before he expired, the King ordered the execution of Anak, his brother, and also their wives and children. The murderers were caught by a river, where they were slain and their bodies were thrown into the water.

One of Anak's relatives saved Gregory and his brother, who were infants, and hid them in his home. There was a revolt in Armenia, and King Artasirus of Persia was able to conquer Armenia and bring it under his rule. As for Arak's sons: one was taken to Persia, and Gregory was sent to the Roman Empire.

When he reached adulthood, Gregory lived in Caesarea in Cappadocia, where he was converted to the Christian Faith. Gregory married, and had two sons, but soon was left a widower. Gregory raised his sons in piety. One of them, Orthanes, later became a priest, and the other, Arostanes, was tonsured as a monk and went into the wilderness to live in solitude.

In order to atone for the sin of his father, who had murdered the father of Tiridates, Gregory entered into the latter's service, and was a faithful servant to him. Tiridates, who was serving in the Roman army, loved Gregory like a friend, but when he learned that Gregory was a Christian, he became angry. Saint Gregory, however, ignored his master's unjust wrath.

When the Goths attacked the Roman Empire, the Prince of the Goths challenged the Emperor to single combat. The Emperor was afraid to fight the Prince, so he had Tiridates put on his armor and take his place. Tiridates defeated his adversary without using his sword, and led him as a captive to the Emperor. Then the entire Gothic army was defeated. In gratitude, the Emperor made Tiridates King of Armenia. When Tiridates offered sacrifice to his "gods" for his new position, he wanted Gregory to sacrifice with him. Gregory refused, and so Tiridates ordered that he be tortured.

The Saint was suspended head downward, with a stone about his neck, and for several days they choked him with a foul-smelling smoke, they beat and ridiculed him, and forced him to walk in iron sandals inset with nails.

During these torments, Saint Gregory sang Psalms. In prison the Lord healed all his wounds. When Gregory stood before the King cheerful and unharmed, he was astonished and ordered that the torments be repeated. Saint Gregory endured them, not wavering, with his former determination and bearing. They then poured hot tin over him and threw him into a pit filled with snakes, scorpions, and other poisonous creatures. The Lord, however, spared His chosen one, and he was left unharmed.

Some pious women kept him alive for fourteen years by feeding him with bread, secretly lowering it into the pit. A holy angel appeared to the martyr, strengthening and encouraging him. During this time King Tiridates killed the holy virgin Saint Ripsimia (Ριψιμία, or Ριψίμη), the Eldress Gaianḗ (Γαϊανή), and 32 other Virgin Martyrs (some sources say 35) from Asia Minor. Tiridates, who seemed to have lost his mind after this, recovered six days later. Then the wrath of God struck King Tiridates, his associates, and the soldiers who had participated in the execution of the virgins. Beset by demons, their appearance resembled wild boars, as once happened to Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 4:30). Running through forests and fields, they tore their clothes and devoured their own flesh.

Saint Gregory was taken from from the pit, and then he was washed, dressed in clean clothes, and fed. Then he was led to the King. Everyone bowed before him, begging him to ask God to heal the King as well as the others responsible for killing the Holy Virgin Martyrs. First, the Saint asked about their relics, which remained unburied for nine days. Saint Gregory buried the bodies, and then began preaching to the people, urging them to turn away from the darkness of idolatry and toward Christ. The people came to believe in Christ, and wanted to build a large church. When it was completed, Saint Gregory had the relics of the holy nuns brought into it. Then he led King Tiridates to the church before the bodies of the Saints whom he had slain, so that they might pray to Christ for him. He repented, and at once his face was restored to its original appearance once more.

Soon all of Armenia was converted to Christ. The temples of the idols were destroyed, and churches for the worship of the only true God were built. Saint Gregory ordained priests, established schools, founded monasteries, and provided for the good order of the Church.

After this, Saint Gregory went into the wilderness, where he ended his earthly life in a manner pleasing to the Lord. His son Aristanes was made a bishop in Cappadocia, and was one of the 318 Holy Fathers of the Council of Nicea.

Senior Airman Mark A. Forester, Combat Controller, 21st Special Tactics Squadron, killed in action on September 29, 2010, while leading a rescue team into an ambush in Uruzgan Province, Afghanistan, trying to save a fallen comrade. He was 29, from Tuscaloosa, Alabama.

Forester's path to Special Tactics ran through faith before it ran through the military. He was serving as a full-time missionary in California when 9/11 happened, an event he later cited as one of the reasons he chose to enlist. He got his college degree first, then joined the Air Force in June 2007, choosing to go in enlisted rather than as an officer because he knew it would give him a better shot at deploying. He wanted the toughest job the military could offer, and Combat Controller was exactly that.

On the day he died, Forester and a team of four Green Berets and eight Afghan National Army soldiers were advancing on a suspected ambush position in Jangalak Village when they were hit by heavy machine gun and RPG fire from roughly 30 armed insurgents. Pinned down, Forester stepped out from behind cover, fired a smoke grenade to mark the enemy position, and directed AH-64 Apache gunships onto the fighters, all while fully exposed to fire. He was killed while trying to reach and save Sergeant 1st Class Calvin Harrison, a wounded soldier from his own patrol. He was posthumously awarded the Silver Star, having already earned a Bronze Star with Valor just weeks earlier for a separate engagement near Forward Operating Base Cobra.

His older brother Joseph, also an Airman, later recalled visiting the Special Tactics schoolhouse after Mark's death and being shown a mural, painted by a fellow student who remembered Mark spending his weekends and evenings training in the gym while everyone else left base. In 2021, the 24th Special Operations Wing dedicated a building at Hurlburt Field in his name. A man who joined to fight terrorism and gave everything trying to bring a brother home. First There. Never forgotten.

text:
First Love Devotions September 30 Morning - Charles Spurgeon inspired
“Sing out the honor of His name; Make His praise glorious” (Psalms 66:2)

Saints are supposed to “continually offer the sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of our lips, giving thanks to His name” (Hebrews 13:15), and “rejoice always, pray without ceasing, in everything give thanks; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you” (1 Thessalonians 5:16–18).

For the Christian, praising God isn’t something you do just when things are going great. God deserves to be praised, even when you’re chained to the wall of a prison. “At midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them. Suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken; and immediately all the doors were opened and everyone’s chains were loosed” (Acts 16:25–26). 

When your back’s against the wall, praising God is the best thing you can do. King Jehoshaphat faced a huge invading army, so he sought the Lord, proclaimed a fast, and the people humbled themselves. Then a prophesy came forth, “Do not be afraid nor dismayed because of this great multitude, for the battle is not yours, but God’s” (2 Chronicles 20:14–15). But the king didn’t relax. He “appointed those who should sing to the LORD, and who should praise the beauty of holiness, as they went out before the army … Now when they began to sing and to praise, the LORD set ambushes” for the enemy, and they were defeated (2 Chronicles 20:21–22).

So, “rejoice in the LORD, O you righteous! For praise from the upright is beautiful. Praise the LORD with the harp; Make melody to Him with an instrument of ten strings. Sing to Him a new song; Play skillfully with a shout of joy” (Psalms 33:1–3).

Trump’s Top 25 Achievements: The List Every Conservative Should Know and Use
Donald Trump doesn’t have an accomplishment problem. Republicans have an information problem. It’s on each of us to change that.
With the midterms coming, an astonishing number of Republican voters cannot name three things President Trump has accomplished. Which is remarkable when you consider that Donald Trump has accomplished more in a year and a half than any other president ever did in four.
Indeed, he has accomplished so much, so fast, across so many fronts that most people cannot keep up. The Enemedia buries the victories, while Republicans do an abysmal job of explaining them.
So here is the cheat sheet. It barely scratches the surface. And yet each and every item here is a game-changer, and your befuddled black-pilling friends need to know it.
This is not a list of promises. It’s a list of laws enacted, cases won, policies implemented, agreements secured, and measurable results.
You don’t have to memorize all 25. Learn five. And when somebody says Trump “hasn’t done much,” show them the receipts.
Trump Restored American Safety and Sovereignty
1. He made the border a real border again.
In a matter of months, Trump reduced illegal border crossings to their lowest level in half a century. Catch-and-release is finished. The wall is going up and even being expanded, “Remain in Mexico” is back, and the Administration reduced releases into the country by an incredible 99.9 percent.
2. He reversed mass migration.
America recorded negative net migration in 2025 for the first time in at least half a century. So far, nearly 3 million illegal aliens have left the country, whether voluntarily or involuntarily: more than 675,000 forcibly deported and the rest “self-deported.”
Many of those self-deportations were facilitated by the President’s innovative program to offer plane tickets and cash bonuses for illegals to leave, not only incentivizing good behavior but significantly reducing the cost of deportations. Citizenship and the law actually mean something again.
3. He signed the Laken Riley Act — and required detention of criminal illegal aliens.
Named for an innocent girl murdered by an illegal alien, the Laken Riley Act requires federal authorities to detain illegals arrested for theft, burglary, shoplifting, assaulting police, or any crime causing death or serious injury. It also lets states sue officials who refuse to enforce it.
Laken Riley should still be alive. This law will prevent tragedies like hers.
4. History’s biggest drop in violent crime, and the lowest violent crime rate in 126 years.
According to FBI data, violent crime in America dropped an incredible 9.7 percent in 2025 — the largest one-year decline in history. Murder fell 18.1 percent, robbery fell 18.5 percent. And America’s violent crime rate is its lowest since 1900.
This is what happens when you put the National Guard on the streets in crime-ridden blue cities: fewer victims, safer streets, and better futures for America’s poorest.
Trump Launched an American Industrial Supercycle
5. He made the 2017 tax cuts permanent…and better.
The One Big Beautiful Bill locked in the largest tax cut in modern history, including the doubled standard deduction, the expanded Child Tax Credit, and 100 percent expensing for factories and equipment. It also delivered No Tax on Tips, No Tax on Overtime, an abolition of most taxes on Social Security benefits, and major relief for seniors.
Every Democrat voted no. With the 2017 act set to expire in December 2025, that would have resulted in the largest tax hike in American history.
6. He repealed 129 regulations for every new one.
In fiscal 2025, federal agencies finalized 646 deregulatory actions and just five regulatory actions: 129-to-1, and in nearly every case, the “one” was to repeal the others! OIRA says the savings exceeded those of Trump’s entire first term. That is more freedom, lower costs, and less bureaucratic sabotage.
Of these, the crown jewel was the repeal of Obama’s 2009 “Endangerment Finding”, the legal foundation for the Green New Scam’s vehicle mandates. EPA calls it the largest deregulatory action in American history and estimates that by itself, it will save Americans more than $1.3 trillion. Trump also killed the federal EV mandate, restored Americans’ freedom to buy the cars and trucks they actually want, and even eliminated the incentives behind the almost universally hated start-stop button.
7. He secured $18 trillion in announced investment commitments.
That’s nearly two-thirds the size of the entire American economy, building American factories, chip plants, data centers, energy projects, steel mills, shipyards, and supply chains employing American workers. Apple, Meta, NVIDIA, Micron, Hyundai, U.S. Steel, Ford, Taiwan Semiconductor, and many corporations and sovereign wealth funds are betting big on Trump’s America.
No President has ever done anything remotely like it. And it’s just getting started.
8. He made “reshoring” and “reindustrialization” real, not a slogan.
Ford is moving Lincoln production out of China. Toyota is shifting Tacoma production from Mexico to Texas. GM, Honda, Mercedes-Benz, Stellantis, and others are expanding U.S. production. The capital equipment pouring into the country is the machinery that’s building the growing boom.
9. He replaced lopsided trade deals with balanced, reciprocal trade.
Trump used tariffs as leverage to reverse 80 years of lopsided trade deals that favored everyone but America, and to win new or improved agreements with trading partners accounting for more than half of global GDP. Those agreements open foreign markets, attack non-tariff barriers, defend strategic industries, and make it more profitable to build in America than to export American jobs.
10. He shifted global energy dominance from the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of America.
Once the world’s largest energy importer — “exporting” $700 billion a year to our enemies — America now outproduces Saudi Arabia and Russia combined. The U.S. is also setting new records in oil, natural gas, and LNG exports, becoming the first country ever to export more than 100 million metric tons of LNG in a year.
Trump also opened land, accelerated permits, expanded pipelines and export terminals, and made American energy a tool for prosperity and peace.
11. After four decades of nuclear paralysis, Trump brought five new reactors online in a single year.
For more than 40 years, not one new privately developed non-light-water reactor reached criticality in America. Trump ordered at least three by July 4, 2026. DOE delivered four by the deadline, then a fifth just one month later.
Decades of zero. One Trump summer: five. That is a genuine nuclear renaissance.
Trump Made Elections Matter Again
12. He broke the Deep State’s power to defy the elected branches.
In Trump v. Slaughter, the Supreme Court ruled for the first time in 90 years that Article 2, Section 1 is still part of the Constitution: the President may fire subordinate officials in the executive branch, overturning the 1935 precedent that insulated “independent” agencies from voters’ control.
Ever wonder why elections often seem to change nothing? How about one President and 5,000 political appointees vs. 2.8 million unfireable, unaccountable bureaucrats? THAT is the “Deep State”.
Trump then made that victory real. For the first time in a century, all policy-making bureaucrats can now be fired for misconduct, incompetence, or defying lawful directives. The permanent bureaucracy no longer gets to veto the voters.
13. He ended nationwide injunction abuse.
In Trump v. CASA, the Supreme Court sharply limited nationwide injunctions. A single, local, district judge should not be able to block a national policy for everyone, everywhere; and yet that’s exactly what they’ve done, nonstop, ever since Trump (and only Trump) took office in 2017.
In restricting that unconstitutional power, the Court kneecapped the Black Robe Bureaucracy’s favorite tool of unlawful judicial supremacy.
14. He shut down USAID as a left-wing slush fund and shadow government.
USAID had become a taxpayer-funded machine for exporting abortion, gender ideology, censorship, and left-wing politics. It had a bigger budget than the CIA and the State Department combined, absolutely no accountability whatsoever, and a penchant for overthrowing governments.
Trump terminated it — completely — and moved real humanitarian aid under the State Department. Immediately, seven socialist Latin American governments lost re-election. Coincidence?
15. He shrank Federal employment to its lowest level in 60 years.
From a high under Biden, the federal workforce is now its smallest since 1966. Workforce reductions, agency closures, and spending cancellations mean fewer bureaucrats paid to resist the voters.
What’s more, when Biden left office, 94 percent of federal employees “worked” from home. The Trump administration cracked down: as Elon Musk put it, “you can work from the office or you can pretend to work somewhere else.”
16. He expelled DEI from the federal government.
Trump eliminated federal DEI offices and barred race- and sex-based preferences across the executive branch. Government hiring and contracting are returning to merit and equality under the law, ending the grotesque Democrat idea that “fighting discrimination” requires the federal government to discriminate.
He Defended Faith and Family
17. He delivered sweeping pro-life reform.
In his first term, Trump delivered the judges that overturned the abominable Roe v. Wade. Hardly anyone believed it could be done, or that Trump would do it. But he did, and a half-century nightmare finally ended.
Since returning to office, Trump has enforced the Hyde Amendment prohibiting the use of federal funds to pay for abortions, reinstated and expanded the Mexico City Policy prohibiting federal funding of foreign abortions, ended federal fetal-tissue research, strengthened conscience protections, protected Medicaid from funding large abortion providers, and pardoned 23 pro-life activists prosecuted by Biden’s weaponized Justice Department.
He’s also done everything within the Executive Branch’s power to defund Planned Parenthood. It would be nice if Congress did likewise.
No President has ever done more to protect life. No one.
18. He got men out of women’s sports, and restored biological reality to federal policy.
The United States government once again officially recognizes two sexes: male and female. Trump ended federal support for the chemical and surgical gender mutilation of children, stopped taxpayer funding of such irreversible abominations, and forced more than three dozen health systems to end or suspend their programs as well.
Trump also enforced Title IX as written: women and girls deserve their own teams, trophies, scholarships, and locker rooms. The NCAA and other athletic organizations changed their rules in response. After years of Democrats doing everything they could to destroy women’s sports and ruin girls’ lives, Trump’s administration protects women and girls again.
19. He enacted America’s first nationwide school-choice program — and launched Trump Accounts.
As part of the President’s One Big Beautiful Bill, Trump enacted America’s first-ever nationwide school choice program. The new Education Freedom Tax Credit helps fund scholarships for tuition, books, and other educational costs.
That’s on top of the new Trump Accounts, which give every child a tax-advantaged stake in America’s future, including a $1,000 federal seed for eligible newborns. Parents gain power. Bureaucracies lose it. And children learn first-hand about free markets and future orientation.
20. He targeted anti-Christian bias and discrimination.
Trump created the White House Faith Office, Religious Liberty Commission, and Task Force to Eradicate Anti-Christian Bias. He restored conscience protections and made clear that Christians do not surrender their First Amendment rights merely by entering public life.
He Restored Peace Through Strength and Put America First
21. He forced NATO to stop freeloading and increase defense spending by 250 percent.

25. He restored the warrior ethos — and reversed the recruiting crisis.
After years of missed targets under Biden, every active military component met or exceeded its 2025 recruiting goal. Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth refocused the newly renamed Department of War on actually winning wars, while pouring resources into shipbuilding, munitions, drones, missile defense, and America’s atrophied industrial base.
Young Americans once again believe their Commander-in-Chief is worth serving. And they’re showing up en masse.
Now Act Like It Matters
Those are not tweets or campaign promises. They are changes in law, power, investment, sovereignty, culture, and the structure of the Republic itself. And they’re just the top 25: I could give you hundreds more.
Midterms are turnout elections. We do not need to convince Democrats to love Donald Trump. We need Republicans and friendly independents to understand what is at stake — and to show up.
And let’s be clear. When you say (as some of you will) “the Republicans need to do a good enough job telling this story”, you’re pointing at yourself. You are “the Republicans.” The Democrats don’t rely exclusively on their elected officials to tell their story: everyone from their media lackeys to their lowest-level supporters are constantly spreading their “news”, whatever that “news” happens to be.

This is called “black-pilling.” It’s a loser mindset, and if you engage in it, you deserve to lose: horribly, painfully, personally. And guess what: you will, unless people who are serious step up to save you. Which is frankly pathetic, but for the rest of our sakes, necessary.

Take the time to learn at least five of these victories. Share this list with someone who needs it. And vote as though the most consequential Presidency in modern history depends on what you do.
Because it does.
