text:
Mary, the “Strong Woman” — Why Michael Matt’s Point Is More Catholic Than His Critics Admit

When Michael Matt calls Our Lady the “ultimate feminist,” one may certainly debate the terminology. But the more important question is what he means by it—and he explains that himself: he points to Mary’s role as Co-redemptrix and to her fiat, through which she freely accepted her part in the redemption of the whole human race, including men. This is not a meaning supplied by his defenders; it is the explanation Matt himself gives.If he is not defending modern ideological feminism, but rather the restoration of the dignity, responsibility, and authentic strength of womanhood, then the idea is not un-Catholic at all. In fact, it touches on a very ancient Christian theme.

“You Need to Lead Us Back to Sanity”

In the passage as reported, Matt addresses the women with the words: “You need to lead us back to sanity.” He describes Our Lady as the “ultimate feminist,” connecting that provocative expression to her cooperation in humanity’s redemption and her acceptance of God’s calling through her fiat.

That explanation matters. Read together, these statements suggest something quite different from the claim that women should take power because they are inherently better than men. Rather, Mary is presented as the supreme example of a woman whose faithful acceptance of her vocation benefits the whole human race—including the men who need her maternal help.

The standard is not feminism by which Mary is judged, but Mary by whom claims about the greatness of women are judged.

Likewise, there is a difference between asking women to replace men and asking them to lead men back to sanity. The latter can mean calling men back to faith, responsibility, self-sacrifice, and obedience to God. Understood this way, the appeal is not to a rivalry between the sexes, but to their restoration.

From the earliest centuries, the Church has understood Mary as the New Eve. St. Irenaeus of Lyons wrote that the knot of Eve’s disobedience was untied by Mary’s obedience. Eve used her freedom against the divine order; Mary used her freedom in faithful acceptance of it. This contrast belongs to the Church’s ancient understanding of salvation, not to a modern campaign against men. (Against Heresies, III, 22, 4.) Neues Advent

“Be it done to me according to thy word.” (Luke 1:38, Douay–Rheims.) Douay-Rheims Bibel Online

This does not mean, of course, that Mary takes the place of Christ. Christ alone is the Redeemer. Yet God willed that a woman should cooperate freely and uniquely in His plan of salvation. Vatikans Webseite

And precisely here we find the Catholic answer both to the degradation of women and to the assumption that a woman must become more like a man in order to possess dignity. Her feminine vocation is not an obstacle to her greatness. Vatikans Webseite

The Fiat: A Woman’s Obedience That Is Anything but Passive

Irenaeus goes further than the familiar image of the knot. In the same passage, he describes the obedient Virgin as “the cause of salvation, both to herself and the whole human race.” His account leaves no room for treating Mary’s consent as insignificant or merely decorative. Her obedience is an active, momentous participation in the salvation of humanity. (Against Heresies, III, 22, 4.) Neues Advent

St. Bernard of Clairvaux gives this truth a magnificent dramatic expression. In his homily on the Annunciation, he pictures Adam, Abraham, David, and the whole human family awaiting the Virgin’s answer. The patriarchs themselves stand in need of what God wills to accomplish through a woman’s consent. Bernard urges her:

“Let humility be bold, let modesty be confident.”

— In Praise of the Virgin Mother, Homily IV, 8–9. Agape Bibelstudium

That is a profoundly Catholic image of feminine strength: humility without paralysis, modesty without helplessness, obedience without passivity.

This is the traditional Marian vision of the Co-redemptrix that gives Matt’s appeal its force. Mary’s fiat is not a declaration of independence from God’s order. It is her wholehearted acceptance of responsibility within it. Her greatness does not consist in refusing to serve, but in freely embracing her vocation as the Mother of the Saviour. Her example can therefore inspire women to take responsibility without turning that responsibility into a struggle against men. Vatikans Webseite

The woman who calls herself the handmaid of the Lord is not a passive instrument. Her service is a freely accepted mission, and the whole human family benefits from her answer.

When Men Fail, Holy Women Do Not Remain Silent

Catholic history supplies memorable examples of women who acted when others hesitated, or when those in authority needed to be recalled to their duties.

St. Joan of Arc led men into battle without ceasing for a moment to be profoundly feminine, remaining faithful to her consecration to God. St. Catherine of Sienaurged Gregory XI to return from Avignon to Rome. St. Hildegard of Bingen called clergy to fidelity and reminded even an emperor that he remained subject to God’s judgment. Their spiritual strength did not depend on denying their womanhood. Vatikans Webseite

Sacred Scripture likewise gives us Deborah, Judith, and Esther: a prophetess who summoned a man to fulfil God’s command, a widow who rebuked the elders’ failing trust, and a queen who accepted the danger of interceding for her people. These are not portraits of women whose holiness consists in never speaking when men hold authority. (Judges 4; Judith 8; Esther 4.) Douay-Rheims Bibel Online

Such action need not be rebellion against order. It can be a service to the restoration of order.

The Wedding Feast at Cana expresses another aspect of this beautifully. Mary notices the problem: “They have no wine.”She brings the need to Jesus and directs the servants toward Him: “Do whatever he tells you.” (John 2:3–5.) USCCB

This is an image of feminine spiritual leadership: Mary takes the initiative, but her initiative directs others toward Christ rather than displacing Him.

Cana is not an example of Christ failing. It is an example of Mary bringing human need to Him and directing others to obey Him. Her initiative serves His authority rather than competing with it. That distinction is precisely what makes the example relevant here.

A Woman’s Service Includes Calling Authority Back to Its Duty

The crucial mistake is to confuse service with the mere execution of another person’s instructions.

A wife’s service is not exhausted by carrying out her husband’s wishes or performing tasks within the home. She is a responsible moral person, not an instrument relieved of judgment and conscience. Her husband’s responsibilities do not abolish her own.

This is not a modern concession reluctantly imposed on Catholic tradition. In Casti Connubii, Pius XI teaches that marital submission preserves a woman’s liberty and dignity, does not make her a minor, and does not require compliance with requests contrary to reason or her dignity as a wife. He then states:

“In fact, if the husband neglect his duty, it falls to the wife to take his place in directing the family.”

These are the words of a 1930 encyclical defending Christian marriage, not a manifesto against it. (Casti Connubii, §§27–28.) Vatikans Webseite

The implication is important: a woman can serve rightful authority by reminding the man who exercises it what he ought to do, what he ought to command, and what he must not permit himself to do.

A mother who challenges a father’s unjust treatment of their children is not thereby attacking fatherhood. She may be defending its proper purpose. A wife who calls her husband away from wrongdoing is not necessarily refusing her vocation; she may be fulfilling one of its most demanding responsibilities.

At such a moment, her greatest service may be not to execute his wishes, but to help him correct them.

St. Thomas Aquinas supplies the broader principle. In his discussion of fraternal correction, he distinguishes the exercise of punitive authority from charitable admonition. Someone without jurisdiction over a superior can nevertheless offer correction when it is needed. Such correction must be governed by charity, appropriate circumstances, and respect—not contempt or a desire to humiliate. (Summa Theologiae, II–II, q. 33, a. 4.) Neues Advent

Applied to family life, this means that correction is not automatically an attempt to seize control. It can be an act of fidelity to a shared good. Nor does it transfer responsibility for a man’s conduct to his wife: he remains responsible for his choices.

Participation in Authority Is Not a Rebellion Against It

The Marian image brings this principle into sharper focus. In the traditional language of the Co-redemptrix, Mary’s service is a real participation in Christ’s saving work. She does not stand outside His mission as a passive spectator.

Pius XII explicitly connects her association with Christ in the work of redemption to her participation in His royal dignity: the New Eve is associated with the New Adam, and her queenship expresses that association. Her service and her greatness are not opposites. (Ad Caeli Reginam, §§35–39.) Vatikans Webseite

By analogy, a wife’s union with her husband is not merely an obligation to receive instructions. It is a participation in their common vocation and in the responsibility of directing their family towards its proper good.

She can share in the exercise of family authority without competing for headship. Leo XIII describes her place beside her husband with precisely this distinction: “not, indeed, as a servant, but as a companion.” Her obedience does not abolish her dignity or reduce their union to a relationship between an employer and an instrument. (Arcanum, §11.) Vatikans Webseite

Pius XI’s image of the husband as the head and the wife as the heart likewise presents marriage as a living unity. The heart is not external to the body’s life. Indeed, the same encyclical safeguards her freedom and dignity and expressly entrusts her with directing the family when her husband neglects his duty. (Casti Connubii, §§26–29.) Vatikans Webseite

The wife’s intelligence, conscience, counsel, and initiative therefore belong within the family’s responsible direction, not outside it. Her contribution need not begin only after a decision has already been made.

This participation includes helping her husband discern what ought to be done, what ought to be commanded, and what must never be commanded at all. When she calls him away from injustice, she need not be setting herself against his authority. She may be helping to restore that authority to the purpose that makes it rightful. This applies St. Thomas’s principle that charitable correction does not require jurisdiction over the person corrected. Neues Advent

Her service is therefore not merely to carry out a decision, but also to help ensure that the decision is worthy of being carried out.

A wife who protects her children from their father’s misuse of authority is not thereby rejecting fatherhood. She is defending the good that fatherhood exists to serve.

As Mary’s participation manifests the fruitfulness of her union with Christ, so, by analogy, a wife’s active cooperation should manifest the fruitfulness of her union with her husband. She does not honour that union by surrendering her conscience, but by bringing her whole person—her fidelity, wisdom, courage, and love—into its service.

The Double Standard: Correcting the Pope, Silencing the Wife

Here a certain style of online defence of tradition needs to examine its own consistency.

The “internet knight” who readily admonishes ecclesiastical authorities, yet treats a wife’s correction of her husband’s wrongdoing as inherently rebellious, faces a serious contradiction. If charitable correction can serve authority in the Church, it cannot become intrinsically hostile to authority merely because the person offering it at home is a woman.

A neo-traditionalist cannot consistently argue that reverence for the papal office permits respectful reminders of its duties, while reverence for a husband requires silence about his misuse of responsibility.

One cannot praise Catherine for reminding a pope of his obligations and then condemn a wife merely for reminding her husband of his.

Papal authority and marital responsibility are not identical. The comparison concerns one principle, not an equivalence of offices: respecting authority does not require pretending that its exercise can never need correction.

The opposite error is the argument, sometimes associated with Catholic “neoconservatism,” that the mere possession of an office should settle the matter. Applied consistently to Avignon, that reasoning would have told Catherine to remain silent: Gregory was the pope, and therefore his decision to remain there should admit no admonition.

Yet Catherine’s example joins profound reverence for the papacy with an insistent appeal that its holder fulfil his responsibilities. Her efforts to bring Gregory XI back to Rome did not arise from indifference to the Church, but from devotion to it. Vatikans Webseite

Likewise, he is the husband or he is the father is not a sufficient answer to a well-founded objection to wrongdoing. An office identifies a responsibility; it does not turn every act of its holder into a rightful act.

Neither every criticism nor every refusal is justified. But neither is every admonition insubordination. The question is whether it serves truth, charity, and the proper good of those concerned.

Feminism Is Not Answered by Making Women Small

Not everything contained in feminism is false, nor is every grievance to which it gives voice illegitimate.

Where women have been reduced to silence, treated as instruments, or denied responsibilities that properly belong to them, resistance can be a natural response to a disorder already present on the other side. A reaction may itself become disordered without the injustice that provoked it ceasing to be real.

Recognizing this does not require approving feminist ideology. It requires acknowledging wrongs against women that the Church herself has condemned. John Paul II expressly acknowledged women’s historical marginalization, the denial of their dignity, and their reduction to servitude. He treated these as failures requiring correction, not as features of Christian order to be defended. (Letter to Women, §§3–6.) Vatikans Webseite

A Catholic defence of order must reject both the rebellion against rightful authority and the corruption of authority into domination.

It is not enough to condemn a woman’s rejection of her duties while ignoring a man’s misuse of his own. Nor can we restore order by defending the very imbalance against which a legitimate grievance arose. One disorder does not become good merely because it has provoked another.

Here the teaching of St. Augustine provides the essential distinction: evil is not an independent substance, but a corruption or deprivation of good—privatio boni. The task is therefore not merely to identify what has become disordered, but to recognize the good that the disorder damages or distorts. (Enchiridion, §§11–14.) Neues Advent

Applied to this question, the distinction is clear: the desire to be treated with dignity, to exercise responsibility, to protect one’s children, and to have a meaningful voice within marriage is not itself a rebellion against God’s order.

These goods must not be discarded merely because they have also been claimed in support of mistaken conclusions. What is good must be recovered; what is false must be rejected; what has become disordered must be restored to its proper place.

Where modern feminist thought treats sexual difference as something to erase, or understands relations between men and women primarily as an antagonistic struggle for power, it conflicts with Catholic anthropology. Recognizing that conflict, however, does not require denying women’s dignity, initiative, or responsibility. The Church’s own account of cooperation between the sexes rejects both antagonism and the reduction of women to passivity. (Letter on the Collaboration of Men and Women in the Church and in the World, §§2–4, 13–16.) Vatikans Webseite

One need not reduce feminism’s complex history to a single cause to recognize the problem with a one-sided understanding of authority: the man commands, the woman executes, and her voice becomes suspect whenever it calls his conduct into question.

To answer feminist errors by defending that imbalance is to leave a genuine grievance unanswered.

We do not overcome those errors by making women smaller. We answer them by restoring to women the dignity, duties, voice, and responsibility that properly belong to them—and by restoring male authority to its proper purpose: service to the good, rather than the satisfaction of the man who exercises it.

That means more than praising women in the abstract. It means acknowledging that their service can include initiative, counsel, admonition, protection of the vulnerable, and correction of an abuse of authority.

Where male authority degenerates into domination, irresponsibility, or convenience, there truly is disorder. John Paul II’s reading of Genesis expressly identifies domination as a distortion of the relationship between man and woman, not its fulfilment. (Mulieris Dignitatem, §10.) Vatikans Webseite

The remedy is neither to abolish responsibility nor to make its misuse untouchable. It is to restore responsibility to its proper purpose.

Recovering a genuine good does not mean approving the errors attached to it. Augustine’s principle is not a blanket justification for any movement. It invites discernment: preserve what is true, reject what is false, and restore the good to its proper order.

Read alongside the fiat, Matt’s appeal can be understood in precisely this restorative sense: women are not being asked to liberate men from their responsibilities, but to help bring them back to those responsibilities.

The Greatness of Womanhood

That is why Matt’s expression may be disputed while the underlying thought remains recognizably Catholic.

Mary does not replace Christ or assume the apostolic office. Yet her consent is active, her fidelity steadfast, and her presence at the Cross inseparable from her maternal participation in her Son’s mission. Douay-Rheims Bibel Online

The Christian woman, therefore, need not become a copy of the man, nor must she be reduced to a passive spectator. She can admonish, educate, resist wrongdoing, lead, encourage—and, when necessary, remind men of the responsibilities they have neglected.

Her service is not always to tell a man that he is right. Sometimes it is to help him become right.

Not by overthrowing the divine order, but by helping to restore it.

text:
Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito Recuses Himself From a Major Climate Case | Stephen Green, PJ Media

Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito has recused himself from Suncor Energy (U.S.A.) Inc. v. County Commissioners of Boulder County, a major climate change case scheduled for oral arguments, about a week before the court is scheduled to take up the case.

Supreme Court Clerk Scott Harris announced Alito’s decision on September 28 in a brief letter to the parties, stating that the justice “has determined that he will not continue to participate.” Alito was supposed to hear the case on October 5, the first day of the court’s 2026–27 term.

The letter offered no explanation for the last-minute recusal, which follows months of pressure from environmental activists over Alito’s financial investments in the energy sector, despite him not owning any shares in the case’s parties.

Alito had previously resisted calls to step aside.

The case centers on whether state tort law allows Colorado local governments to hold oil and gas companies financially liable for their alleged contributions to climate change. Boulder County and other local governments are seeking damages from Suncor Energy and ExxonMobil, arguing that the companies contributed to climate-related harm. The Supreme Court’s ruling could affect similar lawsuits filed against energy companies nationwide.

Despite not owning stock in either Suncor Energy or ExxonMobil, Alito does hold investments in other energy companies, including ConocoPhillips and Phillips 66. Environmental activists have argued that a ruling limiting climate liability could also financially benefit those companies.

In May, a coalition of environmental and judicial watchdog organizations urged the Senate Judiciary Committee to investigate Alito’s participation in the case. They cited his “substantial holdings in individual oil and gas companies” and warned that his involvement could undermine public confidence in the court’s impartiality.

The green activists also questioned why Alito had previously recused himself from a related petition involving the same companies, but initially declined to step aside from the current case. The groups argued that the broader financial implications of the litigation warranted his recusal.

A Supreme Court spokesperson responded that Alito had no financial interest in any party to the case and that the court’s legal counsel had advised him that recusal was not required.

Alito’s earlier recusal from related climate litigation also drew scrutiny. In 2023, he stepped aside when the Supreme Court rejected appeals in the Colorado case alongside similar petitions involving other energy companies, including ConocoPhillips and Phillips 66. The court later said that Alito had “inadvertently recused” himself, because it considered the petitions alongside cases involving companies in which he held financial interests.

In January, Alito withdrew from Chevron USA Inc. v. Plaquemines Parish, Louisiana, a dispute over whether federal contractors can transfer certain cases from state to federal court. In that case, Harris explicitly cited Alito’s financial interest in ConocoPhillips, the parent company of Burlington Resources Oil and Gas Company.

The Supreme Court’s code of conduct, adopted in November 2023, directs justices to recuse themselves when their impartiality might reasonably be questioned. The code includes cases involving a justice’s financial interest in a party or the subject matter of a proceeding. Justices do not have to publicly explain their decisions to recuse themselves.

Alito’s withdrawal leaves only eight justices to hear the climate case. A potential 4–4 split would leave the lower court’s ruling in place without establishing a nationwide Supreme Court precedent on the legal questions surrounding state climate litigation and federal preemption.

The Supreme Court has not announced any changes to the October 5 oral argument schedule.

text:
Sarah Paine sees two rival definitions of security.

Historian Sarah Paine distinguishes between continental and maritime security paradigms. Continental powers tend to see neighboring states as threats. Security then means military strength, territorial depth and, often, expansion across surrounding land.

Maritime powers begin from a different premise. Their strength comes from protected trade, alliances, legal rules and networks that allow wealth to accumulate over time. The goal is not simply to control more territory, but to make exchange more secure and predictable.

Paine connects these paradigms to competing economic outcomes. War destroys wealth, while trade, insurance, credit, banking and mutually accepted legal rules can help countries specialize and accumulate it. Her practical test is whether other participants benefit enough to sustain the strategy.

Geography shapes pressures but does not dictate destiny. Land borders and coastlines create different vulnerabilities and opportunities, while institutions and political choices determine how states respond. Oceans remain important channels for trade, communications and military deployment.

Russia and Switzerland illustrate her contrast: both are continental European states, yet one pursued repeated territorial expansion while the other largely protected itself, followed international rules and prospered without pursuing territorial expansion. Britain offers Paine’s clearest maritime example: it used its island geography and the Royal Navy to protect trade and prevent invasion.

The framework changes how power should be assessed. Territory and military reach matter, but so do productive capacity and durable relationships. A strategy that consumes both may look powerful while weakening the foundations of power.

Does Paine’s test of shared benefits explain why maritime networks can outlast territorial expansion?

Diplomacy is still noisy, but physical Gulf barrels are flowing again, so oil is yo-yoing in the low $100s rather than melting up. Equities and crypto are in a holding pattern into PCE: cooler inflation extends the relief in yields and risk assets, while a sticky print revives the hike scare. Raffaele Sansoni Galeoti Riario (3 May 1461 – 9 July 1521) was an Italian cardinal of the Renaissance, mainly known as the constructor of the Palazzo della Cancelleria and the person who invited Michelangelo to Rome. He was a patron of the arts. He was also the first adolescent to be elevated in the College of Cardinals in the history of the Holy See.[1]

Engagement in the plot against Leo X and death
In June 1517, Cardinal Petrucci and others conspired against Pope Leo X (Giovanni dei Medici). Cardinal Riario refused to participate in the plot but was at least aware of Petrucci's intentions to murder the Pope and did nothing to prevent it. Leo was notified about the plot, arrested the conspirators and ordered their execution. Riario, whose entanglement in the Pazzi conspiracy had not been forgotten by the Medici Pope, secured his head only by surrendering his palace beside San Lorenzo in Damaso to the Pope. Leo transferred it to his cousin Giulio de' Medici, Vice-Chancellor of the Holy See, who rendered it the seat of the Apostolic Chancery. Thus the Palazzo Riario was henceforward known as Palazzo della Cancelleria.

Riario died in Naples, at the age of sixty. His tomb is located in the Basilica dei Santi Apostoli in Rome.

Revelation 17:1 The state of the Church militant being declared, now followeth the state of the Church overcoming and getting victory, as I showed before in the beginning of chapter 10. The state is set forth in 4 chapters. As in the place beforegoing I noted, that in that history the order of time was not always exactly observed, so the same is to be understood in this history, that it is distinguished according to the persons of which it treateth, and that in the several stories of the persons is severly observed in the time thereof. For first is delivered the story of Babylon destroyed, in this and the next chap. (for this Babylon out of all doubt shall perish before the 2 beasts and the Dragon). Secondly is delivered the destruction of both the two beasts, chap. 19. And lastly of the Dragon, chap. 20, in the story of the spiritual Babylon are distinctly set forth the state thereof in this chap. and the overthrow done from God, chap. 18. In this verse and that which followeth is a transition or passage unto the first argument, consisting of a particular calling of the Prophet (as often heretofore) and a general proposition.

Revelation 17:1 The sentence that is pronounced against this harlot.
Revelation 17:3 Henceforth is propounded the type of Babylon, and the state thereof in 4 verses. After a declaration of the type, in the rest of this chap., in the type are described two things, the beast (of whom chap. 13), in verse 3, and the woman that sitteth upon the beast, verses 4, 5, 6. The beast in process of time hath gotten somewhat more than was expressed in the former vision. First in that it is not read before that he was appareled in scarlet, a robe imperial and of triumph. Secondly, in that this is full of names of blasphemy: the other carried the name of blasphemy only in his head. So God did teach that this beast is much increased in impiety and injustice and doth in this last age, triumph in both these more insolently and proudly than ever before.
Revelation 17:3 A scarlet color, that is, with a red and purple garment: and surely it was not without cause that the Romish clergy were so much delighted with this color.
Revelation 17:4 That harlot, the spiritual Babylon, which is Rome. She is described by her attire, profession and deeds.
Revelation 17:4 In attire most glorious, triumphant, most rich, and most gorgeous.
Revelation 17:4 In profession, the nourisher of all, in this verse, and teaching her mysteries unto all, verse 5, setting forth all things most magnificently: but indeed most pernicious besotting miserable men with her cup, and bringing upon them a deadly giddiness.
Revelation 17:5 Deceiving with the title of religion, and public inscription of mystery: which the beast in times past did not bear.
Revelation 17:5 An exposition: in which S. John declareth what manner of woman this is.
Revelation 17:6 In manner of deeds: She is red with blood, and sheddeth it most licentiously, and therefore is colored with the blood of the Saints, as on the contrary part. Christ is set forth imbrued with the blood of his enemies; Isa. 3:1.
Revelation 17:6 A passage unto the second part of this chapter, by occasion given of S. John, as the words of the Angel do show, in the next verse.
Revelation 17:7 The second part or place, as I said, verse 1. The narration of the vision, promised in this verse, and delivered in the verse following. Now there is delivered first a narration of the beast and his story, unto verse 14. After, of the harlot, unto the end of the chap.
Revelation 17:8 The story of the beast hath a triple description of him. The first is a distinction of this beast from all that ever hath been at any time: which distinction is contained in this verse: The second is a delineation or painting out of the beast by things present, by which he might even at that time be known of the godly, and this delineation is according to his heads, verses 2, 10, 11. The third is an historical foretelling of things to come, and to be done by him: and these are ascribed unto his horns, verses 12, 13, 14. This beast is that Empire of Rome, of which I spake, chap. 13:11, according to the mutations and changes whereof which then had already happened, the holy Ghost hath distinguished and set out the same. The Apostle distinguisheth this beast from all others in these words. The beast which thou sawest, was and is not. For so I expound the words of the Apostle for evidence’s sake as I will further declare in the notes following.
Revelation 17:8 The meaning is, that beast which thou sawest before (Rev. 13:1) and which yet thou hast now seen, was, (I say was) even from Julius Caesar in respect of beginning, rising up, station, glory, dominion, manner and stock, from the house of Julius: and yet is not now the same, if thou look unto the house and stock for the dominion of this family was translated unto another, after the death of Nero from the other unto a third, from a third unto a fourth, and so forth was varied and altered by innumerable changes. Finally, the Empire is one, as it were one beast: but exceedingly varied by kindreds, families, and persons. It was therefore (saith S. John) in the kindred or house of Julius: and now it is not in that kindred, but translated unto another.
Revelation 17:8 As if he should say, Also the same that is, shall shortly not be: but shall ascend out of the depth, or out of the sea (as was said, Rev. 13:1) that is, shall be a new stock from amongst the nations without difference, and shall in the same state go unto destruction or ruin, and perish: and so shall successively new Princes or Emperors come and go, arise and fall, the body of the beast remaining still, but tossed with so many and often alterations, as no man can but marvel that this beast was able to stand and hold out, in so many mutations. Verily no Empire that ever was tossed with so many changes, and as it were with so many tempests of the sea, ever continued so long.
Revelation 17:8 That is as many as have not learned the providence of God, according to the faith of the Saints, shall marvel at these grievous and often changes when they shall consider, the selfsame beast, which is the Roman Empire, to have been, not to be, and to be and still molested with perpetual mutation, and yet in the same to stand and continue. This in mine opinion is the most simple exposition of this place, and confirmed by the event of the things themselves. Although by the last change also, by which the Empire, that before was civil became Ecclesiastical, is not obscurely signified by these words: of which two, the first exercised cruelty upon the bodies of the saints: the other also upon their souls: the first by human order and policy, the other under the color of the law of God, and of Religion, raged and imbrued itself with the blood of the godly.
Revelation 17:9 An exhortation preparing unto audience, by the same argument, with that of Christ: He that hath ears to hear, let him hear. Wherefore, for mine own part, I had rather read in this place, Let there be here a mind, etc. So the Angel passeth fully unto the second place of this description.
Revelation 17:9 Very children know what that seven hilled city is, which is so much spoken of, and whereof Virgil thus reporteth, And compasseth seven towers in one wall: that city it is, which when John wrote these things had rule over the kings of the earth: It was and is not, and yet it remaineth this day, but it is declining to destruction.
Revelation 17:9 This is the painting out of the beast by things present (as I said before) whereby S. John endeavored to describe the same, that he might both be known of the godly in that age, and be further observed and marked of posterity afterwards. This delineation hath one type, that is, his heads, but a double description or application of the type: one permanent from the nature of itself, the other changeable, by the working of men. The description permanent, is by the seven hills, in this verse, the other that fleeteth, is from the seven kings, verses 10, 11. And here it is worthy to be observed, that one type hath sometimes two or more applications, as seemeth good unto the holy Ghost to express either one thing by divers types, or divers things by one type. So I noted before, of the seven spirits, Rev. 1:4. Now this woman that sitteth upon seven hills, is the city of Rome, called in times past of the Greeks, … i. of seven tops or crests, and of Varro, septiceps, i. of her seven heads (as here) of seven heads, and of others, septicollis, i. standing upon seven hills.
Revelation 17:9 The beginning of these Kings or Emperors is almost the same with the beginning of the Church of Christ, which I showed before, Rev. 11:1. Namely from the year 35, after the passion of Christ, what time the Temple and Church of the Jews was overthrown. In which year it came to pass by the providence of God that that saying The beast was and is not, was fulfilled before that the destruction of the Jews immediately following came to pass. That was the year from the building of the city of Rome, 109, from which year S. John both numbered the Emperors which hitherto hath been, when he wrote these things, and foretelleth two others next to come: and that with this purpose, that when this particular prediction of foretelling of things to come, should take effect the truth of all other predictions in the Church might be the more confirmed. Which sign God of old mentioned this in the Law, Deut. 18, and Jeremiah confirmeth, Jer. 28:8.
Revelation 17:10 Whose names are these: the first, Servius Sulpicius Galba, who was the seventh Emperor of the people of Rome, the second Marcus Salvius Otho, the third Aulus Vitellius, the fourth, Titus Flavius Vespasianus, the fifth, Titus Vespasianus his son of his own name.
Revelation 17:10 Flavius Domitian son of the first Vespasian. For in the latter end of his days S. John wrote these things, as witnesseth Irenaus, Lib. 5 adversus hareses.
Revelation 17:10 Nerua. The Empire being now translated from the family of Flavius. This man reigned only one year, four months, and nine days, as the history writers do tell.
Revelation 17:11 This is spoken by the figure synecdoche, as much to say as that head of the beast which was and is not, because it is cut off, and Nerua in so short time extinguished. How many heads there were, so many beasts there seemed to be in one. See the like speech in Rev. 13.3
Revelation 17:11 Nerua Traianus, who himself in divers respects is called here the seventh and the eighth.
Revelation 17:11 Though in number and order of succession he be the eighth, yet he is reckoned together with one of these heads, because Nerua and he were one head. For this man obtained authority together with Nerua, and was Consul with him, when Nerua left his life.
Revelation 17:11 Namely, to molest with persecutions the Churches of Christ, as the histories do accord, and I have briefly noted, Rev. 2:10.
Revelation 17:12 The third place of this description as I said, verse 18, is a prophetical prediction of things to come which the beast should do, as in the words following S. John doth not obscurely signify, saying, which have not yet received the kingdom, etc. For there is an Antithesis or opposition between these kings, and those that went before. And first the persons are described, in this verse, then their deeds in the two verses following.
Revelation 17:12 That is, arising with their kingdoms out of the Roman beast: at such time as that political Empire began by the craft of the Popes greatly to fall.
Revelation 17:12 Namely, with the second beast whom we called before a false prophet, which beast, ascending out of the earth got unto himself all the authority and power of the first beast, and exerciseth the same before his face, as was said, Rev. 14:11, 12. For when the political Empire of the West began to bow downwards, there both arose those ten kings, and the second beast took the opportunity offered to usurp unto himself all the power of the former beast. These kings long ago, many have numbered and described to be ten and a great part of the events plainly testifieth the same in this our age.
Revelation 17:13 That is, by consent and agreement, that they may conspire with the beast, and depend upon his beck. Their story is divided into three parts, counsels, acts, and events. The counselors some of them consist in communicating of judgments and affections: and some in communicating of power, which they are said to have given unto this beast in this verse.
Revelation 17:14 With Christ and his Church, as the reason following doth declare, and here are mentioned the facts and the events which followed for Christ’s sake, and for the grace of God the Father towards those that are called, elected, and are his faithful ones in Christ.
Revelation 17:15 This is the other member of the narration as I said verse 7, belonging unto the harlot, showed in the vision, verse 3. In this history of the harlot, these 3 things are distinctly propounded, what is her magnificence in this verse, what is her fall, and by whom it shall happen unto her, in the two verses following: and lastly, who that harlot is, in the last verse. This place which by order of nature should have been the first, is therefore made the last, because it was more fit to be joined with the next Chap.
Revelation 17:15 That is, as unconstant and variable as the waters. Upon this foundation sitteth this harlot as Queen, a vain person upon that which is vain.
Revelation 17:16 The ten Kings as verse 12. The accomplishment of this fact and event, is daily increased in this our age by the singular providence and most mighty government of God. Wherefore the facts are propounded in this verse, and the cause of them in the verses following.
Revelation 17:17 A reason rendered from the chief efficient cause, which is the providence of God, by which alone S. John by inversion of order affirmeth to have come to pass, both that the Kings should execute upon the harlot, that which pleased God, and which he declared in the verse next beforegoing: and also that by one consent and counsel, they should give their kingdom unto the beast, etc., verses 13, 14. For as these being blinded have before depended upon the beck of the beast that lifteth up the harlot, so it is said that afterward it shall come to pass, that they shall turn back, and shall fall away from her when their hearts shall be turned into better state by the grace and mercy of God.
Revelation 17:18 That is, Rome that great City, or only City (as Justinian calleth it) the King and head whereof was then the Emperor, but now the Pope, since that the condition of the beast was changed.

text:
People look at old photographs of Dubai, see very few buildings, and conclude that there was nothing here. Apparently, history only counts when it leaves something tall enough to photograph.

Dubai makes much more sense when you understand that it is a city of merchants. Its openness has been built over generations, through the practical business of dealing with people from elsewhere.

Around the turn of the twentieth century, taxes and government intervention were pushing traders away from the Persian port of Lingah. Dubai’s rulers welcomed them, lowered trade barriers and offered land and protection. Sheikh Maktoum bin Hasher invited newcomers into his majlis to understand what their businesses needed. More than a century ago, attracting talent already involved sitting down and listening.

Those merchants brought their families, their contacts, their languages and their customs. Bastakiya, now known as Al Fahidi, takes its name from Bastak in Iran. Its famous wind towers owe much to the architectural traditions those families brought with them. What arrived from abroad became part of Dubai’s heritage.

The same happened with language. Gulf sailors and shopkeepers used Hindi, Urdu, Farsi and Swahili through their trading relationships. Words entered everyday Emirati speech. Generations of exchange became embedded in how people spoke.

A merchant has a very practical incentive to understand you. Your language helps him negotiate. Your customs help him avoid offending you. Your country might contain his next customer. Curiosity pays, and being permanently offended by foreigners is a fairly expensive business strategy.

Over generations, that changes a city. You can remain attached to your own culture while becoming comfortable with someone else’s. In 1958, Sheikh Rashid granted land and permission for Dubai’s Shri Krishna Temple, years before the discovery of oil.

My favourite illustration of this mentality is less glamorous: dredging the Creek. By the 1950s, accumulated silt was preventing larger vessels from entering. Sheikh Rashid assembled financing through merchants, loans and customs revenues, and work began in 1959. Dubai borrowed money to make it easier for the world to arrive.

Oil was discovered in 1966; production began in 1969. The commercial instinct was already there. Money would give it extraordinary scale.

That is what I appreciate about the place I now call home. Underneath the spectacular buildings, I recognise something familiar: the merchant’s understanding that someone else’s success can create an opportunity for you.

Dubai’s overnight success has taken generations. You can build a tower relatively quickly. Becoming a place where people are willing to bring their families, their savings and their ambitions takes much longer.

text:
Roberto Duran wins a 10-round unanimous decision over Tony Biglen at Memorial Auditorium in Buffalo, New York on September 30, 1992.

Duran knocked Biglen down twice but there were boos in the later rounds when it became apparent that he wouldn't win by a knockout.

Duran came into this off of a TKO loss to Pat Lawlor that followed his decision loss to Sugar Ray Leonard.

15-6-1 with 10 KO wins, this would be the final fight of Tony Biglen's five-year (1987-92) career.

From The Colorado Springs Gazzette in 2019:

The night Palmer High grad went toe to toe with Roberto ‘El Diablo’ Duran

As a teen in Colorado Springs, Tony Biglen sat beside his father, Owen, on the family couch on White Mountain Drive and watched his boxing hero, the wicked and magnificent Roberto Duran.
Duran rose to sinister heights, even by boxing standards. He reveled in his nickname, “El Diablo.” Yes, the devil. After watching “El Diablo” pulverize an opponent, heavyweight great Joe Frazier was asked if this outlaw puncher reminded him of anyone.
“Yeah,” Frazier said. “Charles Manson.” Manson, of course, orchestrated a series of 1969 murders that terrorized Los Angeles.
On a cold night in Buffalo on Sept. 30, 1992, 27 years ago Monday, Tony found himself watching Duran. Owen, as usual, was by his side.
But this viewing carried a petrifying twist. Tony was preparing to step in the ring to face Duran in a middleweight match with Owen as his manager, trainer and motivator. Tony, a 1977 Palmer High grad, was 31 years old and working full time as an electrician in Denver. He had been paid $20,000 to travel to western New York to get knocked out by Duran. That was the promoter’s plan.
Tony and Owen devised a different scheme. Tony would not run from Duran. He would remain true to his boxing philosophy and battle the man known for his “Hands of Stone.”
Hey, we’ve all seen “Rocky.” In the movies, Tony wins the fight. In reality, the tale is not so sweet, only close. Tony veered perilously close to getting knocked out in the fourth round, but dug deep to survive and stand tall when the fight ended after 10 rounds. He was smiling, blood trickling from his mouth, as the final bell rang.
Tony and Owen sit on a sunny Saturday in the family garage at Federal Heights, midway between downtown Denver and Boulder. They never watched a full video of the fight, but details remain fresh.
Owen is likely the only father to arrange for his son to fight Duran, voluntarily placing his flesh-and-blood in the ring against a boxer who once kneed and punched an opponent in the groin at the same time.
“I was a fighter,” Tony says. “I didn’t care.”
I was sitting ringside that night in Buffalo and saw the moment when the Biglen plan flirted with humiliation and disaster.
In the fourth round, Tony was plotting a big punch and took a step toward Duran. He walked into a crushing right hand, and Duran instantly unloaded a wicked left hook, catching Tony flush in the cheek. He toppled to the mat. He had fought 24 times but never been hit with such force. His face throbbed. His mind was a haze. The end seemed near.
Somehow, Tony rose to his feet.
“There’s only a fraction of fighters in the world who could have got up after a combination like that,” Owen says.
Duran was hungry for a knockout, and for a few seconds Tony looked in supreme danger.
Remember, his father was in his corner. In boxing, a trainer can save his fighter by throwing a white towel in the ring, which translates as surrender.
Owen held the towel as he looked carefully at his son’s eyes. He wanted to protect his son, but not too much. For a few seconds, he struggled with his decision. Finally, he could see Tony regain his senses, and the towel remained in his hand.
After the round, Duran strutted to his corner, but Tony offered a surprise. “Vamos, Viejo,” Tony said. Translation: Come on, old man.
As the fight progressed, Tony gained strength and even tagged Duran with a savage right in the late rounds. Tony had finished other fighters with the same punch. Duran’s head snapped back, but he quickly flashed a smile. Tony realized he was battling a boxing superhero.
When the fight ended, Tony walked toward his corner and his father and looked up to see Duran standing in front of him. Duran sometimes ridiculed beaten opponents, even spitting on those he had vanquished. Tony braced himself for an insult.
Duran kissed him on the cheek and whispered: “You are a (expletive) tough dude.”
A few minutes later, Biglen found a pay phone. He wanted to tell his family in Denver that he had gone the distance with Duran. I was standing next to Tony and Owen when he picked up the phone.
Gone the distance? Owen had a grander plan.
“No, Tony,” Owen said. “Tell ‘em this. Tell ‘em you kicked Duran’s butt, and the officials robbed you. Tell ‘em that. It wasn’t on TV. Nobody back home saw it. They’ll never know. Tell ‘em you kicked his butt. What the hell. They’ll never know.”
After the fight and the phone call, Duran treated Tony to Corona beers in the hotel bar, and took photos of Tony with Mia, the mother of El Diablo’s six children.
“I had gotten respect from a lion in the game,” Tony says in the garage as his father nods with pride. Their boxing journey traveled from couch to ring. Tony survived a toe-to-toe clash with his highly dangerous hero. It had been a bloody, beautiful night.
Tony returned to Denver and his life as an electrician. He never fought again.
(In the accompanying picture, Tony and Owen Biglen hold the fight card from Sept. 30, 1992, the night Tony fought boxing great Roberto Duran in Buffalo. Tony is a 1977 graduate of Palmer High School.)

text:
$CVNA: The US used car market is enormous (approximately 20 million vehicles sold annually), but online penetration remains low. Traditional dealership models are inefficient and offer a poor customer experience. High interest rates and rising new car prices and ages have ironically strengthened the demand for online alternatives that offer greater accessibility, affordability, and speed. Carvana competes with CarMax and traditional dealership groups (Lithia, etc.), with its core difference being its vertically integrated end-to-end e-commerce model: website car selection, financing, logistics, remanufacturing, and home delivery. The bottleneck has shifted from demand to inventory and remanufacturing capacity.

Product and Qualification Highlights: End-to-end online experience: Nationwide inventory display, 7-day returns, home delivery, and same-day delivery available in some cities (e.g., Twin Cities).

Remanufacturing and Auction Synergy: Continuously integrating Carvana-level refurbishment capabilities into ADESA auction platforms (Brasher’s, Charlotte, etc.), while expanding megasites to improve turnover and supply.

Financial Closed Loop: Retail auto loans, VSC/GAP/insurance and other ancillary products contribute high-margin "Other Income"; partnerships with companies like Ally expand receivables purchase limits.

Scale Metrics: Website inventory approximately 78,000 vehicles (end of Q2), average monthly unique visitors approximately 21.8 million; brand and logistics network form a competitive moat.

Q2 2026 (ending June 30) set multiple records: retail sales of 197,325 vehicles (+38% YoY), revenue of $7.376 billion (+52%), gross profit of $1.384 billion (+30%), GAAP operating profit of $680 million, net profit of $513 million (margin 7.0%), adjusted EBITDA of $769 million (margin 10.4%). GPU slightly decreased to approximately $7,014, mainly due to structure and base effect. Full-year adjusted EBITDA guidance is $2.7-3 billion (higher than $2.24 billion in 2025), with Q3 sales expected to rise again sequentially.

Jefferies data shows August sales growth of approximately 41%, and the first three weeks of September around 40%, with Q3 potentially recording the largest outperformance since early 2025. Three new remanufacturing megasites opened in Q3, and inventory growth remained at approximately 30%. Q3 earnings are expected in late October.

Core Investments: Demand is not a bottleneck; capacity expansion translates to growth: Sales have grown by 35%+ for several consecutive quarters, and management aims for annual sales of 3 million vehicles in the medium to long term.

Operating Leverage Realized: SG&A/vehicle has decreased after sales increased, GAAP has been consistently profitable, and net debt/EBITDA is approximately 1x, resulting in a significantly improved balance sheet.

Industry Market Share Shift: The integration of online, manufacturing, and financing is more difficult to replicate than pure brick-and-mortar stores or pure platforms.

Short term (1–3 months) $78–88 USD

text:
The FlyDubai flight incident is now being assessed as a terror attack. And perhaps also, as a Sukkot miracle.

While we don’t have a complete or confirmed understanding of the situation yet, here is the emerging picture:

The incident began Wednesday morning, when the Flydubai flight with 174 passengers was traveling from Dubai to Tel Aviv. While approaching Israel, the Boeing 737 suddenly transmitted 7700, the international general emergency code, followed by 7500 — the code for a hijacking or unlawful interference. 

The aircraft then went into a terrifyingly steep descent, losing roughly 13,000–16,000 feet (about 4–5 kilometers) before eventually stabilizing. It diverted toward Saudi Arabia as Israeli Air Force fighter jets were scrambled. Prime Minister Netanyahu and Defense Minister Katz held urgent security consultations, while the IDF chief of staff reportedly consulted with the heads of the Shin Bet and Mossad. 

At first, Israeli officials believed the emergency might have resulted from a fight between the two pilots. But according to the latest information reported by Amit Segal, following situation assessments and testimony from passengers, Israel is now treating the incident as a full-fledged terrorist attack.

According to those reports, the co-pilot repeatedly stabbed the captain inside the cockpit. Crew members and Israeli passengers then managed to break into the cockpit and overpower the attacker. Israeli passengers described finding the cockpit covered in blood and said that they helped take control of the situation.

A senior Israeli official says the co-pilot is now being questioned, and that indications are mounting that his intention was to seize control of the aircraft and crash it with the passengers aboard. Authorities are also reportedly investigating whether the alleged attacker is from one of the Gulf states (some rumors say Oman).

The aircraft ultimately made a safe emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. All passengers are safe. 

Israel is now working to bring the passengers home. El Al offered to send a rescue flight to Saudi Arabia — which would be a first for the Israeli airline — while Israel is currently preparing to send an Israeli Air Force aircraft instead.

After a tense morning with all Israelis glued to the screen in prayers, we thank G-d for the good news. All passengers are safe, and a potentially disastrous terror attack was prevented. 

Pictured:

A photo from the plane, now grounded in Saudi Arabia, shows a passenger with a shirt covered in blood. The story is not yet clear, but it seems that the passenger had assisted in taking control of the situation in the cockpit.

text:
Lipsync Video Three: Helen Ferguson’s April 7, 1914 Affidavit and the Leo Frank Defense

Helen Ferguson’s April 7, 1914 affidavit raises a serious question about what was happening behind the scenes after Leo Frank’s August 1913 conviction.

Ferguson had testified for the State. She later swore two efforts were made to get her either to leave Atlanta or change her testimony. The first involved an offer of $100, plus her board and expenses, if she would leave Atlanta while Frank sought a new trial. The second was far more involved. Ferguson said a young man approached her under a false name, courted her, talked about marriage, introduced a detective as his father, and then helped pressure her to change her testimony about Mary Phagan’s pay envelope.

This was not Ferguson talking years later. She signed the affidavit under oath on April 7, 1914, less than eight months after Frank’s trial.

What Ferguson Had Said at Trial

Helen Ferguson had been a young factory worker and a friend of Mary Phagan. At Frank’s trial she testified about Mary’s pay envelope. Ferguson said she had tried to collect Mary’s pay from Leo Frank, but Frank refused to give it to her.

Her testimony helped explain why Mary personally returned to the National Pencil Company factory on Saturday, April 26, 1913.

After the trial, Ferguson said people tried to change her story.

First Attempt: $100 to Leave Atlanta

Ferguson said the first effort involved money.

Not long after the trial, she was walking to work when a young man approached her on a street corner. Ferguson described him as Jewish, about thirty years old, with a light mustache and light curly hair.

According to Ferguson, he offered her $100, plus her board and all expenses, if she would leave Atlanta. He told her Frank was expected to receive a new trial soon.

Ferguson refused and walked away.

She did not name this first man in her affidavit.

The point is simple. Ferguson swore someone offered her money and living expenses to leave Atlanta while Frank’s lawyers were trying to overturn his conviction.

Ferguson Says Her Foreman Had Already Pressured Her

Ferguson also described problems at the Marcus-Loeb Overall Company, where she had worked under a foreman named Mr. Levin.

She said Levin had tried, prior to Frank’s trial, to get her to testify for Frank instead of against him. Ferguson said she became afraid of Levin and later left the job.

By December 1913, she was working at the Clarke Woodenware Company on Foundry Street.

According to Ferguson, a second effort to reach her began there.

A Young Man Calling Himself “J. W. Howard”

Ferguson said she was leaving work one afternoon with another girl when a young man walked up and greeted her by name.

She told him she did not remember him.

The man introduced himself as “J. W. Howard.” He claimed he had worked at Block’s while Ferguson worked there and said he had wanted to meet her.

Ferguson accepted his story.

A night or two later, he took her to a show. He continued seeing her and, according to Ferguson, began talking about love almost immediately. She said she had known him only about two days when he started making romantic advances.

Ferguson later learned his real name was Jimmy Wrenn.

Wrenn Introduces His Supposed Father

A few days later, Ferguson and “Howard” were walking downtown when they met a large, heavy man with a round face.

Wrenn introduced the man as his father.

Ferguson later said the supposed father was C. W. Burke, a detective working with people connected to Frank’s defense.

According to Ferguson, Burke began attacking the Atlanta police and city detectives, calling them crooks and saying they were no good. The conversation then moved to the Frank case.

Ferguson said Burke wanted her to make a new statement.

She refused.

As Ferguson and Wrenn left, Burke told Wrenn to bring her to the office later because he wanted to talk with her.

Love, Marriage, and an Affidavit

Ferguson said Wrenn met her outside the Clarke Woodenware Company around 9 o’clock one night after she finished extra work.

According to Ferguson, Wrenn talked about caring for her and wanting to marry her. At the same time, he kept asking her to sign an affidavit about the Frank case.

Ferguson did not want to go to an office with him. She said Wrenn kept pushing, telling her his “father” was waiting for them.

She finally went with him.

The Grant Building Meeting

Ferguson said Wrenn took her into a large gray building on Broad Street, which she believed was the Grant Building. They rode the elevator upstairs and entered an office where Wrenn’s supposed father was waiting.

Ferguson remembered seeing the name “J. H. Porter” on the office door. She later learned Porter’s office was next to Leo Frank attorney Luther Rosser’s office.

According to Ferguson, Wrenn and Burke again asked her to change her statement.

Their request was very specific.

They wanted Ferguson to say Frank had refused to give her Mary Phagan’s pay envelope at a different time from the time she had given in her testimony.

Ferguson refused. She said she had told the truth and was not going to change it.

“I’d Hate to Be the Main One to Put the Rope Around Frank’s Neck”

Ferguson said Wrenn then tried another approach.

According to her affidavit, he told her:

“I’d hate to be the main one to put the rope around Frank’s neck.”

Ferguson answered she could not help it because she had only told the truth.

She said Wrenn continued talking about loving her and wanting her to change her statement for him. Ferguson said she became worried and wanted to leave the room.

If her sworn account is accurate, this was not a simple interview with a witness. Ferguson was describing a young man using a false name, romance, talk of marriage, and emotional pressure while asking her to change sworn testimony in a murder case.

Ferguson Mentions Jim Conley

During the meeting, Ferguson mentioned being afraid of Jim Conley.

According to Ferguson, Wrenn and Burke then stopped pushing her to change her testimony about Frank and prepared another affidavit, this one about Conley.

Ferguson said she signed it to satisfy them.

The Conley affidavit described an earlier event in which Conley approached her while she was picking up boxes on the Saturday prior to Mary’s murder. Ferguson said Conley offered to help her, but she dropped the boxes and ran because she was afraid of him.

Ferguson did not deny signing this affidavit. Her April 1914 statement explains why she signed it. She said she refused to change her testimony about Frank but agreed to sign a statement about Conley so the men would stop pressing her.

Wrenn Tries to Kiss Her

After the affidavit was finished, Wrenn drove Ferguson home in an automobile. She said he continued talking about loving her.

Near her home, Ferguson said Wrenn tried to kiss her.

She hit him in the mouth.

According to Ferguson, his romantic behavior cooled quickly after this. He took her to her door, said good-bye, and she saw him only once more.

“J. W. Howard” Was Jimmy Wrenn

A few days later, Ferguson said people who had seen her with the young man told her his real name was Jimmy Wrenn, not J. W. Howard.

She also learned Wrenn had worked at the National Pencil Company and was connected with lawyers and detectives working for Frank.

This part of Ferguson’s story goes far beyond a defense investigator openly asking a witness questions. According to her, Wrenn approached her under a false name, claimed to know her from an earlier job, took her to shows, talked about love and marriage, and then tried to get her to change her testimony.

The “Father” Was Detective C. W. Burke

Ferguson said she discovered the supposed father’s identity several weeks later.

After the Conley affidavit was released to newspapers, a reporter visited her home and described C. W. Burke. Ferguson said the description matched Wrenn’s supposed father.

Other people later gave her similar descriptions. Ferguson said she became sure Burke was the man she had met and believed she could identify him again.

She also learned the J. H. Porter office where Wrenn had taken her was in the Grant Building next to Luther Rosser’s office.

What Ferguson Was Accusing Them of Doing

Ferguson’s April 7 affidavit makes a very direct charge.

She said someone first offered her $100, plus board and expenses, if she would leave Atlanta while Frank sought another trial. After she refused, Jimmy Wrenn approached her under the false name J. W. Howard, courted her, talked about marriage, and introduced detective C. W. Burke as his father.

Ferguson said Wrenn and Burke then took her to an office and tried to get her to change the timing of her testimony about Mary Phagan’s pay envelope. She refused. When she mentioned being afraid of Conley, they prepared a different affidavit about Conley, which she signed.

Her accusation was not simply, “The defense questioned me.”

She was saying people connected with Frank’s side tried to move her out of Atlanta, tried to change a key part of her testimony, hid their identities from her, and used a young man’s supposed romantic interest to gain her trust.

Those are very specific charges.

She named Jimmy Wrenn. She named C. W. Burke. She gave the false name “J. W. Howard.” She described Burke posing as Wrenn’s father. She named the Grant Building. She remembered “J. H. Porter” on the office door. She said Porter’s office was next to Luther Rosser’s. Most of all, she said exactly what they wanted changed: the time connected with Frank refusing to give her Mary Phagan’s pay envelope.

Why the Pay-Envelope Time Was So Serious

This was not some small side point.

Ferguson’s trial testimony dealt directly with Mary’s pay. She said she had tried to collect Mary’s envelope from Frank and he refused to give it to her. Mary later went to the factory herself on Saturday, April 26, to collect her wages.

Changing when this happened could weaken Ferguson’s trial testimony and change how the defense presented the reason Mary had to return to the factory.

According to Ferguson, this was the part of her story Wrenn and Burke wanted changed.

She refused.

A Witness Who Would Not Change Her Story

Ferguson admitted signing the affidavit about Jim Conley. She did not try to hide it. Instead, she gave an explanation for how it happened and why she signed it.

What she refused to do, according to her April 7 affidavit, was change her testimony about Leo Frank.

She said no to the $100 offer.

She said no when Burke asked for a new statement that falsified the evidence.

She said no when Wrenn talked about Frank being innocent.

She said no when Wrenn said he hated to see her help put the rope around Frank’s neck.

She said no even while Wrenn was talking about loving her and marrying her.

On April 7, 1914, Helen Ferguson put the whole story under oath and signed her name to it.

AFFIDAVIT:

Lipsync Video Three: Helen Ferguson Affidavit April 7th, 1914 and the Leo Frank Defense Machinations

Her affidavit for the state follows:

ATLANTA, GEORGIA, FULTON COUNTY — Personally appeared before the undersigned Miss Helen Ferguson, who, on oath, after being duly sworn, deposes as follows:

Since the [Leo] Frank trial last summer [1913], in which I gave testimony that was against Leo M. Frank, two attempts have been made either to get me to leave the city or change my testimony—the first by money, and the second by having a ‘young man make love to me and offering to marry me.

Shortly after the trial I left home one morning to go to my work, and on a street corner a young man, who was a Jew, came up to me and said he would give me $100 and pay my board and all expenses if I would leave Atlanta, as Frank was going to get a new trial some time soon, he said. I refused, and turned and walked away. That's about all he had time to say to me.

He had a light mustache and light, curly hair, and looked like a man about 30 years old.

The second attempt, after the money offer failed, occurred in December, during the two weeks just before Christmas. I was working then at the Clarke Woodenware Company, on Foundry street, having left the Marcus-Loeb Overall Company because I was afraid of the foreman whom I worked under, Mr. Levin, who tried before the trial to get me to swear for Frank and not against him, so that I was afraid of him and left soon afterward.

When I left my work at the Clark Woodenware Company one afternoon in December, I was walking down the street with another girl when a young man, whom I afterwards found out to be Jimmy Wrenn, stepped up to us and said: “Howdy do, Miss Ferguson.” I said: “I don't remember you,” and he answered: “This is Mr. J. W. Howard; don't you remember when you worked at Block's? I worked there, too, and wanted to meet you then, but didn't have a chance.” And so that was the way I met him.

A night or two later he took me to the show and also met me several other times, and was always mighty nice to me, just like a young man is, you know. I hadn't known him more than two days before he began to make love to me. A few days after I met him we were walking up town together when we met a big, heavy fellow, with a big, round face, who was standing on the corner, and whom I have since found out was Mr. C. W. Burke, the detective. Jimmy Wrenn—or Howard, as he called himself at that time, stopped and introduced me to him as his father. We stood on the corner and talked for several minutes. The “father” got to talking about the couple who were caught spooning on the Capitol steps and from this he began to say awful things about the police, saying they were “no good,” and that the city detectives were “crooks” and other such things. He said something about wanting me to make a new statement in the Frank case, and I said: “No, sir.”

And then, as we turned to leave, he said to Mr. Howard: “Bring her up to the office tonight. I want to talk to her anyhow.”

That night Mr. Howard came out to the Clark Woodenware Company at 9 o'clock, when I got off from work, to take me to town to see a show. There were about half a dozen of us girls who did extra work until 9 o'clock a few nights for a while before Christmas.

Jimmy was making real love to me that night—said a lot about caring for me and wanting me to marry him, but he kept on wanting me to sign an affidavit about the Frank case first. I didn't want to go up to any office with him, but he insisted so strongly, and said his father was waiting for us, that he just made me go. He took me up in that big gray-colored building on Broad street. It was the Grant building, I believe. He took me up the elevator, and there in an office his “father” was waiting for us. I remember seeing the name “J. H. Porter” on the door of the office.

They asked me again to change my statement in the Frank case and say it was some other time that Mr. Frank had refused to give me Mary Phagan's pay envelope than the time I said it was. They said that Frank was an innocent man and that everybody knew it. But I said I had told nothing but the truth and wasn't going to change it, and then Jimmy said: “Well, I'd hate to be the main one to put the rope around Frank's neck,” and I said I couldn't help that since I had only told the truth.

Then he talked some more about loving me so much, saying he wished I'd do it for him, until I was worried a good deal and wishing I was out of the room. While we were talking about the Frank case in this way I happened to tell them that I was afraid of Jim Conley. They then dropped the talk about my evidence and fixed up an affidavit for me to sign about Conley, which I signed, in order to satisfy them. I simply said in this how Conley had approached me the Saturday before Mary Phagan was killed, when I was picking up some boxes and had offered to help me, and I had dropped the boxes and run because I was afraid of him.

When we got that affidavit fixed up we left. It seemed like we had been there an awful long time. Jimmy brought me home in an automobile that night and kept on talking love to me, and just before we got home he tried to kiss me, and I hit him in the mouth. That seemed to cool him down and he brought me to the door and said good-bye.

I have never seen him but once since that night. I found out a few days later that his real name was Jimmy Wrenn and not Howard. I found it out from a number of persons who had seen me with him and who knew all about his working at the National Pencil factory and working with the lawyers and detectives for Frank.

It was several weeks afterward before I found that his “father” was the detective, C. W. Burke. When they decided that the time had come for giving my affidavit to the papers a newspaper reporter came out to the house to see me about it. He told me how the affidavit had been given out through Burke and described him to me, and the description made it very plain that he was none other than the “father.” I also learned then that the office of J. H. Porter was up in the Grant building right next to Mr. Luther Rosser's. I have found out in other ways that the “father” was Mr. Burke, many other people describing him to me exactly, and I know I could recognize Jimmy's “father” again the minute I saw him.

HELEN FERGUSON,

sworn to and subscribed before me this

7th day of April, 1914.

(Signed) L. L. HILDEBRAND,

Notary Public, Fulton County, Georgia.

text:
Federal Judge Blocks Utah’s VPN Crackdown | Bruce Gil, Gizmodo

Utah tried to crack down on one of the biggest workarounds to its online age-verification laws, however, a federal judge just blocked the effort.

U.S. District Judge David Barlow granted a preliminary injunction on Sept. 24 blocking a new provision of Utah’s age-verification law aimed at people who use VPNs to hide their location.

The ruling is part of a lawsuit brought by Aylo, the parent company of Pornhub.

Barlow found that Aylo was likely to succeed in arguing that the provision violates the Constitution’s dormant Commerce Clause, which limits states from imposing excessive burdens on interstate commerce. The judge found that Utah’s law would effectively force websites to verify users beyond the state’s borders.

The ruling comes as governments around the world, including dozens of U.S. states, have increasingly passed laws in recent years requiring some form of age verification to access certain types of online content, usually pornography.

These laws typically require users to prove their age by either uploading a government ID or through a third-party age-verification service. Utah has required adult sites to use age-verification systems since 2023.

But VPNs have long offered a simple way around these restrictions. They can route a user’s internet traffic through another location, making someone in Utah appear to be connecting from another state or country.

Utah aimed to close that loophole this year. A new law known as the Online Age Verification Amendments took effect in May, updating the state’s 2023 age-verification law.

The new provision stated that a person is considered to be accessing a website from Utah if they are physically located in the state, regardless of whether they use a VPN or any other method to hide their location.

The Electronic Frontier Foundation warned at the time that holding companies liable for verifying the age of users in Utah, including those using VPNs, is technically unrealistic because websites generally cannot determine a VPN user’s actual location reliably. According to the group, that could force websites to either “ban all known VPN IPs, or to mandate age verification for every visitor globally.”

Aylo filed its lawsuit shortly before the new provision took effect. The company argued similarly that because there is no way to determine every internet user’s physical location with certainty, the law could effectively require it to age-verify all its users around the world to make sure none of them are actually in Utah.

Barlow largely agreed with that argument. In his ruling, he wrote that the law requires companies like Aylo to “geolocate its website users with perfection to avoid liability.”

Utah Attorney General Derek Brown’s office, on the other hand, argued that the statute does not require perfection, but rather reasonable efforts to determine which users are actually located in Utah.

Still, Barlow wasn’t convinced. He wrote that the court has to “analyze the statutory text the Legislature passed into law, not just the Attorney General’s proposed enforcement of it.”

The injunction only blocks the new provision targeting users who hide their location. Utah’s broader age-verification law remains in effect while the lawsuit moves forward.

Aylo and the Utah Attorney General’s Office did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
